    Onboarding guide

    12. API Hosting, Middleware, Idempotency & DTO/Contract Mapping

    What this group covers. This is the ASP.NET Core edge of the framework: the layer that turns an HTTP request into a domain call and turns a Result back into an HTTP response. Almost everything here lives in MMCA.Common.API (the presentation layer that sits above Infrastructure in the dependency flow, see primer §1), with a handful of transport-agnostic collaborators in MMCA.Common.Application (ICorrelationContext, IEntityDTOMapper<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>), MMCA.Common.Infrastructure (CorrelationContext, JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler), and MMCA.Common.Shared (the DTO vocabulary and SupportedCultures). The group has seven interlocking concerns: the composition root that registers the whole edge; the middleware pipeline every request flows through, itself expressed as ordered data rather than a hard-coded call sequence; the error translation that keeps every failure shaped like RFC 9457 Problem Details; the controller hierarchy that hands a module ready-made CRUD, export, auth, recovery, and service-discovery endpoints; the write-safety controls (idempotency keys and conditional writes) that make a retried or racing write predictable; the contract surface (DTO/request mapping, JSON conversion, model binding, correlation, tenancy, feature gating, output caching); and the well-known endpoints that make an extracted service self-describing. Read the group as the reusable ASP.NET host a downstream service (Store, ADC, Helpdesk, or an extracted microservice) drops into place so its own code is nothing but modules. Its central rubric column is [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] (consistent, versioned, standardized contracts and error shapes), with heavy supporting roles for [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability], [Rubric §11, Security], [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability], [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], and (since ADR-027) [Rubric §27, Internationalization].

    The composition root: AddAPI, the builder extensions, and the module-host pair. A host wires the edge through two static extension classes. DependencyInjection's AddAPI (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:45) registers MVC controllers with the global UnhandledResultFailureFilter (DependencyInjection.cs:50), the internal OversizeFormResourceFilter at its own filter order (:53, so a form body over the endpoint's limit answers 413 rather than model binding's 400) and ReturnHttpNotAcceptable = false (:49), wires two JSON converter factories into the serializer options, the EnumerationJsonConverterFactory (DependencyInjection.cs:60, registered here because a concrete enumeration does not inherit the base class's [JsonConverter] attribute) and StronglyTypedIdJsonConverterFactory (DependencyInjection.cs:66, registered for the same reason so a wrapped identifier serializes as the bare primitive it wraps, ADR-115), adds the XML formatters (DependencyInjection.cs:68), optionally installs the ModuleControllerFeatureProvider when a ModulesSettings instance is supplied (DependencyInjection.cs:70-74), binds IdempotencySettings with ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() when configuration is supplied (DependencyInjection.cs:76-82, ADR-070), registers the two scoped action filters IdempotencyFilter and OwnerOrAdminFilter (DependencyInjection.cs:87-88, scoped because they depend on scoped services), turns on feature management with targeting through CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor and the DisabledFeatureHandler (DependencyInjection.cs:108-110), and registers the edge error-localization boundary (AddErrorLocalization, called at DependencyInjection.cs:113 and declared at :125, with AddErrorResources<TResource> at :144 for each module's own .resx set). Three sibling methods on the same class complete the picture: AddCommonExceptionHandlers (DependencyInjection.cs:157) registers the Problem Details service and the five exception handlers in most-specific-first order (:162-166), AddServerAuthSessionCookie (DependencyInjection.cs:182) registers the Blazor Server host's SSR cookie reader (CookieTokenReader, :188) plus the singleton CookieSessionRefresher (:194, singleton so its in-flight map is shared across requests), and AddModuleHealthChecks (DependencyInjection.cs:220) turns ModuleLoader discovery results into module-{Name} health checks, tagged module so /health?tag=module filters them (Healthy for enabled modules at :224-229, Degraded for the disabled ones at :232-238). WebApplicationBuilderExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.cs:24, a partial class split across that file plus WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs and WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs) carries the identical builder-side setup every service shares: header-based API versioning through the api-version header (AddCommonApiVersioning, line 39, reader at line 48, v1.0 assumed when the header is absent at line 46, ADR-046), rate limiting (AddCommonRateLimiting, three overloads at WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:374, :392, and :414), Brotli and Gzip compression at CompressionLevel.Fastest (AddCommonResponseCompression, line 68, both providers pinned to Fastest at lines 77 and 82 because these are dynamic per-request payloads on fractional vCPUs), OpenAPI (line 101), CORS (line 132, ADR-082, with the two policy names as constants at lines 27 and 30 and the allow-any-origin policy selected only in Development by the pipeline's CORS step, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:98-100), and the two JWT bearer registrations: in-process AddCommonAuthentication (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:134) for the Identity host and AddForwardedJwtBearer (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:52) for extracted services that validate against a remote JWKS. Two smaller helpers keep a service host's Program.cs honest. ModuleHostExtensions's AddModuleHost (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/ModuleHostExtensions.cs:51) collapses the settings-bind plus loader construction every module-hosting service repeated verbatim, and answers with a ModuleHostContext (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/ModuleHostContext.cs:21) carrying the bound settings, the loader, and RegisterModules (ModuleHostContext.cs:66) as a step the host hands to its own application pipeline: discovery is deliberately not run inside AddModuleHost, because it has to sit between AddApplication() and AddApplicationDecorators() at a host-chosen position (ModuleHostContext.cs:13-19, ADR-014). JwtAuthorityExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Auth/JwtAuthorityExtensions.cs:15) reads the authority every non-issuer service validates against and throws when the AppHost never injected it (GetRequiredJwtAuthority, :36, throwing at :41-43), because a host that boots without one answers every authenticated request with a 401 that looks like a token problem instead of a wiring problem. JwtAudience (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Auth/JwtAudience.cs:17) applies the same rule to the audience those hosts hand to AddForwardedJwtBearer: RequireConfigured (:28-32) returns the value read from Jwt:Audience (ConfigKey, :20) or throws naming the key and its Jwt__Audience environment-variable form, and the intended call shape carries no ?? fallback, so a hard-coded default can never boot a service with an audience nobody configured (JwtAudience.cs:8-15, a shape ForwardedJwtAudienceTestsBase pins in each consumer). Only one DI ordering rule is load-bearing in the whole host, and it belongs to the CQRS pipeline group, not here: AddApplicationDecorators (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:88) must run last so Scrutor can decorate handlers that are already registered. The API registrations themselves are order-independent. This is the [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] story: versioning, compression, rate limiting, and CORS are configured once and inherited by every service instead of copy-pasted per host.

    The request pipeline is data, not prose. Middleware order is behavior in ASP.NET Core, so the framework does not leave it to each host's Program.cs, and it no longer even leaves it as a fixed sequence of Use... calls. WebApplicationExtensions's UseCommonMiddlewarePipeline (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationExtensions.cs:49) and its Action<MiddlewarePipelineBuilder> overload (WebApplicationExtensions.cs:61) both route through one private ApplyPipeline that seeds the defaults, lets the host adjust them, validates the result, and only then applies each step (WebApplicationExtensions.cs:171-181). The steps themselves are MiddlewarePipelineStep records (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineStep.cs:21), each a stable Name plus an Action<WebApplication> Configure delegate, both null-validated on construction (MiddlewarePipelineStep.cs:27 and :30); because a step is inert data until someone runs it, the whole order is assertable without building a host. MiddlewarePipelineBuilder (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:15) owns the list: CreateDefault (MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:31) seeds the eighteen framework steps in order (:34-150) and InsertBefore, InsertAfter, Replace, and Remove (:161, :178, :198, :219) let a host address any of them by name, which is why MiddlewarePipelineStepNames (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineStepNames.cs:14) is public contract rather than an implementation detail: renaming a constant there is a breaking change, and the declaration order of those constants (:17-74) is the runtime order. Read it top to bottom and you have the edge: exception handler, correlation id, request localization, pre-forwarded capture, forwarded headers, HTTPS redirection, response compression, routing, CORS, authentication, tenant resolution, rate limiting, the soft-deleted-user filter, authorization, output cache, the JWKS and OIDC discovery endpoints, and finally the controllers. Four of those adjacencies are load-bearing, and Build (MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:260) re-checks them before a single step is applied (the Require... calls start at :254): the pre-forwarded capture must run immediately before UseForwardedHeaders or the captured scheme and host are no longer the ones the connection saw; authentication must run immediately before tenant resolution because the claim strategy reads HttpContext.User; authentication must precede the rate limiter (ADR-019) because GlobalRateLimitPartition keys on the authenticated principal and an unauthenticated pipeline would see every request as anonymous; and forwarded headers must precede the HTTPS redirect so the redirect decision reads the proxy-reported scheme. A violation throws InvalidOperationException at startup with the offending order printed (:320-321 and :335-336), and an invariant binds only when both of its steps are still present (:315 and :330), so dropping a whole capability stays legal while reordering a pair does not. Two more decisions are worth internalizing from the default step list. The HTTPS redirect is wrapped in a UseWhen that skips only cleartext HTTP/2 (MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:84-86, through the public IsCleartextHttp2 predicate at :350), because extracted gRPC services speak HTTP/2 cleartext (h2c) and a 307 would break the call; the exemption is keyed on the protocol Kestrel negotiated rather than on the Content-Type, because this step runs before routing and a header is caller-supplied, so a forged application/grpc cannot buy a plaintext response while every browser-reachable request (HTTP/1.1, or HTTP/2 over TLS) is still redirected (:79-84). And the forwarded-headers step (:69) takes its options from CommonForwardedHeaders (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/CommonForwardedHeaders.cs:27), the framework's one forwarded-headers posture: X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, and X-Forwarded-Host by default (DefaultHeaders, :33-34), with the known-proxy and known-network allowlists cleared (Create, :42, clearing at :49-50) so cloud reverse proxies are trusted regardless of their internal IPs. That is safe only because the posture assumes the ingress is the only thing that can reach the container (CommonForwardedHeaders.cs:19-20) and because the pre-forward scheme and host were already stashed in HttpContext.Items under the two keys declared at WebApplicationExtensions.cs:25 and :36. Server-rendered UI hosts adopt the identical posture through CommonForwardedHeadersExtensions's UseCommonUiForwardedHeaders (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/CommonForwardedHeadersExtensions.cs:24), called first in the UI pipeline before anything reads the scheme, the host, or the client address, so every host behind the same ingress reads them the same way (CommonForwardedHeaders.cs:6-11); the gateway keeps its own dependency-free copy of the values because it does not reference this package (:23-24). Hosts freeze their own resulting order with the opt-in fitness function MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:31), whose default expectation is the framework list verbatim (:40-57), so a reorder fails a fast unit test instead of surfacing as an unreachable jwks_uri or a rate cap that never engages (ADR-079). Alongside the pipeline, UseCommonRequestLocalization (WebApplicationExtensions.cs:74) builds the culture options from SupportedCultures (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Globalization/SupportedCultures.cs:9: en-US as the default at line 12 and the full en-US plus es list at line 18, with the qps-Ploc pseudo locale at line 28 added in Development only, WebApplicationExtensions.cs:81-84) so edge error localization runs under the caller's culture, and the companion MapCultureEndpoint (WebApplicationExtensions.cs:103) serves the GET /culture/set switch that Blazor UI hosts map; its bool httpOnly overload (WebApplicationExtensions.cs:116) controls the culture cookie's HttpOnly flag, which the parameterless form leaves off because a WebAssembly client reads the cookie on startup, while a Server-only host can turn it on (:97 and :109) (ADR-027). Turning order into inspectable, validated data is [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability], [Rubric §14, Testability] and [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] in one move.

    Rate limiting: one always-on partition, one named policy, and an optional shared counter. The global limiter is active on every request and rejects with 429 above RateLimitingSettings.GlobalPermitLimit (default 300 requests per minute, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/RateLimiting/RateLimitingSettings.cs:28) per authenticated user: GlobalRateLimitPartition (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:172) routes anonymous traffic to AnonymousPartition (line 83), and health, liveness, /.well-known/*, and gRPC traffic bypass the limiter outright (IsRateLimitBypassed, lines 67-71). The gRPC arm of that exemption is keyed on the routed endpoint rather than on the request's Content-Type (IsGrpcEndpoint, line 128): a header is caller-supplied, so stamping application/grpc on an ordinary request would otherwise hand any authenticated account the no-limiter partition, and endpoint metadata comes from the host's own MapGrpcService registrations instead (the predicate runs after UseRouting, which the pipeline order guarantees). Anonymous callers are exempt everywhere except a real-time hub path, where AnonymousPartition meters them per client IP at RateLimitingSettings.AnonymousHubPermitLimit (default 60, RateLimitingSettings.cs:95) over the configured HubPathPrefixes (default /hubs, RateLimitingSettings.cs:87, matched by IsAnonymousHubRequest at WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:112) and otherwise returns a no-limiter partition (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:102): a gateway cannot meter /hubs at the edge, because the hub authenticates from a query-string token the edge cannot read (ADR-024), so an anonymous negotiate flood would be counted nowhere at all. Because the global limiter otherwise no-ops for anonymous callers and account lockout is per-email, a password spray (one password, many email addresses) from a single source would otherwise be unthrottled. The framework closes that gap with the named auth-ip policy (RateLimitPolicyAuthIp, WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:49), whose partition selector AuthIpRateLimitPartition (line 326) is a per-client-IP window defaulting to 30 requests per minute (RateLimitingSettings.cs:35) and fails open on an unattributable IP (line 331) rather than collapsing every such request into one shared bucket, which would throttle the in-process test server to a standstill. Unlike the other named limiters, this one is not left for each app to attach: AuthControllerBase carries [EnableRateLimiting(WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimitPolicyAuthIp)] on both LoginAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:78) and RegisterAsync (AuthControllerBase.cs:103), and PasswordResetAuthControllerBase<TForgotPasswordCommand, TResetPasswordCommand> carries it on both recovery endpoints (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/PasswordResetAuthControllerBase.cs:78 and :102), as does EmailConfirmationControllerBase<TSendCommand, TConfirmCommand> on both of its anonymous actions (EmailConfirmationControllerBase.cs:81 and :109), so every consumer inherits spray protection by construction, while RefreshAsync (AuthControllerBase.cs:164-166) is deliberately left unthrottled because refresh is periodic and automatic and Blazor Server circuits issue it server-side from one shared host IP. A consumer that inherits the base without calling AddCommonRateLimiting fails at startup on an unregistered policy, which is the loud failure rather than the silent one. Two knobs sit on top of that baseline, both reachable only through the IConfiguration overload (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:403) that binds the RateLimiting section. Algorithm (RateLimitingSettings.cs:49) selects the RateLimitAlgorithm enum (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/RateLimiting/RateLimitAlgorithm.cs:8): FixedWindow is the default and cheapest but lets a caller spend an allowance twice across a boundary (RateLimitAlgorithm.cs:10-15), while SlidingWindow divides the same one-minute window into SegmentsPerWindow segments (default 4, RateLimitingSettings.cs:58) and smooths that burst away at the cost of one counter per segment. And Distributed (RateLimitingSettings.cs:68) swaps the in-memory counter for RedisFixedWindowRateLimiter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/RateLimiting/RedisFixedWindowRateLimiter.cs:41), so a limit means the same thing behind a load balancer as it does on one node. All three choices funnel through one private factory, CreateLimitedPartition (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:259), which takes the Redis path only when an IConnectionMultiplexer is actually registered and otherwise falls through to the in-memory limiters rather than failing startup (the multiplexer probe at line 261). The Redis limiter is worth reading for its deliberate compromises. It stores one counter per partition per window under rl:{partitionKey}:{unixMinute} (RedisFixedWindowRateLimiter.cs:164), where the framework partition key leads with the application namespace so two applications sharing one Redis do not share a counter (:24-28). The increment and the 65 second TTL (KeyTtlSeconds, line 60) run as one Lua script (IncrementScript, lines 50-53), so no failure between them can leave a key with no expiry, and only the increment that creates the key sets the TTL, because re-stamping it on every request would slide the window forward for a caller who keeps hitting it (:44-48); the skew past the window length means clock drift between instances cannot hand a partition a fresh allowance mid-window (:56-58). The increment is not transactional with the permit decision, so a simultaneous burst can overshoot slightly, accepted in exchange for one round trip per request (:31-33). The synchronous AttemptAcquireCore never decides (lines 142-146): the ASP.NET Core middleware calls it first on every request, so granting there would admit every request uncounted and deciding there would block a request thread on a Redis round trip, which is why it returns a not-acquired lease and the real decision happens in AcquireAsyncCore (line 149, reasoning at :127-138). And any Redis fault permits the request and logs at most one warning per window across the process (lines 179-187), because rate limiting protects capacity and must never itself become the reason a healthy request is rejected. RedisRateLimitLease (RedisFixedWindowRateLimiter.cs:214) is the lease type it hands out: Acquired and Undecided are shared statics (lines 219 and 226) so a permitted request allocates nothing, while Rejected (line 250) allocates per call because it carries the time until the partition's window resets (TimeUntilNextWindow, line 198) as RetryAfter metadata, which the rate-limiter OnRejected callback turns into the 429's Retry-After header (:208-212); a request larger than the whole allowance is rejected with no hint, since no later window could hold it (lines 155-160). The auth-ip policy stays per-instance whatever Distributed says (allowDistributed: false, WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:354): per-account lockout already backs it, and a login throttle that fails open on a Redis outage is a worse trade than one that stays local (ADR-019 for the layering, and ADR-029 for the brute-force half). This is [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] handled once at the edge.

    Correlation, tenancy, and the soft-deleted-user gate: three ambient facts established once. CorrelationIdMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs:20) reads the X-Correlation-ID request header (the constant lives at CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs:23), falling back to the current W3C trace id then ASP.NET's TraceIdentifier (lines 41-43), after cutting a caller-supplied value to MaxLength (64, the width of the persisted correlation columns, line 26) and discarding it unless every character is printable ASCII (Sanitize, lines 61-64), so a hostile header is neither echoed back nor persisted. It writes the id onto the scoped ICorrelationContext (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/ICorrelationContext.cs:8, implemented by CorrelationContext, which self-seeds from the correlation id of the enclosing background hop when one is being delivered and otherwise from a new GUID, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CorrelationContext.cs:13), and echoes it back through Response.OnStarting (CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs:46-50). That single id is what the CQRS logging decorators read (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/LoggingCommandDecorator.cs:18 and :24) and stamp onto every log scope through the Command {CommandName} [Module: {ModuleName}] [CorrelationId: {CorrelationId}] scope definition (LoggingCommandDecorator.cs:88-89), so one request is traceable end to end, and by module. TenantResolutionMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/TenantResolutionMiddleware.cs:37) is the HTTP half of ADR-073: it tries each configured strategy in order (claim, then header; the TenantResolutionStrategy.Host option is defined but deliberately returns null rather than being guessed at, lines 105-121) and publishes the winner on the scoped ITenantContext that the persistence query filter, save interceptor, and per-tenant database routing all read (line 70). Two decisions mirror the soft-deleted-user middleware below. It is wired unconditionally but inert by default, because TenancySettings resolves to defaults with Enabled false in a host that never called AddMultiTenancy (line 62). And it fails closed: with Tenancy:RequireTenant on, a request that resolves no tenant is rejected at line 83 and answered 400 with an RFC 9457 body naming the claim and header it looked at (lines 133-146), because an unscoped request would read across every tenant, which is the exact outcome tenancy exists to prevent; an explicit RequireTenant opt-out lets the request run as a system caller instead (lines 75-81), and health, liveness, and discovery paths are excluded so probes still answer before any tenant exists (lines 89-94). SoftDeletedUserMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:40) enforces business rule BR-133: an authenticated caller whose account was soft-deleted is rejected with a bare 401 (lines 110 and 171), checked first against a deleted-user marker read from the shared cache store rather than this replica's local copy (GetFromSharedStoreAsync, SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:94-96), because whichever replica handled the delete is the one that wrote it. The marker lives for 15 minutes (SoftDeletedUserCache.MarkerDuration, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUserCache.cs:32, written at SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:160) so it outlives any access token issued before the delete, and the database answer is cached only when it says deleted: a cached "not deleted" would sit in each replica's local copy and outlive a delete made on another replica (lines 133-135) (ADR-047). It resolves ISoftDeletedUserValidator lazily from RequestServices (line 114) instead of as an InvokeAsync parameter, so a service that does not host Identity still honors the marker and otherwise passes the request through (lines 115-122) rather than 500-ing on every call: an explicit nod to the [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] extraction path. And unlike tenancy it fails open: a cache read that throws falls back to the validator query (lines 95-103), and a validator query that throws lets the request continue (lines 143-150), because failing closed would turn any cache or database blip into a total outage for every authenticated request, while the exposure it buys back is bounded by the access-token lifetime. All three middlewares are [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] (correlation), [Rubric §11, Security] (deleted-account lockout), and [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] (tenant scoping) concerns handled once at the edge instead of in every controller.

    Errors become Problem Details, through two channels and one table. Failures reach the client two ways. Thrown exceptions are caught by the handler chain registered in AddCommonExceptionHandlers (DependencyInjection.cs:157-166), evaluated most-specific-first: OperationCanceledExceptionHandler (499 Client Closed Request, OperationCanceledExceptionHandler.cs:46), DomainExceptionHandler (400, DomainExceptionHandler.cs:32), DbUpdateExceptionHandler (409 at line 41 with a deliberately generic detail so database schema names never leak, DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:43-45, after counting a concurrency conflict on ConcurrencyConflictMetrics at :36-39), ValidationExceptionHandler (400 at line 33 with FluentValidation errors grouped by property name into the errors extension, ValidationExceptionHandler.cs:46-54), and finally GlobalExceptionHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/GlobalExceptionHandler.cs:30), which is the 500 catch-all (line 102) plus two special cases. A CrossTenantWriteException is answered 400 with a fixed title and detail that name nothing the exception carries (constants at :36 and :44-46, handled at :54-72), because echoing a tenant id back tells an unauthorized caller which tenant owns the row it just tried to write, and it is logged as a warning rather than an error because a tenant-scoped API refusing an untenanted write is routine. A BadHttpRequestException raised by Kestrel or model binding keeps the status it already carries (413 Payload Too Large for a body over the endpoint's limit, typically 400 otherwise) and is likewise logged as a warning, because a malformed or oversize request is a caller fault (handled from :74). Business failures that travel as Result.Failure rather than as exceptions are mapped by ApiControllerBase's HandleFailure (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/ApiControllerBase.cs:49), which falls back to a 500 when the error list is empty (lines 39-45) and otherwise derives the status from the most severe error present rather than the first (line 48), so an aggregate built by Result.Combine cannot be downgraded by error ordering: a 403 or a 500 travelling alongside a validation error still answers 403 or 500, and equal ranks keep the earliest error (the ranking is documented at ApiControllerBase.cs:36-44 and lives in ErrorTypeSeverity in MMCA.Common.Shared, so the gRPC edge classifies the same aggregate identically). The safety net UnhandledResultFailureFilter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/UnhandledResultFailureFilter.cs:22, an IAlwaysRunResultFilter) catches any action that accidentally returned a failed Result as a 200 body, logs a warning, and rewrites it as the correct error (lines 28-49). All of those paths converge on ErrorHttpMapping (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ErrorHttpMapping.cs:14), whose FrozenDictionary<ErrorType, int> (lines 20-32) is the single source of truth mapping each ErrorType (Validation, Invariant and Failure to 400, NotFound to 404, Conflict to 409, Unauthorized to 401, Forbidden to 403, UnprocessableEntity to 422, TooManyRequests to 429, Unexpected to 500) to a status code, with 400 as the fallback for anything unmapped (lines 38-39) and the list-taking overload at lines 51-52 applying the severity ranking. Its BuildErrorsExtension (line 62) localizes each Error's human message at the edge through IErrorLocalizer (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Localization/IErrorLocalizer.cs:9), keyed by the stable Code, leaving Code, Type, Source, and Target verbatim so clients can still branch on them, and leaving the original English message untouched when no localizer is registered (line 66). ErrorLocalizer (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Localization/ErrorLocalizer.cs:13) walks the registered ErrorResourceSource (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Localization/ErrorResourceSource.cs:13) list in registration order (lines 23-30: the framework's own ErrorResources (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Resources/ErrorResources.cs:9) anchor first, then each module's resources added through AddErrorResources, DependencyInjection.cs:144) and falls back to the caller's message when no source knows the code (line 32). This is [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] (one consistent RFC 9457 shape) meeting the [Rubric §1, SOLID] discipline of never duplicating the mapping, and [Rubric §27, Internationalization] at the one boundary where a machine-readable code becomes human prose.

    The controller hierarchy: generic CRUD earned by inheritance. A module gets working endpoints by subclassing one generic base and supplying its type parameters (ADR-034). ApiControllerBase is the root: [ApiController], HandleFailure, nothing else. EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/EntityControllerBase.cs:33) adds the read surface (GetAllAsync at line 110, paged at line 154, lookup at line 317, GetByIdAsync at line 361) over an IEntityQueryService<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>, with field projection through a fields query parameter, X-Pagination header metadata (written at line 188), and a page size clamped to MaxPageSize (resolved per request from IOptions<ApplicationSettings>, defaulting to 500 and clamped again to the query pipeline's own EntityQueryPipeline.MaxUnboundedResultLimit, so the pagination metadata and the export loop never assume a page size the pipeline does not serve, lines 52-66). That header has exactly one owner: PaginationHeaderExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Pagination/PaginationHeaderExtensions.cs:12), a public static class whose extension(HttpResponse) block (line 19) adds AppendPaginationHeader (line 27), holds the header name as HeaderName (line 17), and serializes the page's PaginationMetadata with JsonSerializerOptions.Web, so camelCase property names (line 32). A controller that serves a page outside EntityControllerBase therefore emits the identical header instead of re-declaring the name and the serializer settings (PaginationHeaderExtensions.cs:7-11). AggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:29) extends it with an [Idempotent] POST create (lines 75-76) that returns 201 with a Location resolved before the result is returned (lines 91-98): the named by-id route (GetByIdRouteName, defaulting to Get{EntityName}ById at line 57) when the derived controller declares it, and otherwise the new id appended to the collection path the POST was made to, where the inherited GET {id} answers. The Location is never left to the result, because a CreatedAtRoute naming an undeclared route throws only when the result executes, after the entity was saved, which would answer a 500 for a create that had succeeded (AggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:67-74). Its DELETE dispatches DeleteEntityCommand<TEntity, TIdentifierType> and returns 204 (lines 106-119), and CrudEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest, TUpdateRequest> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/CrudEntityControllerBase.cs:55) closes the set with the conditional PUT {id} (attributes at lines 87-89, the six documented response codes at :90-96, the token read at :102, and a fresh ETag on the way out at :111). The interfaces IEntityControllerBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (IEntityControllerBase.cs:14) and IAggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest> (IAggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:15) describe those shapes for testing and documentation. The generic constraints tie the tower together: TEntity derives from AuditableBaseEntity<TIdentifierType> for reads and from AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> for writes, TEntityDTO implements IBaseDTO<TIdentifierType>, and TCreateRequest implements ICreateRequest (IEntityControllerBase.cs:17-18, IAggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:20-22, AggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:42-45). Alongside the CRUD tower sit ten special-purpose bases: AuthControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:49, anonymous login, register, and refresh over IAuthenticationService, lines 69-130, plus the [Authorize] revoke at lines 152-154 and the multi-device pair GET my-sessions (line 183) and POST revoke/{sessionId:guid} (line 216), whose current-device flag comes from the access token's own sid claim so no client state is involved, ADR-097); PasswordResetAuthControllerBase<TForgotPasswordCommand, TResetPasswordCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/PasswordResetAuthControllerBase.cs:43), a sibling of that base rather than an addition to it because each app's own AuthController already occupies the single-inheritance chain (it derives straight from ApiControllerBase, PasswordResetAuthControllerBase.cs:45), serving POST forgot-password (line 75) and POST reset-password (line 99); both are anonymous by necessity since the caller has lost the credential, forgot-password always answers 202 whether or not the address exists (line 92) so the response never reveals which addresses hold accounts, and each app supplies its own command record through a one-line factory (:61 and :69, ADR-091); EmailConfirmationControllerBase<TSendCommand, TConfirmCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/EmailConfirmationControllerBase.cs:43), a second sibling built the same way for the same single-inheritance reason (EmailConfirmationControllerBase.cs:16-19), serving POST send-email-confirmation (line 78) and POST confirm-email (line 106), both [Idempotent], both anonymous because the link is followed from a mail client with no session and an unconfirmed account may be unable to sign in (:23-27), and both behind auth-ip (lines 79-81 and 107-109); send answers 202 on every well-formed request so the response never reveals which addresses hold accounts (:30-32), and the two command records stay app-side behind one-line factories (CreateSendCommand at :61, CreateConfirmCommand at :69, ADR-116); UserAccountAuthControllerBase<TChangePasswordCommand, TChangePreferencesCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/UserAccountAuthControllerBase.cs:41), which subclasses AuthControllerBase purely additively (line 46) and adds the self-service account endpoints PUT password (line 86), PUT preferences (line 112), and GET preferences (line 138), taking the two mutation commands as type parameters because each app owns its own command record while the preferences query is shared (UserAccountAuthControllerBase.cs:48-49); OAuthControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/OAuthControllerBase.cs:56, the Google, GitHub, and Apple external-provider challenges at lines 103, 113, and 126, the GET complete provider callback at line 145 and the POST exchange redemption at line 230, whose single-use exchange code, cached for two minutes at OAuthControllerBase.cs:87, keeps tokens out of the redirect URL; a multi-replica host passes an IDistributedLock to the four-argument constructor so the code is read and burned inside that lock (lease and wait at lines 80-81) and two replicas redeeming the same code at once cannot both mint a token pair, while the three-argument constructor (line 90) keeps an unlocked read-then-burn that is single-use only per replica (:35-40); ADR-036 and ADR-043); DataExportControllerBase<TQuery> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Privacy/DataExportControllerBase.cs:61), the data-subject access and portability endpoint (ADR-076), which serves GET {userId}/export (line 79) as a real file download rather than an inline body (returned through File(...) at line 111, with an invariant user-data-{userId}-{yyyyMMdd}.json name derived from the package's own GeneratedOn, documented at lines 132-133 and built at line 141), gated by both an [Authorize] and a [FeatureGate] on PrivacyFeatures.DataExport (lines 59-60) while the handler independently enforces owner-or-privileged-role, and abstract only because each app owns its own query record (CreateQuery, line 126); LegalAcceptanceControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Legal/LegalAcceptanceControllerBase.cs:45), the signed-in user's Terms of Service standing behind a class-level [Authorize] (line 44): a GET that reads the caller's standing against the configured current version (line 59) and an [Idempotent] POST that records an acceptance (lines 93-94), both on LegalAcceptanceRoutes.Action, with the current version resolved from options (CurrentTermsVersion, line 54) and the derived controller supplying only the route, the DataExportControllerBase precedent (:19-21); and ServiceInfoControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/ServiceInfoControllerBase.cs:30), whose dual-version /ServiceInfo returns ServiceInfoResponse for the deprecated v1.0 (line 51) and ServiceInfoV2Response for v2.0 (line 54, a superset adding the supported and deprecated version lists held at lines 32-33), proving the versioning machinery works across versions ([MapToApiVersion] at lines 40 and 46). The last two are the administration surface, and both are gated on a capability rather than a role name, so the framework never has to know an app's role vocabulary. UsersAdminControllerBase<TUserDto> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:43) carries a single class-level [HasPermission(AdministrationPermissions.ManageUsers)] (line 42) over GET {userId} (line 55), the view-only GET {userId}/sessions (line 76, served by the framework's IUserSessionsAdministrationService injected into that action at line 82), the POST {userId}/lock and POST {userId}/unlock pair (lines 103 and 123), and PUT {userId}/roles (line 144), the rest over the app's own IUserAdministrationService<TUserDto>. The user roster is not an action here: it is the app's own generic paged entity endpoint (UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:20-23). A host that grants the permission to nobody serves endpoints that deny everyone, which is the safe direction. RolesAdminControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/RolesAdminControllerBase.cs:61, gated on AdministrationPermissions.ManageRoles at line 60) reports each role's compiled and stored permissions (GET at line 80, GET {role} at line 121), publishes the permission catalog (GET catalog at line 102), and writes a stored set through PUT {role}/permissions (line 143), recording the caller through an overridable ResolveChangedBy (line 162). Two refusals on that write are the ones to memorize, both 400: a set that names ManageRoles itself is rejected, because granting from here would make access to role administration a matter of data and deleting the row would lock every operator out of the screen that could restore it, and a set naming anything outside the catalog is rejected rather than stored as a row no endpoint will ever check. All of these carry the same note: class-level routing and versioning attributes are not reliably inherited, so the per-service sealed subclass supplies them. This is the clearest [Rubric §5, Vertical Slice] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] payoff in the presentation layer: a module writes a DTO, a mapper, and a short sealed subclass, and inherits a fully paged, filterable, exportable, error-mapped REST resource, with [Rubric §30, Compliance & Data Governance] covered by the DSAR base.

    Export is a route, not a content negotiation. EntityControllerBase.ExportAsync (EntityControllerBase.cs:253-258) streams the same filtered collection the paged endpoint serves as an RFC 4180 CSV download, page-looping the query service server-side (ADR-078). It is a distinct path rather than an Accept: text/csv variant for two reasons stated in the source: the public output-cache policy varies by query string but not by Accept, so a cached JSON body could be replayed to a CSV request, and AddAPI sets ReturnHttpNotAcceptable = false, so a negotiation miss would fall back to JSON silently instead of returning 406 (EntityControllerBase.cs:198-203). The work is split in two. The controller keeps the HTTP concerns (the action, the row scope, the file name, and the headers) and hands the format to EntityCsvExporter<TEntityDTO> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Export/EntityCsvExporter.cs:17, an internal static class whose own summary draws that line at :11-14), which owns which DTO properties can be exported, how a page of rows becomes CSV records, and the paging loop that streams every page under a row ceiling (WriteAsync, line 116, invoked from EntityControllerBase.cs:280). Its record-writing primitive is CsvWriter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Export/CsvWriter.cs:44), a deliberately hand-written internal helper: it quotes only when RFC 4180 requires it (WriteField, line 203, with the trigger set as a SearchValues<char> at line 71), terminates records with CRLF regardless of host OS (line 58), formats cells invariantly so the same row produces the same bytes on every machine (FormatCell, line 141, which writes a Money cell as its amount plus ISO 4217 code through FormatMoney at line 173), and writes a UTF-8 BOM explicitly (line 55, through WriteByteOrderMark at line 82, paired with the preamble-free encoding at line 65) because Excel reads a BOM-less UTF-8 CSV in the machine's ANSI code page. Two guards run before any byte is written. Columns a CSV cannot represent faithfully, binary concurrency tokens and every non-string collection property, are computed once per closed DTO type and dropped (UnexportablePropertyNames at EntityCsvExporter.cs:31, the type test IsExportableType at :238-241); value objects and other class-typed properties are deliberately kept, because CsvWriter renders each as a value (Money as amount and currency code, Currency as its code, any other record as compact JSON rather than its compiler-generated ToString, :26-29). And a caller who names one of those dropped properties in fields= gets an Error.InvalidEntityField validation failure rather than a quietly missing column (ValidateFields, EntityCsvExporter.cs:61, called first thing in the action at EntityControllerBase.cs:266-268). Then the exporter renders into an in-memory buffer rather than the response body (a StreamWriter over a MemoryStream, EntityCsvExporter.cs:132-135) and copies each page to the body with awaited writes only (DrainAsync, :209-221), because the synchronous CSV writer would otherwise flush synchronously whenever its buffer filled, which Kestrel rejects (:104-108). Nothing reaches the body until the first page has succeeded: headers, BOM, and the header row go out only then (:157-164), and a first-page failure comes back as a plain failed Result (:144-145), which is what keeps the "a failure on page one still returns Problem Details" path honest (EntityControllerBase.cs:301-302). A failure on a later page can no longer change the status, so the exporter logs it through the controller (LogExportPageFailure, EntityControllerBase.cs:702) and ends the file with an explicit # export incomplete after N rows line (EntityCsvExporter.cs:147-151, text at :363) rather than letting it pass for a complete export of fewer rows. The row ceiling is announced up front through the X-Export-Row-Limit header (constant at EntityControllerBase.cs:522, default 100,000 at line 472, overridable per host through MaxExportRows at lines 79-87, written alongside the Content-Disposition attachment name in BeginExportResponse at lines 619-625, the name being a UTC {controller}-{yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ}.csv built at lines 635-638) with a # export truncated at N rows notice written as a final body line (EntityCsvExporter.cs:192-195, text at :357), because headers are frozen the moment the first byte flushes; when the ceiling lands exactly on a page boundary the exporter consults the page's TotalItemCount instead of issuing one more query just to find out (:182-188), and a short page ends the loop only when that total agrees, because the query pipeline can clamp a full page below the requested size and stopping there would truncate the file with no marker (IsLastPage, :229-230). Row scoping is a shared hook rather than an export-only one: GetReadSpecificationAsync (EntityControllerBase.cs:627-629) is what all five read actions apply (both GetAllAsync overloads, the lookup, GetByIdAsync, and the export, :535-541), resolved once per request so one instance filters every page of an export loop (:567-568). It is asynchronous because row scoping is rarely a pure function of the principal (:547-552), it returns GetExportSpecification(), itself null by default (line 601), and the lookup, which takes a predicate rather than a specification, receives the same scope as its Criteria (:310-315, passed at line 328). So an export or a dropdown can no longer drift wider than the list it mirrors, and a scoped GetByIdAsync answers a filtered-out row with 404 rather than 403 so the read cannot become an existence oracle (:562-564). The default differs by surface on purpose. The JSON read endpoints stay unscoped until a controller overrides one of the two hooks, but the export is fail-closed: when no scope resolves it queries nothing and answers 403 carrying ExportRowScopeRequiredErrorCode (Export.RowScopeRequired, line 487; the check at lines 272-274, the error built by UnscopedExportRefused at :608-613), unless the controller deliberately overrides AllowUnscopedExport (false by default, line 508) for rows every caller who can reach the endpoint may see, such as reference data or an admin-only table. A controller that forgot to scope its export therefore serves no rows rather than every row (:231-238). That is a [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] and [Rubric §11, Security] pairing worth reading closely.

    Idempotency for safe retries. Write endpoints are made replay-safe by IdempotentAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotentAttribute.cs:16), a one-line ServiceFilterAttribute that resolves the scoped IdempotencyFilter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotencyFilter.cs:68) from DI (ADR-017). The filter runs at two MVC stages. As an IAsyncResourceFilter it runs before model binding, the last point at which the body can be made replayable, and calls EnableBuffering only when an Idempotency-Key header is actually present (lines 119-125), so ordinary traffic pays nothing. As an IAsyncActionFilter it does the real work (line 128): with no key the action simply runs (lines 132-136); with one, it derives the cache key from the caller's user id claim (or anon: plus the remote IP), the HTTP method, the route template, and the client-supplied key, joined on newlines and SHA-256 hashed so the key length stays bounded (BuildCacheKey, lines 485-498). Scoping to the caller stops one user's cached response from being replayed to another; scoping to method plus route stops one key from colliding across endpoints that share a cache instance. It also hashes the buffered request body (ComputeRequestBodyHashAsync, line 182, rewinding the stream on both sides so model binding still sees it) and binds that hash to the record. The flow is then a lock-free fast path (TryReplayAsync called at line 143), then the guarded section. The guard is an IDistributedLock resolved from RequestServices when the host registers one (lines 148-156), because a per-process lock only serializes duplicates that land on the same replica and both deployed apps run more than one; a host with no distributed lock falls back to the striped KeyedSemaphoreStripe (field at line 90, used from line 201) rather than a per-key semaphore table that would grow unbounded or race on removal. Under the distributed lock the filter waits LockWait (5 seconds, line 104) for a lease living LockTimeToLive (30 seconds, line 97), double-checks the cache, and runs the action. Four outcomes are worth memorizing. A hit replays the stored IdempotencyRecord (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotencyRecord.cs:14, a status code plus JSON body plus the request-body hash) with an X-Idempotent-Replay: true header (line 383, through IdempotencyHeaders), as a bare StatusCodeResult when the stored body is empty so a replayed 204 does not acquire a content type (lines 384-391). A key reused with a different payload is answered 422 Unprocessable Entity rather than replayed (line 376 and BodyMismatchResult at 322-333), because replaying would tell the client a genuinely new write succeeded when nothing ran. A duplicate that cannot take the lock within the wait and finds nothing cached gets 409 Conflict (lines 263-269 and InFlightDuplicateResult at 301-312), which is retryable and honest rather than a second execution. And a cache or lock that faults is swallowed: the request runs without the guarantee and the degradation is counted (lines 255, 364, and 439), because deduplication is an optimization over an at-least-once client retry and must not become an outage of every write endpoint. Only 2xx results are stored, and only the two shapes the record can represent: an ObjectResult or a body-less StatusCodeResult such as NoContent() (BuildRecord, line 448), for IdempotencySettings.CacheExpirationHours (default 24, constrained to the range 1 to 168, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotencySettings.cs:15-16) through ICacheService (line 430). Replaying a transient 500 for a whole retention window would defeat the retry the header exists to enable. All three behaviors are observable: IdempotencyMetrics (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotencyMetrics.cs:16) publishes idempotency.replayed (line 36), idempotency.conflict tagged kind=body_mismatch or in_flight (lines 24, 29, and 41), and idempotency.degraded (line 46) on the MMCA.Common.Idempotency meter (line 19), so a sustained degraded rate says out loud that deduplication is effectively off. The one thing the filter cannot do is notice an endpoint that forgot to opt in, which is what NonIdempotentAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/NonIdempotentAttribute.cs:23) exists for: it attaches no pipeline stage and changes no behavior, it only records a required Justification string (line 28), and its sole consumer is the PostActionsDeclareIdempotencyIntent fitness function (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Cqrs/ArchitectureRules.Idempotency.cs:44, matching at :72-73), which fails the build unless every POST action carries either [Idempotent] or this attribute. That is why AuthControllerBase reads the way it does: all five of its POST actions (login, register, refresh, revoke, and the per-session revoke) carry a written reason for staying outside the contract (AuthControllerBase.cs:76, :94, :125, :153, and :217), since replaying a stored token pair would hand a retrying client credentials minted for an earlier call or already invalidated by rotation (a retried register hits the email-exists 409 instead, which is the correct answer), and replaying a cached 204 would report success for a revoke that never ran. OAuthControllerBase's POST exchange opts out for the same reason, since it burns a single-use code (OAuthControllerBase.cs:290). This is a [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability], [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] and [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] control: at-least-once retry from a gateway or a flaky client cannot create duplicate resources, and "no idempotency here" is always a recorded decision rather than an omission nobody noticed.

    Conditional writes: the ETag round trip, and only the header. Idempotency keys make a retried write safe; the concurrency token makes a racing write safe, and the HTTP way to state that precondition is If-Match (ADR-035). The token travels in exactly one place. IConcurrencyAware (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/DTOs/IConcurrencyAware.cs:15) is the read-side contract: a byte[] RowVersion declared init (line 19), rendered as the response ETag and echoed back by the client in its next write, and its own doc states the rule (lines 9-14): update requests carry no token, a persisted aggregate always has one, and a write that states no precondition is refused rather than falling back to last-write-wins. ConcurrencyETag (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Http/ConcurrencyETag.cs:24, taught with the auth and HTTP primitives in Group 08) is the pure translation layer between the EF Core rowversion byte array and the wire: Format renders it as the weak tag W/"<base64>" (line 44) and TryParse reads one back (line 62), with the header names and the * wildcard as constants (:27, :30, :33). Weak is the honest strength, because a strong tag promises byte-for-byte equality of the representation, which this cannot promise when the same row version renders differently under a fields= projection (ConcurrencyETag.cs:13). The read side emits it automatically: EntityControllerBase.GetByIdAsync calls SetConcurrencyETag (EntityControllerBase.cs:383), which resolves the DTO's RowVersion property once per closed controller type (line 391, so a DTO with no token costs no per-request reflection), reads the token off either the typed DTO or the camelCase dictionary a fields= projection produces (ReadRowVersion, lines 434-443), and writes the header at line 425; the method is protected rather than private (line 417) so a controller serving a row from a custom read emits the same header instead of re-implementing the format, which is where the two halves drift apart and a precondition quietly stops working. The write side is SupportsIfMatchAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Concurrency/SupportsIfMatchAttribute.cs:49), which, unlike IdempotentAttribute, needs no scoped service and therefore implements IAsyncActionFilter directly and needs no DI registration (lines 44-48). Before the action it decodes the header into HttpContext.Items under a public key (TokenItemKey, line 57, written at line 122), which the action reads back through the static RequiredToken (line 68); after the action it rewrites a conflict outcome to 412 Precondition Failed, covering an ObjectResult 409 and a bare StatusCodeResult 409 (lines 143-160) as well as a DbUpdateConcurrencyException the action let escape, which it answers with its own 412 Problem Details and marks handled so the global DbUpdateExceptionHandler never turns it into a 409 (lines 132-140). A given concurrency exception therefore reaches exactly one of those two places, and each records it on ConcurrencyConflictMetrics (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Concurrency/ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:24), so every conflict is counted once (ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:14-17). That internal static class publishes persistence.concurrency.conflict (lines 37-40) on the MMCA.Common.Persistence meter (line 27, duplicated as a literal in MMCA.Common.Aspire because that package has no reference to this one, :8-10), tagged entity_type with the CLR type of the first conflicting entry read from the EF model, so a lazy-loading proxy reports its entity rather than the generated subclass, or unknown when the exception carries no entry (EntityTypeName, lines 55-56). No alert ships on it: a sustained rate on one entity type points at contended rows, which is a design question rather than an incident (:20-21). Three responses make the contract unambiguous. A missing or wildcard If-Match is 428 Precondition Required and the action never runs (lines 109-114 and 164-173), so last-write-wins is not reachable by omission. A malformed tag is a 400 rather than being ignored (lines 116-120 and 176-185), because silently dropping a precondition the client believed it had set is the one outcome worse than rejecting it. And 412 is used rather than 409 because RFC 9110 reserves it for a precondition the client stated in a header (SupportsIfMatchAttribute.cs:36-41). CrudEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest, TUpdateRequest> is where all of it lands: [SupportsIfMatch] on the PUT (CrudEntityControllerBase.cs:91), the token read at :102, and the whole set of outcomes declared as ProducesResponseType at :90-96. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] and [Rubric §8, Data Architecture], with a [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] counter on the conflicts.

    Output caching at the edge, and evicting it across services. Read endpoints that are user-independent by contract can be cached at the HTTP edge even when the UI attaches a bearer token to every request, which the built-in ASP.NET policy refuses to do. PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy.cs:47), registered by name through OutputCacheOptionsExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.cs:6, both overloads at lines 20 and 34), drops that identity bail-out and enables caching for the authenticated request anyway (lines 88-90), varies by every query-string key (QueryKeys = "*" at line 96) so search, paging, filtering and field projection each get their own entry, refuses to store responses that set cookies or are not plain 200s (lines 125-128), and offers a bypassRoles escape hatch so a privileged caller who receives an elevated payload always reads fresh, skipping both lookup and storage (the constructor parameter at line 69, the role test at line 142, applied at lines 88-90, ADR-040). The store behind it defaults to per-replica memory, so a tag eviction on one instance leaves every other instance serving stale bytes. OutputCacheEvictionHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheEvictionHandler.cs:32) closes that gap by consuming the OutputCacheEvictionRequested integration event and calling EvictByTagAsync for each tag against this host's store (lines 38-64); no broker type appears in it (it implements only IIntegrationEventHandler<OutputCacheEvictionRequested>, lines 32-35), so the same handler is reachable from the in-process dispatcher and from the framework's own broker receive path, where a host subscribes with RegisterOutputCacheEvictionConsumer() inside its AddBrokerMessaging configuration (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/IntegrationEventConsumerExtensions.cs:28, shorthand for RegisterIntegrationEventConsumer<OutputCacheEvictionRequested>() at line 32) (ADR-026). Its two behaviors are both deliberate: eviction is per-tag best effort, so a store that throws on one tag is logged and counted rather than rethrown (lines 56-62), because rethrowing would redeliver the message, re-evict every tag that already succeeded, and eventually dead-letter a message whose only consequence is a cache entry that expires on its own TTL anyway; and an OperationCanceledException is explicitly not swallowed (line 56), so host shutdown looks like shutdown rather than an acked message. The failures are visible through OutputCacheMetrics (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheMetrics.cs:16), which publishes cache.eviction.failed tagged by cache tag on the MMCA.Common.OutputCache meter (lines 19 and 29-30), the alert target for cross-service cache coherence: a non-zero rate means this host is serving responses it was told to drop. OutputCacheEvictionExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheEvictionExtensions.cs:27) is the DI half plus the in-process shortcut: AddOutputCacheEvictionHandler (line 111) registers the handler as a singleton through TryAddEnumerable (lines 115-117) so a host and a module that both ask for the behavior get one handler rather than a double eviction, while EvictTagsAsync (line 49) and the log-and-continue TryEvictTagsAsync (line 78) let code already running in this host evict its own tags without publishing an event to itself. One more type exists only because of the cache: ApiVersionReportingResultFilter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/ApiVersionReportingResultFilter.cs:21), an internal IResultFilter that AddCommonApiVersioning adds to every MVC action (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.cs:60). The versioning library writes api-supported-versions and api-deprecated-versions from a Response.OnStarting callback, but the output cache snapshots the headers when the body starts, before those callbacks run, so a cached entry would otherwise be stored and replayed without the report (ApiVersionReportingResultFilter.cs:13-17). The filter reports ahead of the body through whatever IReportApiVersions the host registered (OnResultExecuting, lines 24-40, skipping a response that has already started or an endpoint with no version metadata), so the headers land in the snapshot, the library's own callback finds them present and adds nothing, and a host with ReportApiVersions off still reports nothing. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] with a [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] backstop.

    The contract surface: mapping, JSON, and query filters. The framework maps between the wire and the domain by hand, not through a runtime reflection mapper (ADR-001). Two interfaces in the Application layer define the shape, both in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/IEntityDTOMapper.cs: IEntityDTOMapper<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (line 14) turns an entity into its DTO and supplies a default interface implementation for the collection overload (line 27), and IEntityRequestMapper<TEntity, TCreateRequest, TIdentifierType> (line 42) turns an incoming request into a domain entity through its factory, returning a Result so mapping-time validation (a uniqueness check, for example) is a first-class failure rather than an exception (line 54). Their write-side twin, IEntityUpdateApplier<TEntity, TUpdateRequest, TIdentifierType> (same file, line 79), belongs to the CQRS group because it is what lets one generic update handler own loading, the concurrency token, and the save while the aggregate keeps owning its invariants (IEntityDTOMapper.cs:62-74). All three are auto-registered by module assembly scanning. The query string has one edge helper of its own, QueryFilterModelBinder (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/ModelBinders/QueryFilterModelBinder.cs:24) parses the filters[Prop].operator= and filters[Prop].value= query-string convention into the (operator, value) dictionary the paged read and export endpoints hand to the specification layer, capping one request at MaxFilters = 50 distinct properties (line 34, enforced at lines 61-62, bounding the per-request reflection work a caller can demand from QueryFilterService) and discarding entries missing an operator or a value (line 75). Request bodies that carry a file get the same treatment: FormFileUploadExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Uploads/FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:31) puts the size check, the single exact read, and the refusal error behind one call (:27-28), answering an UploadedFileContent (FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:16, the bytes plus the file name and content type exactly as the client declared them) or, for a CSV import, a CsvUpload (:24) that keeps the raw upload beside the parsed table so a command can store or re-parse it while the edge runs its own validation and dry run (:19-20); the OversizeFormResourceFilter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Uploads/OversizeFormResourceFilter.cs:22) that AddAPI installs reads the form before model binding only for an action that binds one, so the server's "request body too large" refusal reaches the exception handlers as a 413 instead of becoming a model-state 400, and a streaming upload that reads the body itself is never buffered (:9-19). The small shared DTO vocabulary those generics rely on lives in MMCA.Common.Shared: IBaseDTO<TIdentifierType> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/DTOs/IBaseDTO.cs:9, an Id declared with an init accessor at line 13), BaseLookup<TIdentifierType> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/DTOs/BaseLookup.cs:8, a required id at line 12 plus a required display name at line 15, for dropdowns and autocomplete), and the concurrency contract IConcurrencyAware described above. Manual mapping keeps the DTO contract explicit and reviewable: the [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices] position this codebase takes deliberately.

    Feature gating and per-module controller visibility. Three mechanisms let an operator turn surface area on and off without a code change. DisabledFeatureHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/FeatureManagement/DisabledFeatureHandler.cs:14) renders a consistent Problem Details 404 when a FeatureGate-protected action is reached while its flag is off (lines 18-26), so a disabled feature looks like a nonexistent endpoint rather than an error (ADR-031). A percentage rollout needs to be sticky per user rather than random per request, which is what CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/FeatureManagement/CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor.cs:68) supplies: registered by AddAPI through WithTargeting<...> (DependencyInjection.cs:109), it builds the targeting context from the current request's principal, taking the user id from the user_id claim that TokenService emits and falling back to the principal's name (line 86), and taking the groups from the caller's role claims under all three types the JWT middleware may produce (ClaimTypes.Role, role, roles, lines 76-82) because ICurrentUserService is scoped while this accessor is a singleton (DependencyInjection.cs:101-106). An anonymous request yields an empty context (lines 67-74), so a targeted feature is simply off for anonymous callers, and the accessor can never fail a request. A flag's value need not wait for a deployment either. A host that opts in to reloadable flags (AddReloadableFeatureFlags, which binds FeatureFlagOverrideSettings from the FeatureFlags section, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideSettings.cs:6-12) layers StoredOverrideFeatureDefinitionProvider (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/StoredOverrideFeatureDefinitionProvider.cs:31) over the configuration provider: a flag with a stored override answers with the override's definition and every other flag answers from configuration unchanged (:10-12, :43-50), so the FeatureGate decorators keep calling IFeatureManager and an override takes effect on the next evaluation with no restart (:16-18). It fails toward configuration, never toward an exception: an override set that cannot be loaded leaves every flag on its configured value and logs a warning (:24-25, :75-79). The overrides themselves are FeatureFlagOverride rows (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverride.cs:24, created through a Result-returning Create at line 82 and cleared by soft delete at line 134) whose FeatureFlagOverrideMode is Off (the kill switch), On, Percentage, or Targeting (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideMode.cs:12-28), translated into a FeatureDefinition by FeatureFlagDefinitions (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagDefinitions.cs:33). They live in the owning service's own database behind IFeatureFlagOverrideStore, implemented by EFFeatureFlagOverrideStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/FeatureFlags/EFFeatureFlagOverrideStore.cs:33), in a FeatureFlagOverrides table (FeatureFlagOverrideModelBuilderExtensions, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideModelBuilderExtensions.cs:18) that enters the model only when the marker FeatureFlagOverrideModelGate is registered, so a host that never opts in keeps a byte-identical model and sees no migration (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideModelGate.cs:3-11). Reads go through IFeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot, whose FeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:46) holds the whole override table as one entry in the host's ICacheService for OverrideCacheSeconds (default 30, FeatureFlagOverrideSettings.cs:24), keyed by both the application name and the data source so two services sharing one Redis never read each other's snapshot (FeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:27-32), and invalidated by prefix on a write so every replica of a two-level-cache host stops addressing the old snapshot (:18-24, :70-71). The administration half is IFeatureFlagAdministrationService, implemented by the internal FeatureFlagAdministrationService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:30, ListAsync, SetOverrideAsync, and ClearOverrideAsync at lines 45, 62, and 86), which validates a name against the FeatureFlagCatalog (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagCatalog.cs:17, built from the registered FeatureFlagAssembly records at line 9 through FeatureFlagRegistry, which reads every public const string on a static *Features class into a FeatureFlagDescriptor, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagRegistry.cs:17, :35, and :46, each declared with its FeatureFlagAttribute and FeatureFlagLifetime, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAttribute.cs:32). It is exposed over HTTP by FeatureFlagsControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/FeatureFlagsControllerBase.cs:38, gated on AdministrationPermissions.ManageFeatures at line 37: GET at line 49, PUT {name} at line 68, DELETE {name} at line 93). The wire vocabulary is the Shared records SetFeatureFlagOverrideRequest (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/SetFeatureFlagOverrideRequest.cs:18), FeatureFlagOverrideResponse (FeatureFlagOverrideResponse.cs:14), FeatureFlagStatusResponse (FeatureFlagStatusResponse.cs:15), and the FeatureFlagValueKind enum (FeatureFlagValueKind.cs:10) (ADR-031).

    The newer edge surface: opt-in actions, declarative caching, view-as, and the composed host. Several smaller pieces extend the edge without changing a host that ignores them. Two marker attributes opt an entity controller in to extra list actions: SupportsCursorPagingAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Pagination/SupportsCursorPagingAttribute.cs:14, the keyset list served by the query service's GetPageByCursorAsync, :4-11) and SupportsChangeFeedAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Pagination/SupportsChangeFeedAttribute.cs:14, the change feed served by GetChangesSinceAsync, :4-11). Both are enforced by the internal OptInActionAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Pagination/OptInActionAttribute.cs:17), an IActionModelConvention that removes the base action from any controller that did not opt in, so it has no route and no API description (:6-13). Output caching gains two declarative forms: PublicCachedReadsAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/PublicCachedReadsAttribute.cs:42, an IControllerModelConvention) marks the inherited base reads anonymous and output-cached under one named policy and names the by-id route, so a controller no longer overrides a read only to add attributes (:9-21), and EvictOutputCacheAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/EvictOutputCacheAttribute.cs:36, an IAsyncResultFilter) evicts its tags after a 2xx write and before the body is written, evicts nothing on a non-2xx, a GET or HEAD, or an unhandled exception, and logs rather than fails when eviction throws (:12-27). Rate limiting gains RateLimitPartitions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/RateLimiting/RateLimitPartitions.cs:11), partition factories for a host's own policies built on the framework's limiters (:7-9), and the in-memory fixed window now runs through RemainingWindowFixedWindowRateLimiter (MMCA.Common/Source/Build/RateLimiting/RemainingWindowFixedWindowRateLimiter.cs:31), one internal source file linked into each package that runs such a window, which rewrites the 429's Retry-After hint from the whole window length to the time actually remaining (:6-22), handing back a RejectedLease that carries only that hint (:133-137). Read-only support access (ADR-137) has its HTTP half in ViewAsGuardMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:42): for a principal carrying act_sub it refuses every method other than GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS with 403, except the action marked by ViewAsEndEndpointAttribute (:245) and an endpoint marked read-only, and it re-checks that the grant is still live on every request, answering 401 otherwise (:13-33). Unlike the soft-deleted-user gate it fails closed, because an outage then costs one support session rather than a write in someone else's name (:35-39). A service that does not hold the grant store checks the shared-cache ViewAsEndedMarker (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsEndedMarker.cs:32) instead, written only by the end endpoint (:16-26). The controller tower grows to match. Under Controllers/Administration, AuditHistoryControllerBase (AuditHistoryControllerBase.cs:48, GET {entity}/{key} at line 93 behind AdministrationPermissions.ViewAuditTrail at line 47) and ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase (ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase.cs:40, behind ManageUsers at line 39) join the users and roles bases; MachineClientsControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:39, behind ManageClients at line 38: list, create, and rotate, promote, and revoke at lines 48, 68, 93, 115, and 140) manages service credentials that MachineTokenControllerBase (MachineTokenControllerBase.cs:40) exchanges for a token through one anonymous POST behind auth-ip (lines 45-48). Three more self-service sign-in bases follow the same app-owns-the-command pattern as the recovery bases: SignInLinkControllerBase<TSendCommand, TRedeemCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/SignInLinks/SignInLinkControllerBase.cs:35, anonymous sign-in-link and sign-in-link/redeem behind auth-ip, lines 80-83 and 108-111), PasskeysControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Passkeys/PasskeysControllerBase.cs:41, [Authorize] registration and management from line 62, anonymous signin/options and signin behind auth-ip at lines 229-232 and 254-257), and TwoFactorControllerBase<TBeginCommand, TConfirmCommand, TDisableCommand, TRegenerateCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/TwoFactor/TwoFactorControllerBase.cs:60, status, enrollment, confirmation, recovery codes, and disable at lines 92, 119, 150, 190, and 219, every action plain [Authorize] rather than a permission, :28). External sign-in now also accepts generic OIDC providers: each OidcProviderSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/OidcProviderSettings.cs:20) is read from OAuth:Oidc:<Name> (:8-10), the configured set is held by OidcProviderRegistry (OidcProviderRegistry.cs:10, registered only when at least one provider exists, :4-7), and OidcClaimNormalizer (OidcClaimNormalizer.cs:21) maps the validated ID token onto the app's claim shape, keyed by a stable oid or {iss}|{sub} and never by the mutable email (:6-18). On the outbound side, OutboundAddressPolicy (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Http/OutboundAddressPolicy.cs:11) holds an operator-supplied URL to public addresses, at validation time and again at connect time, so a stored webhook target cannot reach the host's own network (:7-9, the IPv6 allow-list at :35-38).
