Finally, the separate MMCA.Common.ServiceHost package composes all of this for an extracted service: ServiceHostBuilderExtensions's AddMmcaServiceHost (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/ServiceHostBuilderExtensions.cs:65) runs the start-up list every extracted host repeated, in the one correct order, taking vendor calls only as callbacks so the package stays cloud-neutral (:21-24, ADR-059); what differs between hosts arrives through MmcaServiceHostOptions (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/MmcaServiceHostOptions.cs:16, defaulting to an HTTP/2 cleartext endpoint at line 42 and ServiceHostAuthentication.ForwardedJwtBearer at line 52), and the returned MmcaServiceHost (MmcaServiceHost.cs:11) is what ServiceHostApplicationExtensions's UseMmcaServiceHostAsync (ServiceHostApplicationExtensions.cs:44) takes to apply the post-Build() pipeline, with the internal ServiceHostOpenApi (ServiceHostOpenApi.cs:10) and ServiceHostProfiling (ServiceHostProfiling.cs:11, the MiniProfiler step) as its helpers. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], [Rubric §11, Security], and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] again, each piece opt-in.

    Per-module controller visibility. Back on the feature-gating thread, at a coarser grain, ModuleControllerFeatureProvider (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/ModuleControllerFeatureProvider.cs:28) removes a disabled module's controllers from MVC discovery entirely, snapshotting the disabled names once (lines 36-39), returning immediately when none are disabled (lines 41-44), and matching a .{ModuleName}. token against the controller's assembly name or namespace (lines 60-81, the dots on both sides preventing a Catalogue false positive on Catalog), so a module switched off in configuration cannot have its routes mapped (they would otherwise 500, since the module's DI services were never registered). Together these are the feature-flag story extended to the HTTP edge and part of the [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] "one codebase, many deployment shapes" design.

    Well-known endpoints, database initialization, and the extraction edge. Several types here exist only so a module can be lifted out of the monolith into its own service (ADRs 004, 007, 008). JwksEndpointExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/JwksEndpointExtensions.cs:15) serves /.well-known/jwks.json (path constant at line 20, mapped at line 33) from IJwksProvider so extracted services validate tokens against the issuer's public keys instead of a shared secret, and OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions.cs:22) serves the minimal discovery document the JWT middleware fetches when AddForwardedJwtBearer sets an authority: it returns 404 when Jwt:Issuer is not configured (lines 62-66), derives jwks_uri from that configured issuer rather than from the inbound request (line 76) so issuer and JWKS URI stay origin-aligned, and disables the camelCase naming policy (line 45) because RFC 8414 field names are snake_case and jwksUri would not be recognized. AddForwardedJwtBearer itself resolves RequireHttpsMetadata in three steps, explicit argument, then the Authentication:JwtBearer:RequireHttpsMetadata key (constant at WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:25), then "true outside Development" (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:64-66); a resolved false outside Development is honored, because an internal-ingress h2c authority genuinely has no HTTPS metadata, but it is never silent: InsecureJwtMetadataWarningStartupFilter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Auth/InsecureJwtMetadataWarningStartupFilter.cs:15) is registered exactly then (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:68-72) and logs one startup warning naming the key (InsecureJwtMetadataWarningStartupFilter.cs:21 with the message at :26-28). It is an IStartupFilter rather than a log line at registration time for a reason worth remembering: while the service collection is being built the logging providers are not configured yet, so a warning written there is dropped (InsecureJwtMetadataWarningStartupFilter.cs:7-13). JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Http/JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler.cs:17) copies the caller's inbound Authorization header onto outgoing HTTP calls, unless one was already set (lines 27-30) and no-oping when there is no ambient HttpContext (lines 32-36), so distributed authorization flows through a service-to-service hop without any handler threading the token by hand: the HTTP twin of JwtForwardingClientInterceptor. DatabaseInitializationExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/DatabaseInitializationExtensions.cs:28) initializes every physical data source the host owns: InitializeDatabaseAsync (line 51) validates the strategy before touching anything (EnsureKnownStrategy, called at line 63 and declared at line 290, which accepts only Migrate or None and otherwise throws naming the valid values through UnknownStrategy at line 302), warms the IEntityDataSourceRegistry so entity-to-database routing is deterministic before the first repository call (lines 70-72), runs EnsureCreated for the migration-less Cosmos, PostgreSQL, and SQLite sources up front (lines 76-106, skipping a PostgreSQL or SQLite source that does configure a migrations assembly, because creating its tables without an __EFMigrationsHistory row leaves every migration both pending and un-appliable), then, under a raised five-minute command timeout so a replica queued behind another's EF migrations lock does not die at the 30-second default (InitializationCommandTimeout, line 37, applied at line 112 through RaiseCommandTimeouts, line 257), applies the configured strategy per migrated source (lines 118-128), where None is the production guard that throws with a per-source breakdown of pending migrations (line 124 into ThrowIfPendingMigrationsAsync at line 359; ADR-030, ADR-006), repeats the same strategy per tenant that keeps its own copy of a source, each in a fresh scope with its tenant set (line 130 into InitializeTenantDatabasesAsync at line 196, ADR-073), and finishes by running the enabled modules' seeders on the default scope only (line 137). Five smaller startup helpers round out the host: OpenApiEndpointExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/OpenApiEndpointExtensions.cs:24) maps the per-version OpenAPI document (MapCommonOpenApi, lines 34-38) and the optional Scalar reference UI (MapCommonScalarUi, lines 52-56), both outside Production only, ApiParameterDescriptorBackfillProvider (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/OpenApi/ApiParameterDescriptorBackfillProvider.cs:43) fills in the placeholder descriptor MVC leaves null on an unbound route token (lines 65-71) so a URL-segment-versioned or {tenant}-templated route cannot turn document generation into a 500, running last by ordering itself at int.MinValue (line 46) and registered exactly once through TryAddEnumerable however many helpers a host calls (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.cs:56 and :103, through the private helper at :124-126), the paired StronglyTypedIdSchemaTransformer (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/OpenApi/StronglyTypedIdSchemaTransformer.cs:24) and StronglyTypedIdParameterTransformer (same file, line 74), both registered by AddCommonOpenApi through a ConfigureAll that reaches every versioned document (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.cs:115-119) and both inert in a host that declares no wrappers: the schema half clears the object schema the default generator produces for a one-property struct and rewrites it as the wrapped primitive's type and format (:38-41, mapped at :46 and :51) so the document matches the bare-primitive wire shape, and the operation half does the same for route and query parameters, which the API explorer describes as plain strings because they bind through a TypeConverter (:74-107, ADR-115), SignalRExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/SignalRExtensions.cs:12) maps NotificationHub at its configured path when push notifications are enabled (lines 22-27), MiniProfilerExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/MiniProfilerExtensions.cs:11) registers MiniProfiler with Entity Framework profiling when ApplicationSettings.UseMiniProfiler is set (lines 16-25), and AppAssociationEndpointExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/AppAssociationEndpointExtensions.cs:15) with AppAssociationOptions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/AppAssociationOptions.cs:9) serve the Android Digital Asset Links and Apple App Site Association documents (paths at lines 18 and 24, mapped at lines 42 and 46) that let a mobile OS hand this host's https links to the installed native app (ADR-043). ExternalAuthExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:30) completes the OAuth half of authentication, staying entirely inert when no provider is configured (lines 47-52), each of Google, GitHub, and Apple gated on its OAuth:{Provider}:ClientId being present (lines 60-73) and throwing at startup when the matching client secret is missing (lines 98-100 and 110-112); Apple has no static secret, so its handler mints one (line 130) and startup throws instead on a missing TeamId, KeyId, or PrivateKeyPem (lines 131-139). Apple also never puts the user's name in its ID token: it posts it once, as the user form field of the first authorization's callback, and never again for that Apple ID, so the Apple scheme hooks OnCreatingTicket to AppleUserNameClaims (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:214-216). That internal static helper (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/AppleUserNameClaims.cs:18) reads the already buffered callback form (AddFromCallbackFormAsync, line 28, the field name held as UserFormField at line 21) and copies name.firstName and name.lastName into ClaimTypes.GivenName and ClaimTypes.Surname (AddFromUserField, line 47, the claims added at lines 75-76), leaving any claim the identity already carries untouched (line 86) and adding nothing for a missing or malformed field (lines 49-52 and 70-73), because the name is best effort and must never fail the sign-in. Without it the account is created with the "User User" placeholders and the real name cannot be recovered on a later sign-in (AppleUserNameClaims.cs:7-16). Taken together these are the [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness], [Rubric §11, Security], and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] concerns that let the same controller code run identically in a monolith and in a fleet of extracted services behind a YARP gateway.

    Where this group sits. Everything above is the outermost ring. It depends downward on the CQRS pipeline and query services (Groups 03 and 05), the auth and caching infrastructure (Groups 08 and 09), the persistence factories (Group 07), the integration-event contracts it consumes (Group 04), and the module system that discovers controllers and drives health checks (Group 14 via ModuleLoader), and it rests on the Result and domain primitives (Groups 01 and 02). Nothing inside the framework depends on it: the app hosts and the gRPC transport group (Group 13) call into it. AssemblyReference and ClassReference (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/AssemblyReference.cs:8 and :20) are the scanning anchors that let those callers point at this assembly without naming an incidental type. Read the group as the framework's HTTP grammar: the reusable edge every downstream service inherits so its own code stays modules and domain logic, never plumbing.

    AssemblyReference

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/AssemblyReference.cs:8 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: a tiny static class that exposes the MMCA.Common.API assembly handle and its simple name, so convention-based scanners have a stable, refactor-safe anchor into this layer.
    • Depends on: System.Reflection (BCL) only (AssemblyReference.cs:1).
    • Concept introduced (assembly-marker types for convention scanning). Scrutor-based DI registration and the architecture fitness rules both need a stable "anchor" type to say scan the assembly that contains this. Rather than reaching for typeof(SomeIncidentalClass).Assembly, a dedicated AssemblyReference makes the intent explicit and survives type moves. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses whether recurring structural problems are solved with named, reusable patterns; here the same two-type marker shape repeats in every layer and module assembly, which is exactly this pattern applied uniformly. [Rubric §33, Developer Experience] assesses how easy the framework is to build on; centralizing one assembly handle per package means every scan call references one obvious token.
    • Walkthrough: two public static readonly fields. Assembly (AssemblyReference.cs:11) is typeof(AssemblyReference).Assembly, resolved once at type initialization. AssemblyName (AssemblyReference.cs:14) is Assembly.GetName().Name with a ?? string.Empty fallback for logging and diagnostics.
    • Why it's built this way: a purpose-built anchor decouples scanning from any incidental type. The pattern is duplicated in every layer so each assembly is self-describing without a cross-layer reference back to a single "well-known" class.
    • Where it's used: module handler/validator/mapper scanning (see ModuleLoader) and the architecture tests' package-assembly pinning.

    ClassReference

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/AssemblyReference.cs:20 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: an empty, instantiable class in the MMCA.Common.API assembly, used where a generic constraint or a typeof(...) needs a concrete reference type from this layer rather than an Assembly instance.
    • Depends on: nothing. See AssemblyReference for the full concept; ClassReference is its type-shaped sibling.
    • Concept: covered under AssemblyReference. Where AssemblyReference.Assembly answers "which assembly", ClassReference answers "give me a class token from that assembly" for APIs whose generic parameter is constrained to a reference type (where T : class).
    • Walkthrough: the whole type is public class ClassReference; (AssemblyReference.cs:20), a body-less class declaration whose doc comment (:17-19) states the intent. It carries no members; its identity is the entire point.
    • Why it's built this way: some registration and scanning helpers take a marker type parameter instead of an Assembly; a dedicated empty class keeps those call sites from accidentally binding to a real domain or controller type.
    • Where it's used: generic registration helpers that need a per-assembly type anchor from the API layer.

    AppleUserNameClaims

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Authentication · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/AppleUserNameClaims.cs:18 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: an internal static helper that recovers the user's given name and surname during a Sign in with Apple callback and adds them to the external identity as ClaimTypes.GivenName and ClaimTypes.Surname claims.
    • Depends on: the ASP.NET Core OAuth ticket context (OAuthCreatingTicketContext), System.Security.Claims, and System.Text.Json. No first-party dependencies. It is plugged into the Apple handler by ExternalAuthExtensions (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:216).
    • Concept introduced (best-effort claim enrichment from a one-time payload). Apple's ID token never carries the user's name. Apple posts it once, as JSON in the callback form's user field, and only on the first authorization; every later sign-in sends an empty field (AppleUserNameClaims.cs:21, :45). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how external identity input is trusted; here the payload is untrusted form data, parsed defensively, and a failure never blocks sign-in.
    • Walkthrough
      • UserFormField = "user" (:21) names the form field.
      • AddFromCallbackFormAsync(OAuthCreatingTicketContext) (:28) is the OnCreatingTicket handler. It returns early when there is no identity or the request is not form-encoded (:30-33), then reads the already buffered form (:35) and delegates to AddFromUserField with the scheme's ClaimsIssuer (:36).
      • AddFromUserField(ClaimsIdentity, string?, string?) (:47) returns on a blank value, parses the JSON, requires an object with a name object, and reads firstName and lastName (:54-68). A JsonException is swallowed (:70-73): the name is best effort and the controller's placeholders apply instead.
      • AddIfMissing (:84) adds a claim only when the value is non-blank and the identity does not already carry that claim type, so an existing claim is never overwritten (:84-91); ReadString (:79) trims string values and ignores non-strings.
    • Why it's built this way: the sign-in must never fail because a cosmetic field is missing or malformed, and the one-time nature of the payload means the only chance to capture it is inside the callback, which is why it hooks OnCreatingTicket rather than the controller.
    • Where it's used: only by the Apple branch of ExternalAuthExtensions (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:216); covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Authentication/AppleUserNameClaimsTests.cs.

    OidcClaimNormalizer

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Authentication · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/OidcClaimNormalizer.cs:21 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: an internal static helper that rebuilds the principal a generic OpenID Connect handler produces from a validated ID token into the claim shape the OAuth controller already reads, so a new OIDC provider needs no app change (OidcClaimNormalizer.cs:5-8).
    • Depends on: System.Security.Claims only (OidcClaimNormalizer.cs:1). It is called from the OnTokenValidated event that ExternalAuthExtensions wires for every OIDC scheme (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:140-144).
    • Concept introduced (provider-neutral identity normalization). Each OIDC issuer names its claims a little differently, and the handler is configured to keep the raw names (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:128-130). This class maps them onto one fixed shape and drops everything else. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how external identity input is trusted; two choices here are trust decisions. The provider key is never the email, which a user or an administrator can change (OidcClaimNormalizer.cs:10-13), and email_verified passes through only when the operator configured the provider with TrustEmail and the token asserts it, so an app that links an external login to an existing account by email does so only for an issuer the operator vouched for (:14-16).
    • Walkthrough
      • EmailVerifiedClaimType = "email_verified" (OidcClaimNormalizer.cs:24) names the one non-standard claim the app reads.
      • Normalize(ClaimsPrincipal, string providerName, bool trustEmail) (:31) starts an empty claim list (:33), adds ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier from ProviderKey when one can be built (:35-39), then copies email, given name, surname, and name, each from the raw OIDC claim name with the mapped ClaimTypes name as a fallback (:41-44). It adds email_verified=true only when trustEmail is set and the token's value parses as true (:46-51). The result is a new principal whose authentication type is the provider name (:53), which the controller passes on as the login provider (:17-18).
      • ProviderKey (:56) returns {tid}|{oid} when both claims are present (:58-63); for Entra ID sub is pairwise per application while oid is the stable user id inside the tenant (:10-12). Otherwise it uses sub (or NameIdentifier) and returns null when there is none (:65-69), qualifies it with the iss claim, falling back to the subject claim's Issuer when iss was not kept and the issuer is not the default (:71-78), and returns {iss}|{sub}, or null when no issuer is known (:80).
      • First (:83-86) returns the first non-blank value across a list of claim types, and AddIfPresent (:88-94) adds a claim, issued by the provider name, only when the value is non-blank.
    • Why it's built this way: keying on {iss}|{sub} rather than the bare sub keeps two issuers from colliding on the same subject value, and building a fresh principal (rather than adding to the handler's) guarantees the controller sees only claims this class vouches for.
    • Where it's used: only by the OIDC branch of ExternalAuthExtensions (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:142). See ADR-036 for the external-login decision.

    OidcProviderSettings

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Authentication · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/OidcProviderSettings.cs:20 · Level 0 · record (internal sealed partial)

    • What it is: the validated configuration of one generic OIDC provider, a positional record of Name, Authority, ClientId, ClientSecret, Scopes, DisplayName, Domains, and TrustEmail (OidcProviderSettings.cs:20-28), plus the static reader that builds the list from configuration.
    • Depends on: IConfiguration, FrozenSet, and a source-generated Regex (OidcProviderSettings.cs:148-149). No first-party dependencies.
    • Concept introduced (fail-fast, configuration-driven provider registration). Any OIDC provider joins by adding an OAuth:Oidc:<Name> section (SectionPath, OidcProviderSettings.cs:31); no code changes. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] both apply: a misconfigured section throws an InvalidOperationException that names the offending key at startup rather than producing a half-working scheme, and a section without ClientId stays inert, the same gate the built-in providers use (:43-52).
    • Walkthrough
      • ReadAll(IConfiguration) (:53) is null-tolerant about the section (:55-56) and reads each child whose ClientId is set (:60). It tracks which provider claimed each email domain and throws when a second provider lists a domain already claimed, because each domain may map to one provider only (:58, :63-69).
      • Read (:77) takes the section key as the name. It rejects a reserved name (:82-86): google, github, and apple (the built-in providers) and complete, exchange, and discover (the controller's own literal routes, which would shadow the challenge), compared ignoring case (:35-41). It also rejects a name that fails ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}$, because the name becomes a URL path segment (:88-92, :148).
      • Authority and ClientSecret are required through Required (:94-95, :131-137). Scopes default to openid profile email when none are configured, and openid is inserted first when a configured list omits it (:33, :97-109). Domains are normalized, blanks dropped, and de-duplicated ignoring case (:111-115). DisplayName falls back to the name (:117, :126), and TrustEmail is true only when it parses as such (:118).
      • NormalizeDomain (:145-146) trims and drops a leading @; case is kept because every comparison is ordinal-ignore-case (:139-142).
    • Why it's built this way: validating eagerly at registration means an operator learns about a typo in a deployment, not at a user's first sign-in, and the reserved-name list keeps a configured provider from silently hijacking a built-in route.
    • Where it's used: read by ExternalAuthExtensions (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:58) and held by OidcProviderRegistry. See ADR-036.

    OidcProviderRegistry

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Authentication · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/OidcProviderRegistry.cs:10 · Level 1 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: an internal lookup over the configured OidcProviderSettings list (primary-constructor parameter, OidcProviderRegistry.cs:10), registered as a singleton only when at least one OIDC provider is configured (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:91-100).
    • Depends on: OidcProviderSettings for the provider list and its NormalizeDomain rule (OidcProviderRegistry.cs:34).
    • Concept introduced (home-realm discovery by email domain). A sign-in page can ask for an email address and route the user to the provider whose Domains claim that address's domain, rather than showing one button per provider. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] is relevant: both lookups return null instead of throwing, so the controller decides the response.
    • Walkthrough
      • Find(string? name) (OidcProviderRegistry.cs:15-18) returns the provider whose name equals the route segment, ignoring case, or null for a blank name or no match.
      • FindByEmail(string? email) (:26) takes the domain after the last @ and returns null for a missing @, an empty local part, or an empty domain (:28-32). It then normalizes the domain and returns the provider whose Domains contains it, exact match ignoring case (:34-37); a subdomain does not match its parent (:20-23).
    • Why it's built this way: the registry is absent in a host with no OIDC configuration, so the controller resolves it optionally and the generic routes stay inert.
    • Where it's used: OAuthControllerBase resolves it from the request services (OAuthControllerBase.cs:188) and calls Find for the generic challenge route (:160) and FindByEmail for discovery (:181).

    ExternalAuthExtensions

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Authentication · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:30 · Level 2 · class (static)

    • What it is: a static class that registers the external OAuth provider schemes (Google, GitHub, Apple), one OpenID Connect scheme per configured OAuth:Oidc:<Name> section, and the short-lived cookie scheme that carries the external principal from the provider callback to the app's OAuth controller. It is the counterpart wiring that AddCommonAuthentication (JWT-only) deliberately leaves out.
    • Depends on: the ASP.NET Core authentication, HTTP, configuration, DI, and OpenID Connect protocol surfaces (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:1-5), plus the provider handlers reached through AddGoogle, AddGitHub, AddApple, and AddOpenIdConnect (:163, :175, :190, :113). First-party, it partners with the app's OAuth controller subclassing OAuthControllerBase, whose ExtractClaims consumes the schemes registered here (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:11-12, :184), reads OidcProviderSettings, registers OidcProviderRegistry, hands each OIDC principal to OidcClaimNormalizer, and names the same signal the UI's ConfigurationOAuthUISettings uses to decide which buttons to render (:16-18).
    • Concept introduced (config-gated, additive auth registration). The single public const string ExternalLoginScheme = "ExternalLogin" (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:36) is shared with the OAuth controller so the sign-in scheme name can never drift between the two halves of the flow. The important property of this class is that it is additive and inert: AddCommonAuthentication registers only the JWT bearer scheme, so without this call the OAuth controller would Challenge and read schemes that are not in the authentication pipeline and the flow would fail at runtime (:14-16), yet a host with no OAuth configuration section keeps the JWT-only default completely untouched. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how authentication, secrets, and trust boundaries are handled; each provider is gated on its ClientId being present, a missing companion secret throws at startup (:166-168, :178-180, :199-207), and a misconfigured OIDC section fails startup naming its key (:45-47, :57-58) rather than silently half-configuring an auth scheme. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] is relevant because the opt-in posture mirrors AddPermissions (ADR-020), and the class doc says so explicitly (:17-20).
    • Walkthrough
      • The public surface is one C# extension(IServiceCollection services) block (ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:38), matching the DI convention described in the primer.
      • AddExternalAuthProviders(IConfiguration configuration) (:50) reads the OAuth section (:52), pulls Google:ClientId, GitHub:ClientId, and Apple:ClientId (:53-55), and reads every OIDC provider eagerly through OidcProviderSettings.ReadAll (:57-58). When all three client ids are empty and no OIDC provider is configured it returns the collection untouched (:62-68), which is what keeps environments without OAuth secrets (most tests, local dev) exactly as AddCommonAuthentication left them (:60-61).
      • When at least one is configured it calls services.AddAuthentication() with no argument (:72). The comment above it is the load-bearing detail (:70-71): the parameterless overload does not reset the default scheme set by AddCommonAuthentication, it just yields a builder to append schemes onto.
      • It then adds the ExternalLogin cookie (:74) and each configured built-in provider in turn, each behind its own non-empty check (:76-89). When OIDC providers exist it adds one scheme per provider and registers a singleton OidcProviderRegistry, which the controller's generic challenge route and home-realm discovery read (:91-100), before returning services for chaining (:102).
      • AddOidcProvider (:112-145) registers an OpenID Connect scheme named after the provider, using its display name (:113): authorization code flow with PKCE (:118-119), signing into ExternalLoginScheme (:120) with callback /auth/callback/<Name> (:121). The sign-out callback and remote sign-out paths are per provider, because the handler defaults are shared and two OIDC providers would otherwise claim the same path (:123-126). MapInboundClaims = false, SaveTokens = false, and GetClaimsFromUserInfoEndpoint = false (:130-132) keep raw claim names (sub, iss, tid, oid, email_verified) for the event and keep the ID token out of the cookie, since nothing downstream reads it (:128-129). The scope list is replaced by the provider's (:134-138), and OnTokenValidated swaps the principal for OidcClaimNormalizer's output (:140-144).
      • AddExternalLoginCookie (:151-160) configures the bridge cookie: name mmca_external_login (:154), HttpOnly (:155), SameSite=Lax (:158, sufficient because the OAuth round trip returns as a top-level GET navigation, which avoids the Secure plus cross-site cost that SameSite=None imposes, :156-157), and a 10-minute expiry (:159).
      • AddGoogleProvider (:162-172) and AddGitHubProvider (:174-187) each set the client id, require the matching ClientSecret or throw (:166-168, :178-180), set SignInScheme = ExternalLoginScheme, pin a fixed CallbackPath (/auth/callback/google at :170, /auth/callback/github at :182), and set SaveTokens = true. GitHub additionally requests the user:email scope (:185) because it does not return the email on the default scope and the controller's ClaimTypes.Email lookup would otherwise fail (:183-184).
      • AddAppleProvider (:189-217) is the one that differs structurally among the built-in providers. Its ClientId is the Apple Services ID, not the app bundle id (:192-194), and Apple has no static client secret at all: the handler mints a short-lived ES256 JWT from the developer's private key, so GenerateClientSecret = true (:198) and TeamId (:199), KeyId (:202), and PrivateKeyPem (:205) are each required-or-throw. The PEM is handed over as a callback returning a ReadOnlyMemory<char> (:208). Scheme, callback path (/auth/callback/apple, :211), and SaveTokens match the other two. It also wires options.Events.OnCreatingTicket = AppleUserNameClaims.AddFromCallbackFormAsync (:216), because the handler reads only the ID token, which never carries the name; Apple posts the name once, in the callback's user form field, on the first authorization (:214-215). See AppleUserNameClaims.
    • Why it's built this way: the cookie is intentionally short-lived and single-purpose. It exists only to bridge the provider callback to the controller's CompleteAsync, which signs it out the moment the local JWT pair is minted (:148-149). Splitting the OAuth scheme registration from AddCommonAuthentication keeps the JWT-only default free of provider secrets, and gating each provider independently means one provider's configuration never disturbs another's. Every provider, built-in or OIDC, signs into the same cookie, so the controller's completion path is shared. See ADR-036 for the external-login decision.
    • Where it's used: called from the host composition of a service that exposes social login; pairs with the app's OAuthController (subclass of OAuthControllerBase). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Authentication/ExternalAuthExtensionsTests.cs and ExternalAuthOidcTests.cs.

    ModuleControllerFeatureProvider

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/ModuleControllerFeatureProvider.cs:28 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: an IApplicationFeatureProvider<ControllerFeature> that removes controllers belonging to disabled modules from MVC's controller discovery, so a module turned off via configuration exposes no routes.
    • Depends on: ModulesSettings (the config-bound enabled/disabled map, ModuleControllerFeatureProvider.cs:4) and the MVC application-parts surface (IApplicationFeatureProvider<ControllerFeature>, ControllerFeature, ApplicationPart, :2-3), plus System.Reflection for the TypeInfo it inspects (:1).
    • Concept introduced (module-aware controller discovery). MVC discovers controllers by scanning referenced assemblies. When a host references a module's API assembly transitively but an operator has disabled that module (Modules:{Name}:Enabled=false), MVC would still map its controllers, and every request to them would 500 because the module's DI services were never registered (ModuleControllerFeatureProvider.cs:19-25). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether modules can be composed and decomposed cleanly; this provider is one boundary that lets a module be switched off without deleting code or breaking the host, complementing the disabled-module stub registrations in the module system. [Rubric §29, Resilience, Reliability & Business Continuity] is relevant: the enable/disable decision is enforced once at the edge rather than checked inside each controller.
    • Walkthrough: the primary-constructor parameter is ModulesSettings modulesSettings (ModuleControllerFeatureProvider.cs:28-29). PopulateFeature (:33) first snapshots the disabled module names once (:36-39) so it does not re-scan the settings dictionary per controller, returns early if none are disabled (:41-44), then materializes the matches and removes every controller matched by IsDisabledModuleController (:46-53). The private static matcher (:60) reads the controller's assembly simple name and namespace, each with a ?? string.Empty fallback (:64-65), and, for each disabled module, tests whether either contains the token .{ModuleName}. (:72). Wrapping the module name in dots is deliberate: it matches .Catalog. inside MMCA.Store.Catalog.API or its .Controllers namespace while avoiding false positives from substrings like "Catalogue" (:69-71). The comparison is OrdinalIgnoreCase on both the assembly name and the namespace (:74-75), and the loop falls through to false when nothing matches (:81).
    • Why it's built this way: matching on the dotted token handles both the MMCA.{Repo}.{Module}.API convention and the legacy {Prefix}.Modules.{Module}.* convention without maintaining a registry of controller types (:14-17). Removing controllers at feature-provider time is earlier than routing, so a disabled module is invisible rather than returning a runtime error.
    • Where it's used: registered by DependencyInjection's AddAPI(modulesSettings) via ConfigureApplicationPartManager (DependencyInjection.cs:72-73), but only when a non-null ModulesSettings is supplied (DependencyInjection.cs:70); pairs with the module system's disabled-stub registrations so cross-module interfaces stay resolvable.

    DependencyInjection

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:26 · Level 11 · class (static)

    • What it is: the primary DI entry point for the MMCA.Common.API layer. Using a C# extension(IServiceCollection services) block (DependencyInjection.cs:28) it adds six methods to IServiceCollection: AddAPI, AddErrorLocalization, AddErrorResources<TResource>, AddCommonExceptionHandlers, AddServerAuthSessionCookie, and AddModuleHealthChecks.
    • Depends on: a broad slice of the API layer plus feature management and localization (DependencyInjection.cs:1-19). Notable first-party types wired here: the Shared-layer EnumerationJsonConverterFactory (aliased, :19, because the Shared and API namespaces both surface converters), and StronglyTypedIdJsonConverterFactory (ADR-115 strongly typed identifiers, serializing wrapper types as their bare primitive), UnhandledResultFailureFilter, OversizeFormResourceFilter (from MMCA.Common.API.Uploads, :15), IdempotencyFilter and IdempotencySettings, OwnerOrAdminFilter and its OwnerOrAdminFilterOptions, ModuleControllerFeatureProvider, CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor and DisabledFeatureHandler, IErrorLocalizer/ErrorLocalizer, ErrorResources/ErrorResourceSource, the exception handlers (OperationCanceledExceptionHandler, DomainExceptionHandler, DbUpdateExceptionHandler, ValidationExceptionHandler, GlobalExceptionHandler), CookieTokenReader and ICookieSessionRefresher/CookieSessionRefresher, the session-cookie options and store (SessionCookieSettings, ISessionCookieStore/SessionCookieStore, from MMCA.Common.API.SessionCookies, :14), and ModuleLoader/ModulesSettings. Externals: Microsoft.FeatureManagement (including its IDisabledFeaturesHandler contract), Microsoft.Extensions.Localization, ASP.NET Core MVC/ProblemDetails/HealthChecks.
    • Concept introduced (layered DI wiring at the API edge). [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses whether each layer registers only its own concerns; this class wires controllers, JSON/XML formatters, filters, feature management, exception handlers, and health checks, all API-layer edges, and reaches down to Application only for ModulesSettings/ModuleLoader (:16-17). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] and [Rubric §17, DevOps] both apply through AddModuleHealthChecks (:220), which projects module state into /health checks tagged module so /health?tag=module reports each module's status (:212-213). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] is relevant: every parameter is optional and defaulted so a host wires only what it needs.
    • Walkthrough
      • AddAPI(ModulesSettings? modulesSettings = null, IConfiguration? configuration = null) (DependencyInjection.cs:45) registers controllers with ReturnHttpNotAcceptable = false, the UnhandledResultFailureFilter global filter, and the OversizeFormResourceFilter at its own FilterOrder, so an oversize form body answers 413 rather than model binding's 400 (:47-54). It adds two JSON converters (:55-67) and the XML DataContract formatters (:68); Currency is not among them because it carries its own converter in Shared (:30-31). The first converter is the load-bearing one for enumerations: concrete enumerations do not inherit the base class's [JsonConverter] attribute because System.Text.Json resolves it with inherit: false, so the factory is registered once here and every Enumeration<T> serializes by Name across the whole API surface (:57-60). The second, StronglyTypedIdJsonConverterFactory (:62-66), does the same job for ADR-115 strongly typed identifiers, so wrapper types serialize as the bare primitive they wrap without the attribute being repeated on every wrapper a consumer declares; in a host that declares no wrappers the factory converts nothing. It then conditionally registers ModuleControllerFeatureProvider when modulesSettings is non-null (:70-74), conditionally binds IdempotencySettings from the config section with data-annotation validation on start (:76-82), and registers the scoped IdempotencyFilter and OwnerOrAdminFilter (:87-88). Scoped is driven by OwnerOrAdminFilter, which takes the scoped ICurrentUserService; IdempotencyFilter takes only a logger and reads the singleton ICacheService from the request's services (:84-86). Right after that it binds OwnerOrAdminFilterOptions with data-annotation validation but deliberately not ValidateOnStart (:90-95): BypassRole is required with no default, the framework knows no role names, so validating at startup would fail every host that never applies the filter; validating on first resolve puts the message in front of the host that actually uses it. Feature management comes next (:97-110) and is worth reading closely: AddHttpContextAccessor() is called first because it is TryAdd-based and therefore safe to repeat, then AddFeatureManagement().WithTargeting<CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor>() registers the feature manager plus the built-in Percentage/TimeWindow/Targeting filters and supplies the targeting audience from the current request's principal, which is what makes a percentage rollout sticky per user instead of random per request; the accessor is a singleton, which is exactly why it reads IHttpContextAccessor rather than the scoped ICurrentUserService. Finally the singleton DisabledFeatureHandler is bound to IDisabledFeaturesHandler (:110) and AddErrorLocalization() is called (:113).
      • AddErrorLocalization() (:125) registers ASP.NET localization (:127), the singleton IErrorLocalizer via TryAddSingleton so a host can substitute its own (:128), and the framework's own ErrorResources source (:129-133). The framework source is registered inline as an ErrorResourceSource with IsFramework = true (:132) rather than through AddErrorResources<ErrorResources>(), so the localizer can consult it last: a module's entry for a code wins over the framework's (:121-122). AddErrorResources<TResource>() (:144) adds a module's resource anchor as another ErrorResourceSource built from an IStringLocalizerFactory (:146-147). This is the ADR-027 edge error-localization extension point, keyed by Error.Code, and modules add their translations additively (:119-122).
      • AddCommonExceptionHandlers() (:157) registers ProblemDetails (adding a requestId extension from TraceIdentifier, :159-161) then five IExceptionHandlers in specificity order (:162-166): OperationCanceled, DomainException, DbUpdate, Validation, and GlobalExceptionHandler as the catch-all. ASP.NET Core invokes them in registration order and stops at the first that handles the exception, hence most-specific first and the 500 fallback last (:153-154).
      • AddServerAuthSessionCookie(string apiBaseAddress) (:182) wires the SSR-prerender auth path: it guards the address (:184), then adds HttpContextAccessor, memory cache, the scoped CookieTokenReader (:186-188), a named HttpClient pointed at the internal API base address (:190-191), and the CookieSessionRefresher as a singleton (:194). The singleton is load-bearing: its in-flight map must be shared across requests for single-flight refresh to work (:193). It then registers the SessionCookieSettings options with no configuration binding, so SameSite and the claims-only browser token keep their default behavior unless the same-origin API proxy in MMCA.Common.UI.Web tightens them on opt-in (ADR-131), and the singleton ISessionCookieStore/SessionCookieStore via TryAddSingleton (:196-199). Last it registers TimeProvider.System via TryAddSingleton (:201-204): the refresher judges access-token expiry against the injected clock, and a Blazor Web host that calls only this method has no AddServices registration to supply one, while TryAdd never displaces a clock the host registered itself. The doc comment is explicit that the address is the internal endpoint, not the browser-facing one (:178-179).
      • AddModuleHealthChecks(ModuleLoader moduleLoader) (:220) adds one health check per module, Healthy for each enabled module (:224-230) and Degraded for each disabled one (:232-239), named module-{Name} and tagged module. It must run after ModuleLoader's DiscoverAndRegister (:216-217).
    • Why it's built this way: bundling the API-edge concerns behind small, defaulted extension methods lets each host opt into exactly the surface it needs (a JWT-only test host skips AddServerAuthSessionCookie; a monolith with no disabled modules passes a null modulesSettings; a host with no idempotency configuration passes a null configuration and keeps the defaults). The exception-handler ordering, the oversize-form filter's 413, the enumeration and strongly-typed-id converter factories, the OwnerOrAdminFilterOptions validate-on-resolve (not on-start) choice, the targeting accessor's singleton lifetime, the refresher's singleton lifetime, and the TryAdd fallback clock for hosts that call only AddServerAuthSessionCookie are the non-obvious, correctness-critical choices, and each carries an inline comment. Error localization is registered automatically by AddAPI so modules only add their own resources additively (ADR-027).
    • Where it's used: called from every service host's composition (Program.cs of the ADC/Store/Helpdesk API hosts and the integration-test hosts) to wire the shared API layer; AddApplicationDecorators() still runs last in the overall sequence (see MMCA.Common/CLAUDE.md DI ordering note).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the relative ordering of AddAPI against AddInfrastructure/AddApplication in a given host is not fixed by this file; only AddApplicationDecorators() last is load-bearing.

    ApiVersionReportingResultFilter

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/ApiVersionReportingResultFilter.cs:21 · Level 0 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: an MVC IResultFilter that writes the api-version report headers (api-supported-versions, api-deprecated-versions) before a result writes its body, so the output cache stores them with the entry (ApiVersionReportingResultFilter.cs:8-12).
    • Depends on: Asp.Versioning (IReportApiVersions, ApiVersionMetadata), Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http, and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters (ApiVersionReportingResultFilter.cs:1-4). No first-party dependencies.
    • Concept introduced (report before the body so the cache snapshot sees it). The versioning library reports from a Response.OnStarting callback, but the output cache snapshots response headers when the body starts, before those callbacks run, so a cache hit replayed the stored headers without the version report (:14-17). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether the contract a client observes is stable; this filter keeps the version headers present on cached and uncached responses alike. Versioning itself is the decision recorded in ADR-046, and the cache that makes the ordering matter is the one configured by OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.
    • Walkthrough: OnResultExecuting (:28-44) returns early if the response has already started (:31-34). Otherwise it reads ApiVersionMetadata from the matched endpoint (:36) and the host's IReportApiVersions from RequestServices (:37); if either is missing it returns (:38-41), else it calls reporter.Report(response, metadata.Map(reporter.Mapping)) (:43). OnResultExecuted is an empty body (:47-49).
    • Why it's built this way: reporting ahead of the body puts the headers in the cache snapshot, and the library's own OnStarting callback then finds them present and adds nothing (:17-18). Resolving IReportApiVersions from DI, rather than writing the headers directly, means a host with ReportApiVersions off still reports nothing (:18-19).
    • Where it's used: added to the global MVC filter collection by WebApplicationBuilderExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.cs:60), right after AddApiParameterDescriptorBackfill() in the versioning setup. See WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.

    ConcurrencyConflictMetrics

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Concurrency · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Concurrency/ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:24 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the OpenTelemetry counter for optimistic-concurrency conflicts: how often a save lost to a moved row version and the request was answered with a conflict, tagged by the entity type that conflicted (ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:6-11).
    • Depends on: System.Diagnostics.Metrics (Meter, Counter<long>) and Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore for DbUpdateConcurrencyException (ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:1-2). No first-party dependencies. Its two recording sites are SupportsIfMatchAttribute and DbUpdateExceptionHandler.
    • Concept: the same "meter a mechanism an operator cannot otherwise see" idea introduced at IdempotencyMetrics and applied to cache eviction at OutputCacheMetrics, here applied to optimistic concurrency (ADR-035). A conflict is a correct outcome for the request that lost, so nothing fails visibly; the counter is what shows contention. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether such a signal is exported. The type doc settles two points worth carrying (:12-23).
      • Counted once, at the two places a conflict becomes a response (:14-17): SupportsIfMatchAttribute answers 412 under an explicit If-Match and marks the exception handled, and DbUpdateExceptionHandler answers 409 for every other endpoint. A given exception reaches exactly one of the two, so each conflict is counted once.
      • No alert ships on it (:20-21): a sustained rate on one entity type points at contended rows (two editors, or a background writer racing user edits), which is a design question rather than an incident.
    • Walkthrough
      • MeterName = "MMCA.Common.Persistence" (:27) and a single static Meter built from it (:35). UnknownEntityType = "unknown" (:30) is the tag value when the exception names no entry; the tag name itself, entity_type, is private (:33).
      • ConflictCounter (:37-40) is a Counter<long> named persistence.concurrency.conflict with unit {conflict}.
      • RecordConflict(DbUpdateConcurrencyException) (:46-47) adds one, tagged with EntityTypeName(exception).
      • EntityTypeName (:55-56) returns UnknownEntityType when exception.Entries is empty, otherwise the CLR name of the first entry's type read from the EF model (Entries[0].Metadata.ClrType.Name), so a lazy-loading proxy reports its entity rather than the generated subclass (:49-52). The tag is bounded by the host's entity vocabulary.
    • Why it's built this way: internal static keeps the instrument out of the package's public surface while the filter and the handler in the same assembly record it. As with OutputCacheMetrics, the meter name is duplicated as a literal in MMCA.Common.Aspire because that package has no reference to MMCA.Common.API, and a host exports the counter by registering the meter, which the Aspire service defaults do (:8-10).
    • Where it's used: twice. SupportsIfMatchAttribute records before replacing the exception with a 412 (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Concurrency/SupportsIfMatchAttribute.cs:186), and DbUpdateExceptionHandler records only for the DbUpdateConcurrencyException kind, leaving unique-key and foreign-key failures uncounted so they do not hide the contention signal (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:34-39).

    EvictOutputCacheAttribute

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/EvictOutputCacheAttribute.cs:36 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: an attribute that is also an MVC result filter. Placed on a write action or on a whole controller, it evicts the output-cache tags it names after the write succeeds, instead of a hand-written eviction call before every return (EvictOutputCacheAttribute.cs:11-14).
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters.IAsyncResultFilter, IStatusCodeActionResult for the result's own status, IOutputCacheStore, and ILogger with a NullLogger fallback (EvictOutputCacheAttribute.cs:1-7). The eviction itself is the best-effort TryEvictTagsAsync verb of OutputCacheEvictionExtensions (:114).
    • Concept introduced (declarative, outcome-aware cache eviction). A public read cached by PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy stays stale until a write drops its tag, so every successful mutation has to evict. Doing that by hand means one eviction call per success branch, and a branch that forgets it serves stale data for a full TTL. The class doc settles three decisions (:15-34).
      • When it evicts (:16-22): as a result filter it runs after the action filters, so it sees the final outcome, after SupportsIfMatchAttribute rewrote a conflict to 412 and after an idempotent replay was produced. A 2xx result evicts every tag BEFORE the response body is written; a non-2xx result, a GET or HEAD, and an unhandled action exception (which skips result filters) evict nothing.
      • Best effort (:23-28): the write has already committed, so a cache-store fault is a Warning, never a failed request, and a host with no IOutputCacheStore registered evicts nothing. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether a post-commit follow-up degrades gracefully; this is the contract ADR-096 states.
      • Once per request (:29-33): tags already evicted are recorded in HttpContext.Items, so a class-level and a method-level instance naming the same tag evict it once. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether a hot path avoids redundant round trips; the dedupe keeps a stacked declaration from doubling store calls. The caching model this serves is ADR-040.
    • Walkthrough
      • [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class | AttributeTargets.Method, AllowMultiple = true, Inherited = true)] (:35). EvictedTagsItemKey (:42) is the HttpContext.Items slot holding the per-request set of evicted tags.
      • The constructor takes params string[] tags (:52), throws ArgumentNullException on null (:54), ArgumentException when the array is empty (:56-57) or a tag is null, empty or whitespace (:59-60), and copies the array (:62). Tags (:66) exposes them read-only, in order.
      • OnResultExecutionAsync (:75) null-guards both arguments, evicts when ShouldEvict says so (:80-83), then always awaits next() (:85), so the eviction lands before the body is written.
      • ShouldEvict (:89) returns false for GET and HEAD (:92-93), then reads the status from the result's own IStatusCodeActionResult.StatusCode, falling back to the response status (:95), and accepts 200 through 299 (:96).
      • EvictAsync (:100) filters the tags through the request's evicted set, keeping only those HashSet.Add accepts (:102-103), returns when none are pending, returns when no IOutputCacheStore resolves (:107-109), resolves ILogger<EvictOutputCacheAttribute> or the null logger (:111-112), and calls store.TryEvictTagsAsync(logger, pending) (:114).
      • EvictedTagsOf (:118) returns the set already stored under EvictedTagsItemKey (:120-121) or creates an ordinal HashSet<string> and stores it (:123-125).
    • Why it's built this way: a result filter, not an action filter, is the one place that sees the status after every action-level rewrite and still runs before the body, which is what lets a 412 from the conditional-write filter evict nothing. Resolving the store and the logger from RequestServices instead of taking them by constructor keeps the attribute usable as a plain attribute with no DI registration.
    • Where it's used: the generic write base relies on it: CrudEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest, TUpdateRequest> documents that a derived controller declares its tags with this attribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/CrudEntityControllerBase.cs:42). ADC's Conference controllers carry it at class level, for example ActivitiesController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Activities/ActivitiesController.cs:42) and SessionAssetsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/SessionAssets/SessionAssetsController.cs:62), and at method level with several tags, for example EventsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventsController.cs:195) and the lifecycle transitions of EventLifecycleController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventLifecycleController.cs:61). Framework coverage is EvictOutputCacheAttributeTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Caching/EvictOutputCacheAttributeTests.cs), and consumers assert their declarations through EvictOutputCacheAssertions in the testing package (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/EvictOutputCacheAssertions.cs).

    OutputCacheMetrics

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheMetrics.cs:16 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the OpenTelemetry instrument set for the output-cache eviction consumer. Today it is exactly one counter, cache.eviction.failed, plus the helper that records it.
    • Depends on: System.Diagnostics.Metrics (Meter, Counter<long>, OutputCacheMetrics.cs:1) only. Its single recording site is OutputCacheEvictionHandler.
    • Concept: the same "meter a degradable mechanism" idea introduced at IdempotencyMetrics, applied to a different failure. Cross-service cache eviction (OutputCacheEvictionHandler) is deliberately best-effort: an eviction that throws is logged and swallowed rather than rethrown, because rethrowing would redeliver the message and eventually dead-letter it. The consequence is that a failing eviction is invisible from the outside, since every request still succeeds and the stale entry simply serves until its TTL. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether an operator can see that: the counter doc names itself the alert target for cross-service cache coherence, because a non-zero rate means this host is serving output-cached responses it was told to drop (OutputCacheMetrics.cs:23-27). It also records the cardinality argument, which is the discipline that keeps a tagged counter affordable: the cache_tag tag is bounded by the host's own tag vocabulary, a small fixed set declared in its output-cache policies.
    • Walkthrough
      • MeterName = "MMCA.Common.OutputCache" (OutputCacheMetrics.cs:19) and a single static Meter built from it (:21). The type doc carries a warning worth reading once and remembering (:10-14): never create a second Meter with this name, because a duplicate instance publishes a parallel set of instruments under the same meter name and a listener enabling one of them silently misses measurements recorded on the other.
      • EvictionFailed (:29-32) is a Counter<long> named cache.eviction.failed with unit {tag}.
      • RecordEvictionFailure(string cacheTag) (:36-37) adds one with a cache_tag tag, so the instrument name and the tag name are spelled in exactly one place.
    • Why it's built this way: internal static keeps the instruments out of the package's public surface while the handler in the same assembly records them. As with IdempotencyMetrics, the meter name is duplicated as a literal in MMCA.Common.Aspire because that package has no reference to MMCA.Common.API (:8-9), and a host exports the instruments by registering the meter, which the Aspire service defaults (ConfigureOpenTelemetry) already do (:6-8).
    • Where it's used: exactly once, in OutputCacheEvictionHandler's catch block (OutputCacheEvictionHandler.cs:61), paired with a Warning log naming the same tag.

    PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy.cs:47 · Level 2 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: a custom ASP.NET Core IOutputCachePolicy for public, user-independent GET/HEAD endpoints that must stay cacheable even when the request carries an Authorization header. It replaces the built-in default policy, which refuses to serve or store a cached response for any authenticated request.
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.OutputCaching (IOutputCachePolicy, OutputCacheContext) and Microsoft.Extensions.Primitives (StringValues) (PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy.cs:1-8), plus three first-party types resolved or called per request: ITenantContext for the tenant-vary key, and IPermissionRegistry with PermissionAuthorizationHandler for the permission bypass. It is registered by OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.
    • Concept introduced (auth-header-tolerant output caching). The framework UI attaches a Bearer token to every outgoing API request, including reads of [AllowAnonymous] endpoints whose payload is identical for every caller. Under the default policy those reads bypass the output cache for any signed-in user and land on the database each time (PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy.cs:16-21). [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether hot read paths avoid redundant work; this policy is a direct performance lever, letting public reads share one cached entry across authenticated and anonymous callers. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses trust boundaries; the class docs are explicit that a cached response is served verbatim to every subsequent caller, so it must be applied only to identity-independent payloads, and the bypassRoles mechanism exists precisely so a privileged role that receives an elevated payload (for example administrators seeing unpublished rows) is never served or stored from the shared cache, and bypassPermissions does the same when the elevated payload is gated by a permission rather than a fixed role, so any caller holding it by claim, by role or by stored grant skips the cache too (:29-39). A second SECURITY remark covers multi-tenancy (:40-45): the tenant-vary rule below is a backstop, not a license, an endpoint whose payload depends on the caller (rather than only on the tenant) still must not use this policy. This is the edge tier of the two-tier caching model (ADR-026); the authenticated-read decision itself is ADR-040.
    • Walkthrough: a TenantVaryByKey = "t" constant (:53) mirrors the t:{tenantId} prefix the caching CQRS decorators use, and four instance fields hold the rest of the config, _expiration, _bypassRoles, _bypassPermissions, _tags (:55-58). Three constructors chain to the last: the params string[] tags overload passes empty bypass-roles and bypass-permissions arrays (:63-64), the (expiration, bypassRoles, tags) overload passes an empty bypass-permissions array (:73-74), and the full (expiration, bypassRoles, bypassPermissions, tags) constructor (:92) guards its inputs (ThrowIfLessThanOrEqual(expiration, TimeSpan.Zero) and null checks on all three arrays, :94-97). All three interface methods are explicitly implemented, so they are reachable only through IOutputCachePolicy. CacheRequestAsync (:106) computes attemptOutputCaching as "is a GET/HEAD request" AND "is not a bypassed caller" (:112-113), enables output caching, sets AllowCacheLookup/AllowCacheStorage to that flag, deliberately turns request coalescing off with AllowLocking = false (:122), sets the expiration (:123), and (matching the built-in default) varies the cache key by every query-string parameter via CacheVaryByRules.QueryKeys = "*" (:127). Locking is off because with it on, concurrent misses for one key wait on the first request's execution, which runs under that request's RequestAborted token: one client disconnecting would cancel the shared query and every waiter would answer 500 with a TaskCanceledException; the cost is that simultaneous misses each run the query once (:118-121). It then resolves the tenant from context.HttpContext.RequestServices and, when one is present, stamps it into CacheVaryByRules.VaryByValues[TenantVaryByKey] (:133-137), an unresolved tenant, single-tenant host or background call, adds nothing; then copies the eviction tags in (:139-140). ServeFromCacheAsync (:146) is a no-op returning ValueTask.CompletedTask. ServeResponseAsync (:150) refuses to store any response that set a cookie or returned a non-200 status (:156-160), the same guard the built-in default applies. Two private helpers close it out. IsCacheableRequest (:165-166) accepts GET or HEAD. IsBypassedCaller(HttpContext) (:172) first returns true when Array.Exists(_bypassRoles, user.HasRole) (:175), returns false when no bypass permissions are configured (:180-183), and otherwise resolves the optional IPermissionRegistry from RequestServices (:187) and asks PermissionAuthorizationHandler.Holds(user, registry, permission) for each bypass permission (:188), the same evaluation the permission handler grants the elevated payload by (:185-186). HasRole is deliberate, not ClaimsPrincipal.IsInRole: IsInRole only matches the identity's own role claim type, so against a provider that emits bare role/roles claims the permission handler would grant the elevated payload while this bypass check missed it, and that response would be stored under the shared public key (:168-171).
    • Why it's built this way: it mirrors the built-in default policy minus exactly one behavior, the authenticated-request bail-out, so its caching, query-key variance, and cookie/status guards stay identical to what developers already expect. Bypass roles and bypass permissions get the default behavior back (no lookup, no storage), which keeps elevated payloads out of the shared cache without disabling caching for everyone. Evaluating a bypass permission through the permission handler's own Holds, rather than a second claim check, means a role granted the permission later (including a stored grant) is bypassed too, so the cache can never answer a caller the endpoint would have given the elevated payload. Stamping the resolved tenant into the vary key means a multi-tenant host's shared cache entry per path+query never crosses tenants, since the same path and query mean different rows per tenant (:129-132). A raw IOutputCachePolicy implementation inherits none of the default policy's behavior, so every guard is re-implemented here.
    • Where it's used: registered as a named policy by OutputCacheOptionsExtensions and referenced from controller actions via [OutputCache(PolicyName = ...)] or, for the base reads of an entity controller, through PublicCachedReadsAttribute. Store's Catalog service registers three such policies with no bypass roles, the products one at 60 seconds because an effective price moves on the clock (MMCA.Store/Source/Services/MMCA.Store.Catalog.Service/Program.cs:59-69); ADC's Conference service registers eleven, most of them with an admin bypass-roles array (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:174-216), including two short 60-second policies, NowNextPolicy (:202) and BookmarkCountsPolicy (:216). Its sessions policy is the one that constructs the policy directly with a bypass permission, ConferencePermissions.SessionAssetsManage, because SessionAssetsController's read answers a holder of that permission with materials the public cannot see (:181-192). Framework coverage is PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicyTests and PublicEndpointOutputCachePermissionBypassTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Caching/). The tags passed here are the same strings OutputCacheEvictionHandler evicts by.

    OutputCacheOptionsExtensions

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.cs:6 · Level 2 · class (static)

    • What it is: registration helpers that add named output-cache policies backed by PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy onto ASP.NET Core's OutputCacheOptions.
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.OutputCaching (OutputCacheOptions, OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.cs:1) and PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy.
    • Concept: this is a thin fluent facade over OutputCacheOptions.AddPolicy, using a C# extension(OutputCacheOptions options) block (OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.cs:8) so the policy registration reads as a first-class option on the options object. See the DI registration extension(T) convention. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] is relevant: the helper gives callers a self-documenting, named entry point instead of hand-constructing the policy at each call site.
    • Walkthrough: two overloads of AddPublicEndpointPolicy. The first (OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.cs:20-21) takes name, expiration, and params string[] tags and registers new PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy(expiration, tags). The second (:34-35) adds a string[] bypassRoles parameter before the params string[] tags and forwards to the three-argument policy constructor, for endpoints whose payload is identical for every caller except one privileged role. Both are expression-bodied and return void, mutating the options in place.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the policy construction behind a named helper means the "apply only to [AllowAnonymous], identity-independent endpoints" guidance travels with the API surface (see the doc comments at :10-16 and :23-29) instead of being re-derived at each registration.
    • Where it's used: called during host composition where the app configures AddOutputCache(...); the registered name is then referenced by [OutputCache(PolicyName = ...)] on controller actions. Store's Catalog service uses the two-argument form (MMCA.Store/Source/Services/MMCA.Store.Catalog.Service/Program.cs:59-69); ADC's Conference service mostly uses the bypass-roles form (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:276-307).

    OutputCacheEvictionHandler

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheEvictionHandler.cs:32 · Level 4 · class (sealed, partial)

    • What it is: the integration-event handler that drops named tags from this host's output cache when another service says the underlying data changed. It is the consumer half of cross-service output-cache coherence.
    • Depends on: IIntegrationEventHandler<in TIntegrationEvent> closed over OutputCacheEvictionRequested (OutputCacheEvictionHandler.cs:35), ASP.NET Core's IOutputCacheStore, ILogger, and OutputCacheMetrics for the failure counter (:1-4).
    • Concept introduced (cache coherence across a service boundary, as a best-effort hint). PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy makes a public read cheap by caching it for minutes at a time. The cost of that is staleness when the data changes, and in a multi-service topology the change usually happens somewhere else: a write in one service invalidates a cached read in another. The framework's answer is an ordinary integration event, so nothing about this handler is broker-specific. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses whether cross-service reactions travel as events rather than as direct calls; the class doc is explicit that no broker type appears here, so the handler is equally reachable from the in-process dispatcher (:8-16). Two failure decisions carry the design.
      • Per-tag best effort (:18-24): each tag is evicted independently and a failure is logged and counted rather than rethrown. Rethrowing would hand the message back to the retry policy and redeliver it, re-evicting every tag that already succeeded, and would eventually dead-letter a message whose only consequence is a cache entry that expires on its own TTL anyway. The doc gives the one-line principle worth remembering: a failed eviction is a staleness window, not a lost fact. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether degraded dependencies degrade the system gracefully instead of failing it; this is the contract ADR-096 generalizes.
      • Cancellation is not swallowed (:25-28): an OperationCanceledException from host shutdown propagates, so the broker receive pipeline sees the shutdown rather than a completed message. This is the same when (ex is not OperationCanceledException) discipline used across the framework's cache-touching code.
    • Walkthrough: the primary constructor takes IOutputCacheStore outputCacheStore and ILogger<OutputCacheEvictionHandler> logger (:32-34). HandleAsync(OutputCacheEvictionRequested integrationEvent, CancellationToken) (:38) null-guards the event (:42), then loops the tags (:44), skipping blank entries (:46-49). Each tag goes through outputCacheStore.EvictByTagAsync(tag, cancellationToken) inside its own try (:51-53) followed by a Debug log (:54). The catch (:56-63) is deliberately broad, filtered only by when (ex is not OperationCanceledException); its comment notes that CA1031 stays at error but does not flag a filtered catch, and S2221 is a suggestion, because an eviction store that throws must not turn a coherence hint into a dead-lettered message (:58-60). It records the failure on OutputCacheMetrics (:61) and logs a Warning naming the tag and stating that responses carrying it stay cached until their own TTL expires (:62, template at :72-75).
    • Why it's built this way: partial plus two [LoggerMessage] declarations (:67-75) gives source-generated, allocation-free logging at Debug for the success path and Warning for the failure path. Keeping the handler free of any broker type is what lets the same class serve both the in-process dispatcher and the broker consumer, which is the extraction property the module system is built around (ADR-007, ADR-008).
    • Where it's used: registered by OutputCacheEvictionExtensions.AddOutputCacheEvictionHandler(). The broker half is RegisterOutputCacheEvictionConsumer() inside the host's AddBrokerMessaging configuration, which wires the generic IntegrationEventConsumer<OutputCacheEvictionRequested> onto this handler; ADC's Conference service calls both (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:280 and MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/ConferenceBrokerConsumers.cs:31); on the far side, ADC's Engagement bookmark path names this handler as the receiver of the OutputCacheEvictionRequested it causes to be published (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application/UserSessionBookmarks/DomainEventHandlers/UserSessionBookmarkCacheEvictionHandler.cs). The tags it evicts are the ones passed to OutputCacheOptionsExtensions.AddPublicEndpointPolicy. Framework coverage is OutputCacheEvictionHandlerTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Caching/OutputCacheEvictionHandlerTests.cs).

    SupportsIfMatchAttribute

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Concurrency · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Concurrency/SupportsIfMatchAttribute.cs:58 · Level 4 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: an attribute that is also an action filter and an application-model convention. It makes a write action conditional: the optimistic-concurrency token comes from the HTTP If-Match header, the header is mandatory, and a conflict outcome is answered with 412 Precondition Failed rather than 409 Conflict. As a convention it also documents those answers in the API description.
    • Depends on: ConcurrencyETag (the header name, the wildcard, and the tag decoder), Error, ErrorHttpMapping and IErrorLocalizer for the problem body, ConcurrencyConflictMetrics for the conflict counter, plus Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters.IAsyncActionFilter, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ApplicationModels (IActionModelConvention, IControllerModelConvention), IApiResponseMetadataProvider, ProblemDetailsFactory, and Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbUpdateConcurrencyException (SupportsIfMatchAttribute.cs:1-12).
    • Concept introduced (conditional writes, and why two conflict statuses are not one). The type doc (:16-56) is the whole design, in five decisions.
      • The token never touches the request model (:22-27, :60-65): the filter decodes the header and puts the bytes in HttpContext.Items under TokenItemKey, and the action reads them from there. A request body therefore never carries a concurrency token, and no request record has to loosen its immutability to receive one.
      • The header is required (:28-34). A guarded mutation without a usable token would be a last-write-wins write, so a request that states no precondition is refused with 428 Precondition Required and the action never runs. A malformed tag is a 400 Bad Request, because the server cannot tell what the caller meant. * counts as no precondition, since it names no particular version.
      • Why 412 and not 409 (:33-41): RFC 9110 reserves 412 for a precondition the client stated in a conditional request header, which is precisely what If-Match is, while 409 stays the answer for a conflict the client did not condition on. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether status codes carry their standard meaning rather than a local one. The doc also names the consequence worth carrying, because the rewrite keys on the outcome rather than on an error code: an endpoint whose 409 means something else (a duplicate key, say) reports that conflict as 412, with the original problem details, error codes included, intact.
      • The attribute IS the filter (:44-48): unlike IdempotentAttribute this needs no scoped service, so it implements IAsyncActionFilter directly and requires no DI registration by the host.
      • The attribute owns its response metadata (:49-55): as an action or controller model convention it appends Problem Details 412 and 428 response types after the action's own, each only when neither the action nor its controller already declares that status. Apply(ActionModel) (:96) collects the declared statuses from every IApiResponseMetadataProvider filter on the action and its controller (:100-104) and adds a ProducesResponseTypeAttribute(typeof(ProblemDetails), status) for each missing one of PreconditionStatusCodes (:69-70, :106-109); Apply(ControllerModel) (:117) runs that for every action of a controller carrying the attribute at class level (:121-124). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] again: the published contract states the answers the filter can produce without each action repeating them.
    • Walkthrough
      • [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method | AttributeTargets.Class)] (:48); TokenItemKey (:57) is the HttpContext.Items slot. RequiredToken(HttpContext) (:68-76) is the action-side accessor: it returns the decoded byte[], or throws InvalidOperationException naming the attribute when the slot is empty. That is deliberate (:64-67): reaching the action with no token means the attribute is missing, which is a wiring mistake rather than a client error.
      • OnActionExecutionAsync (:79) guards its arguments (:81-82), calls TryApplyIfMatch (:84), and returns without running the action when it is false (:84-88), because the 428 or the 400 is already on the context. Otherwise it awaits next() (:90) and passes the outcome to the rewrite (:92).
      • TryApplyIfMatch (:104) reads the header (:106-107), then refuses with PreconditionRequiredResult when the value is blank or is the wildcard (:109-114), refuses with MalformedIfMatchResult when ConcurrencyETag.TryParse cannot decode it (:116-120), and otherwise stores the bytes in HttpContext.Items and returns true (:122-123).
      • RewriteConflictToPreconditionFailed (:130) handles two shapes. A DbUpdateConcurrencyException is first recorded on ConcurrencyConflictMetrics (:137), then replaced with the 412 result and marked ExceptionHandled = true (:132-141).
