Marking it handled is what stops DbUpdateExceptionHandler from mapping it to a 409 like any other DbUpdateException, and it is also why the conflict is counted here: the global handler never sees it (:134-136). An ObjectResult already carrying 409 has both its own StatusCode and its ProblemDetails.Status moved to 412, leaving the body otherwise intact (:145-152); a bare StatusCodeResult 409 is swapped for a 412 (:154-156); anything else falls through untouched (:158-159).
      • The three responses are built by one private helper, Problem (:206-222), which asks the registered ProblemDetailsFactory for the body so the response carries the same diagnostic extensions (traceId) as the rest of the API, falls back to a hand-built ProblemDetails when no factory is registered, and attaches the framework's standard errors extension through ErrorHttpMapping.BuildErrorsExtension with the optional IErrorLocalizer (:218-219). The three call sites differ only in status, title, detail and error: 428 Concurrency.PreconditionRequired (:164-173), 400 Concurrency.MalformedIfMatch (:176-185), and 412 Concurrency.PreconditionFailed (:188-197), each detail line showing a sample tag or telling the caller to re-read and retry.
    • Why it's built this way: making the attribute its own filter keeps adoption to a single line on an action with no host wiring, which matters for a framework whose consumers upgrade in lockstep (ADR-035). Routing the token through HttpContext.Items instead of through the bound model is what removed reflection from the request path entirely: there is no per-type property lookup, and request records stay init-only as the immutability fitness rules require.
    • Where it's used: applied across all three consumer apps on writes whose stale-view risk is real, each action reading the token with SupportsIfMatchAttribute.RequiredToken(HttpContext) a few lines below the attribute. In ADC: the event lifecycle transitions (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventLifecycleController.cs:59, :86), the hand-written PUT actions of EventsController (.../Controllers/Events/EventsController.cs:228), SessionsController (.../Controllers/Sessions/SessionsController.cs:310), SpeakersController (.../Controllers/Speakers/SpeakersController.cs:372) and the other Conference controllers (activities, sponsors, categories, session assets, partners, questions), plus Engagement's SessionQuestionsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/Controllers/SessionQuestionsController.cs:136, :160, :186) and LivePollsController (.../Controllers/LivePollsController.cs:86, :120). In Store: OrdersController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/OrdersController.cs:299, :359), OrderFulfillmentController (.../OrderFulfillmentController.cs:55, :88, :134), GuestOrdersController (.../GuestOrdersController.cs:165) and InventoryItemsController (.../InventoryItemsController.cs:96, :129) in Sales, the Catalog controllers (for example MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Catalog/MMCA.Store.Catalog.API/Controllers/ProductVariantsController.cs:100), and Identity's CustomersController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.API/Controllers/CustomersController.cs:178, :204, :230). In Helpdesk: TicketsController (MMCA.Helpdesk/Source/Modules/Tickets/MMCA.Helpdesk.Tickets.API/Controllers/TicketsController.cs:116, :144, :212). ADC pins the convention with ConditionalWriteConventionTests fitness tests that assert the attribute is present on the endpoints that need it (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API.Tests/Conventions/ConditionalWriteConventionTests.cs:31, and an Engagement twin at MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API.Tests/Controllers/ConditionalWriteConventionTests.cs:13). The read half of the round trip is EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>.SetConcurrencyETag (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/EntityControllerBase.cs:417-425), which gives the client the tag to send back.

    OutputCacheEvictionExtensions

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/OutputCacheEvictionExtensions.cs:27 · Level 5 · class (static, two extension blocks)

    • What it is: two things that travel together. It is the one-method DI registration for OutputCacheEvictionHandler (the container half of the cross-service eviction path), and it is the multi-tag eviction helper pair a mutating controller reaches for right after a write.
    • Depends on: OutputCacheEvictionHandler, IIntegrationEventHandler<in TIntegrationEvent>, OutputCacheEvictionRequested, BestEffort, and ServiceCollectionDescriptorExtensions.TryAddEnumerable (OutputCacheEvictionExtensions.cs:1-8).
    • Concept introduced (two eviction verbs for two call sites). ASP.NET Core's IOutputCacheStore evicts one tag per call, but a single write usually invalidates several (a speaker edit drops both conference:speakers and conference). Rather than a private per-controller helper wrapping a run of EvictByTagAsync calls (:17-21), the framework offers one call that names every tag, in two flavors that differ only in what they do when the cache store is unreachable.
      • EvictTagsAsync propagates the failure. A caller that considers a failed eviction part of its own success uses this one.
      • TryEvictTagsAsync is the best-effort sibling: a Redis outage or a transient network fault becomes one Warning plus one BestEffort metric increment instead of an exception (:60-66). The reasoning is worth internalizing: the mutation this follows has already committed, so surfacing the failure would turn a successful write into a client-visible error while leaving the write in place, and an entry that could not be evicted expires on its own TTL anyway. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] covers exactly this post-commit-follow-up contract (ADR-096).
      • A second detail in TryEvictTagsAsync is easy to miss and load-bearing: eviction runs under CancellationToken.None, not the request token (:67-70, :90). The write has committed, so a client that disconnected mid-response must not abandon the cleanup.
    • Concept (an idempotent registration for a handler that must not run twice). Two lifetime decisions are documented on AddOutputCacheEvictionHandler and both matter. The handler is registered as a singleton, matching the lifetime the module scanner gives every other integration-event handler, so a host that wires it by hand and a module that wires it through the scan agree. And it goes in through TryAddEnumerable rather than AddSingleton, so calling it twice (a host plus a module that both want the behavior) registers one handler rather than evicting every tag twice (:102-108). [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether a shared concern can be opted into safely from more than one place; a plain Add here would double every eviction, harmless in effect but doubling the store round trips and the failure counter.
    • Walkthrough
      • A class-level [SuppressMessage] for CA1708 (:23-26) records a known analyzer trap: with multiple extension(T) blocks in one static class, CA1708 flags the compiler-generated grouping members as case-colliding, and no user-visible identifier differs only by case.
      • EvictOperationPrefix = "output-cache-evict:" (:34) is the prefix of the best-effort operation name. The tag is appended so a failure is attributable to the cache it could not clear, which is also why the doc insists call-site tags stay low-cardinality literals: the name becomes a metric tag (:29-33).
      • extension(IOutputCacheStore store) (:36) holds the two verbs. EvictTagsAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken, params string[] tags) (:49) null-guards store and tags (:51-52) and awaits EvictByTagAsync for each tag in the order given (:54-57). TryEvictTagsAsync(ILogger logger, params string[] tags) (:78) adds a logger guard (:80-82) and routes each eviction through BestEffort.ExecuteAsync with the prefixed operation name, the caller's logger, the eviction as the action, and CancellationToken.None (:86-90).
      • extension(IServiceCollection services) (:95) holds AddOutputCacheEvictionHandler() (:111). It null-guards services (:113), calls services.TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IIntegrationEventHandler<OutputCacheEvictionRequested>, OutputCacheEvictionHandler>()) (:115-117), and returns the collection for chaining (:119). The doc records the one prerequisite (:100-101): AddOutputCache() must have been called, since it supplies the singleton IOutputCacheStore the handler evicts through.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc states the pairing rule plainly (:12-16): this is the DI half, RegisterOutputCacheEvictionConsumer() on the framework's IBrokerConsumerBuilder is the broker half (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/IntegrationEventConsumerExtensions.cs:28, shorthand for RegisterIntegrationEventConsumer<OutputCacheEvictionRequested>() at :32), and a host that wants the behavior calls both. Splitting them is what keeps the handler broker-agnostic, since the DI registration has no messaging dependency at all. Housing the eviction verbs in the same class keeps the write-side helper and the read-side coherence path in one file.
    • Where it's used: ADC's Conference service calls services.AddOutputCacheEvictionHandler() (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:313) alongside the broker registration (:352). No consumer controller calls either verb directly: the one caller is EvictOutputCacheAttribute, which runs the best-effort form after a 2xx write (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/EvictOutputCacheAttribute.cs:114), so ADC's Conference controllers and Store's Catalog controllers name their tags declaratively instead, for example SpeakerCategoryItemsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Speakers/SpeakerCategoryItemsController.cs:51), ProductsController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Catalog/MMCA.Store.Catalog.API/Controllers/ProductsController.cs:46) and CategoriesController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Catalog/MMCA.Store.Catalog.API/Controllers/CategoriesController.cs:33). Framework coverage: OutputCacheEvictTagsTests pins both verbs, including the CancellationToken.None rule and the swallow-versus-throw split (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Caching/OutputCacheEvictTagsTests.cs:59-113), and OutputCacheEvictionHandlerTests pins the double-registration behavior (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Caching/OutputCacheEvictionHandlerTests.cs:107-114).

    PublicCachedReadsAttribute

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Caching · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Caching/PublicCachedReadsAttribute.cs:42 · Level 8 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: a class-level attribute that is also an MVC controller-model convention. On an entity controller it marks the inherited base reads (both GetAllAsync overloads, GetAllForLookupAsync and GetByIdAsync) as anonymous and output-cached under one named policy, and names the by-id route, so a controller no longer overrides a base read only to add attributes (PublicCachedReadsAttribute.cs:8-13).
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization (AllowAnonymousAttribute, IAllowAnonymous, IAuthorizeData), Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ApplicationModels (IControllerModelConvention, ControllerModel, ActionModel, SelectorModel) and Microsoft.AspNetCore.OutputCaching.OutputCacheAttribute (PublicCachedReadsAttribute.cs:1-3), plus EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>, whose read actions it recognizes (:4, :45-50). The named policy it points at is normally a PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy registered through OutputCacheOptionsExtensions (:36-38).
    • Concept introduced (declaring a public cached read surface once, at the controller). A public read cached under PublicEndpointOutputCachePolicy needs two markers on every read action, [AllowAnonymous] and [OutputCache(PolicyName = ...)], and the base reads live in the framework's generic controller, so without this attribute a consumer overrides each inherited read just to decorate it. The class doc settles three decisions (:14-39).
      • What it adds (:15-22): on every selector of a base read it appends the anonymous marker and the output-cache marker, each only when the selector does not already carry one, so an override's own [OutputCache] wins whatever its policy. The by-id read gets a route name unless one is already declared. Nothing is added to the action filters, so the API description changes only by the operationId a new route name produces. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether hot read paths avoid redundant work; this makes the cached shape the one-line default for an entity's public reads, the authenticated-read caching model of ADR-040.
      • What it leaves alone (:23-27): the export, every write, the opt-in cursor and change-feed reads, and every action the application declares itself keep exactly the authorization and caching the controller gives them.
      • What it refuses (:28-34): an override of a base read is still a base read and is marked like an inherited one, so an override that declares its own [Authorize] or permission attribute without [AllowAnonymous] makes the convention throw when the application model is built, because the anonymous marker would silently replace the requirement. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether access-control changes are explicit; this turns an accidental widening of a gated read into a startup failure rather than a public endpoint. A read that needs a gate belongs on a controller without the attribute.
    • Walkthrough
      • [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = true)] (:41). ReadActionNames (:45-50) holds the three base read names via nameof on the open EntityControllerBase<,,>; both GetAllAsync overloads share one name.
      • The constructor takes policyName (:57) and rejects null, empty or whitespace with ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace (:59). PolicyName (:64) exposes it. ByIdRouteName (:71) is an optional init property: null derives Get{EntityName}ById, and empty or whitespace is rejected when the convention runs.
      • Apply(ControllerModel) (:83) null-guards the model, finds the closed EntityControllerBase<,,> in the controller's base chain or throws InvalidOperationException naming the controller (:87-89), throws when ByIdRouteName is set but blank (:91-95), and derives the route name from the first generic argument, the entity type (:97). For every action IsBaseRead accepts (:99) it runs EnsureNoDeclaredAuthorization (:101), notes whether the action is GetByIdAsync (:103), and marks each selector, passing the route name only for the by-id read (:105-108).
      • MarkSelector (:118) adds AllowAnonymousAttribute when no IAllowAnonymous is present (:120-123), adds OutputCacheAttribute { PolicyName = PolicyName } when no OutputCacheAttribute is present (:125-128), and sets the attribute route's name only when a name is wanted and the route model has none (:130-133).
      • EnsureNoDeclaredAuthorization (:146) throws when the action's own attributes carry an IAuthorizeData and no IAllowAnonymous (:148); authorization declared on the controller class is deliberately left alone, the usual shape of gated writes beside public reads (:136-141).
      • FindEntityControllerBase (:156) walks BaseType until it meets a generic type whose definition is EntityControllerBase<,,> (:158-161). IsBaseRead (:171) takes the method's GetBaseDefinition().DeclaringType (:173), so an override still counts as a base read, and requires that declaring type to be a closed EntityControllerBase<,,> and the method name to be one of ReadActionNames (:175-177).
    • Why it's built this way: a controller-model convention runs once when the application model is built, so the markers become ordinary endpoint metadata with no per-request cost, and a misuse (a non-entity controller, a blank route name, a gated override) fails at startup rather than at the first request. Writing to EndpointMetadata rather than to the action filters keeps the published API description unchanged. Adding a marker only when absent lets an individual override opt out of the shared policy by declaring its own [OutputCache]. An unknown policy name is not checked here; it fails at request time exactly as a hand-written [OutputCache(PolicyName = ...)] does (:36-38).
    • Where it's used: fourteen ADC Conference controllers carry it at class level, each beside a class-level EvictOutputCacheAttribute for the write side, for example SessionsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Sessions/SessionsController.cs:44), EventsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventsController.cs:48), SpeakerCategoryItemsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Speakers/SpeakerCategoryItemsController.cs:48) and SponsorsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Sponsors/SponsorsController.cs:39). Framework coverage is PublicCachedReadsAttributeTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Caching/PublicCachedReadsAttributeTests.cs), and ADC asserts its declarations through PublicCachedReadAssertions (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API.Tests/Helpers/PublicCachedReadAssertions.cs). The generic entity-controller decision it builds on is ADR-099.

    DisabledFeatureHandler

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.FeatureManagement · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/FeatureManagement/DisabledFeatureHandler.cs:14 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the one-method handler that decides what a [FeatureGate]-protected controller action returns when its feature flag is off. Instead of ASP.NET Core's default (a bare 404 with no body), it emits an RFC 9457 Problem Details payload so a disabled feature reads the same as any other framework error.
    • Depends on: IDisabledFeaturesHandler and FeatureGateAttribute from Microsoft.FeatureManagement.Mvc (NuGet); ProblemDetails, ObjectResult, and StatusCodes from ASP.NET Core. No first-party dependencies.
    • Concept introduced: feature gating at the HTTP edge. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether every response, success or refusal, follows one uniform contract; this handler makes the disabled-feature path match the ApiControllerBase.HandleFailure shape rather than leaking a framework default. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven Design] covers concerns applied uniformly across endpoints, and feature flags are exactly that. Note the split: this class gates controller actions decorated with [FeatureGate], while FeatureGateCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult> gates CQRS handlers one layer deeper. The two surfaces cover the two entry points into a gated capability, which is precisely the dual-surface enforcement ADR-031 records.
    • Walkthrough: HandleDisabledFeatures(features, context) (DisabledFeatureHandler.cs:17) sets context.Result to an ObjectResult wrapping a ProblemDetails with Status = 404 and a fixed title/detail ("Feature not available", DisabledFeatureHandler.cs:19-24), and also sets the outer StatusCode = 404 (DisabledFeatureHandler.cs:26) so the response code and the body agree. It returns Task.CompletedTask (DisabledFeatureHandler.cs:29): the work is synchronous, there is nothing to await.
    • Why it's built this way: the payload deliberately does not name the disabled feature. An anonymous caller learns only that the endpoint is unavailable, not which flag is off, so the flag set is not enumerable from outside. The features parameter is available but unused for that reason.
    • Where it's used: registered as the app's IDisabledFeaturesHandler singleton inside AddAPI (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:110, immediately after services.AddFeatureManagement().WithTargeting<CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor>() on DependencyInjection.cs:108-109); invoked by Microsoft.FeatureManagement.Mvc whenever a [FeatureGate] action is hit with its flag disabled. In the framework itself that covers DataExportControllerBase<TQuery> while PrivacyFeatures.DataExport is off (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Privacy/DataExportControllerBase.cs:60) and the three notification controllers gated on NotificationFeatures.PushNotifications (Controllers/Notifications/DevicesController.cs:23, NotificationInboxController.cs:27, NotificationsController.cs:28).

The endpoint is anonymous and reached on the service host directly; gateways do not route it (class doc, ServiceInfoControllerBase.cs:12-13).

    • What it is: the base class of the entity and use-case API controllers (the OAuth and service-info bases derive ControllerBase directly, as the class doc at ApiControllerBase.cs:16-21 states). It carries the [ApiController] behavior, the shared HandleFailure that turns domain errors into RFC 9457 Problem Details responses (adding a Retry-After header to a 429 that knows its wait), and the concurrency-token plumbing every controller that serves or conditionally writes a row reuses: SetConcurrencyETag and the two HandleConditionalCommand*Async helpers.
    • Depends on: Error, ErrorType, Result, ErrorHttpMapping (and through it ErrorTypeSeverity), IErrorLocalizer (resolved optionally from RequestServices), RetryAfterHeader (Format), ConcurrencyETag, SupportsIfMatchAttribute (RequiredToken), and ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult>; System.Reflection plus a ConcurrentDictionary for the per-type token-property cache.
    • Concept introduced: centralized error-to-HTTP mapping. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether every endpoint fails the same way; [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] covers keeping the HTTP-translation concern in the presentation layer rather than the domain. This is the boundary where a Result failure from the Application/Domain layers becomes an HTTP status: the domain never knows about status codes, this base owns that mapping. The [ApiController] attribute (ApiControllerBase.cs:22) enables automatic model-state validation, binding-source inference, and ProblemDetails serialization.
    • Concept introduced: the status code is ranked, not positional. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] both bear on this. An aggregate failure built by Result.Combine carries several errors at once, and if the response status came from errors[0] then the order in which handlers appended errors would decide whether a caller saw 403 or 400. HandleFailure therefore hands the whole list to ErrorHttpMapping.GetStatusCode(IReadOnlyList<Error>) (ApiControllerBase.cs:62, mapping at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ErrorHttpMapping.cs:54-55), which resolves the most severe ErrorType present through ErrorTypeSeverity. The ranking is spelled out on the method doc (ApiControllerBase.cs:35-44): Unexpected (500), then Unauthorized (401), Forbidden (403), TooManyRequests (429), Conflict (409), NotFound (404), UnprocessableEntity (422), and finally Invariant/Validation/Failure (400). Equal ranks keep the earliest error, so a same-rank list behaves exactly as a positional selection would. The ranking itself lives in MMCA.Common.Shared on purpose (ErrorHttpMapping.cs:49-50), so the gRPC edge classifies the same aggregate identically. Every error still travels in the response; only the status is ranked.
    • Concept introduced: a 429 that says how long to wait. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]. A refusal such as a sign-in lockout (ADR-029) knows its own duration, carried on Error.RetryAfter. SetRetryAfter (ApiControllerBase.cs:87) acts only when the ranked status is 429 (:89-92), takes the longest RetryAfter among the TooManyRequests errors (:94-96, because retrying before the longest would only be refused again), and writes Response.Headers.RetryAfter through RetryAfterHeader.Format (:97-100) when that delay is positive, so the header uses the same whole, rounded-up seconds the rate limiters send (:79-86). Any other status, or a 429 with no hint, sends no header.
    • Concept introduced: one place that turns a row version into a precondition. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] (ADR-035). A client gets the concurrency token as a weak ETag on a read and hands it back as If-Match on the next write (see SupportsIfMatchAttribute); this base owns both halves so they cannot drift apart.
      • SetConcurrencyETag(object? dto) (:125) is protected, so a custom read action, a hand-built projection, or a conditional write answering with the refreshed value emits the identical header instead of re-implementing the reflection and the base64 format (:118-123). A null row returns at once (:127-128), a row with no or an empty token gets no header (:130-131, because a fabricated tag would invite preconditions the write side cannot honour, :112-117), and otherwise it writes ConcurrencyETag.Format(rowVersion) under ConcurrencyETag.ETagHeaderName (:133).
      • ReadRowVersion (:239) reads the token off the row's RUNTIME shape: a shaped dictionary (a fields= projection) is probed under rowVersion, then RowVersion (:241-246); a typed value goes through RowVersionProperties.GetOrAdd(dto.GetType(), FindRowVersionProperty) (:248). That static ConcurrentDictionary<Type, PropertyInfo?> (:30) resolves each runtime type once, since a type's shape cannot change at runtime (:25-29), and FindRowVersionProperty (:255-260) accepts only a public instance, readable, non-indexer byte[] property named exactly RowVersion. Keying on the runtime type is what lets the helper live on this non-generic base rather than on a DTO-typed one.
      • HandleConditionalCommandAsync<TCommand, TResult> (:153, TResult : Result at :158) and HandleConditionalCommandWithResponseAsync<TCommand, TResponse> (:184) run a conditional write end to end. Each null-guards its handler and command builder eagerly (:160-161, :190-191), reads the token SupportsIfMatchAttribute.RequiredToken(HttpContext) decoded (:163, :193; an action without [SupportsIfMatch] throws InvalidOperationException and the handler never runs, :151-152, :182-183), builds the command from it, and hands off to a private awaited half (:164, :194; the split keeps the argument checks eager, :197, :215). RunConditionalCommandAsync (:198) dispatches (:205), maps a failure through HandleFailure (:206-207), awaits the optional onSuccess follow-up such as a cache eviction (:209-210), and answers 204 (:212). RunConditionalCommandWithResponseAsync (:216) unwraps the value with TryGetValue (:223-224), awaits onSuccess with it (:226-227), emits the refreshed token through SetConcurrencyETag(value) (:229), and answers 200 with the value (:230), so the client already holds the precondition for its next write (ADR-144 relies on that round trip).
    • Walkthrough: HandleFailure(IEnumerable<Error> errors) (ApiControllerBase.cs:49) is protected virtual:
      • Null/empty guard (ApiControllerBase.cs:51-59): with no errors it returns a 500 "Unknown error", treating an empty failure as a programming mistake rather than a domain outcome.
      • Ranked status (ApiControllerBase.cs:62, with the intent stated in the comment just above it at ApiControllerBase.cs:61).
      • Builds a ProblemDetails with that status and a fixed title/detail (ApiControllerBase.cs:64-69), attaches Extensions["errors"] via ErrorHttpMapping.BuildErrorsExtension (ApiControllerBase.cs:72), optionally localized through an IErrorLocalizer resolved with GetService (ApiControllerBase.cs:71, so a host without localization simply passes null), sets the Retry-After header when it applies (ApiControllerBase.cs:74), then returns StatusCode(statusCode, problemDetails) (ApiControllerBase.cs:76).
    • Why it's built this way: one virtual method instead of a switch in every action removes duplication and makes the response shape uniform (ADR-013 for why failures are values rather than exceptions in the first place); keeping it virtual lets a subclass (EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>) wrap it with logging without reimplementing the mapping. The ErrorHttpMapping members are internal static (ErrorHttpMapping.cs:41, :50, :61), which is what lets UnhandledResultFailureFilter reuse the same ranked status mapping and the same errors extension array for a failed Result that an action returned without calling HandleFailure (UnhandledResultFailureFilter.cs:36 and :47). The two bodies are deliberately not identical: the filter labels its ProblemDetails Title/Detail "Unhandled result failure" / "The action returned a Result.Failure that was not mapped to an HTTP error response." (UnhandledResultFailureFilter.cs:42-43) against the base's "Operation failed" / "One or more errors occurred." (ApiControllerBase.cs:67-68), so a response that fell through the filter is distinguishable from one the controller mapped on purpose. Localization is the ADR-027 extension point, keyed by Error.Code and leaving Code/Type/Source/Target verbatim so clients can still branch on them (ErrorHttpMapping.cs:60-63 for the contract, ErrorHttpMapping.cs:62-70 for the projection that honours it).
    • Where it's used: the root of the entity and use-case controller hierarchy. EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>, AuthControllerBase, PasswordResetAuthControllerBase<TForgotPasswordCommand, TResetPasswordCommand>, DataExportControllerBase<TQuery>, and every module controller derive from it directly or transitively; OAuthControllerBase and ServiceInfoControllerBase do not. The architecture rule ControllersInheritApiControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Api/ArchitectureRules.Controllers.cs:66) fails a module controller that derives raw ControllerBase unless it is listed as exempt. The conditional-write helpers are used by ADC's EventLifecycleController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventLifecycleController.cs:72, HandleConditionalCommandAsync) and QuestionsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Questions/QuestionsController.cs:67, HandleConditionalCommandWithResponseAsync) among others, and SetConcurrencyETag directly by ADC's SpeakersController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Speakers/SpeakersController.cs:301). Framework coverage is ApiControllerBaseTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/ApiControllerBaseTests.cs) and ApiControllerBaseConditionalCommandTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/ApiControllerBaseConditionalCommandTests.cs).

    EmailConfirmationControllerBase<TSendCommand, TConfirmCommand>

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Controllers · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/EmailConfirmationControllerBase.cs:43 · Level 6 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the abstract base for the two anonymous email-confirmation endpoints, POST send-email-confirmation and POST confirm-email (ADR-116 is the identity-completions decision it implements; the route names are at EmailConfirmationControllerBase.cs:78 and :106). The app subclass supplies the route prefix, the API version and two one-line command factories; the base owns the HTTP shape.
    • Depends on: ApiControllerBase (base, for HandleFailure), ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> (one handler per action, both returning Result), ICommandWithRequest<out TRequest> (the generic constraints, :46-47), SendEmailConfirmationRequest and ConfirmEmailRequest (the bodies), IdempotentAttribute, and the RateLimitPolicyAuthIp constant on WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.
    • Concept introduced: a sibling controller instead of a longer inheritance chain. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses uniform endpoint conventions; [Rubric §1, SOLID] covers keeping the base closed and the variation in small abstract members. The app's own AuthController already occupies the single-inheritance chain (AuthControllerBase to UserAccountAuthControllerBase<TChangePasswordCommand, TChangePreferencesCommand>), so confirmation ships as a separate controller routed to the same Auth prefix, which reaches the gateway through the existing /Auth route (:13-20). The commands stay app-side, the same split PasswordResetAuthControllerBase<TForgotPasswordCommand, TResetPasswordCommand> uses: the derived controller supplies each through CreateSendCommand (:61) and CreateConfirmCommand (:69), and the base reads the request back only through ICommandWithRequest<TRequest> (:35-38).
    • Concept introduced: anonymous by necessity, and non-enumerating. [Rubric §11, Security] is the angle. Both actions are [AllowAnonymous] because the link is followed from a mail client with no session, and an unconfirmed account may be unable to sign in at all (:23-27). Send answers 202 on every well-formed request: the handler treats an unknown address and an already-confirmed one as success, so the response never reveals which addresses hold accounts, and only a malformed payload reaches 400 through the request validator (:30-33, :78-84). Both carry [EnableRateLimiting(RateLimitPolicyAuthIp)] (:81, :109) and declare the 429 (:84, :113), for the same reason login and recovery do (ADR-019, ADR-029).
    • Walkthrough
      • Primary constructor (:43-45) exposes the two handlers as protected SendHandler (:50) and ConfirmHandler (:53).
      • SendEmailConfirmationAsync (:85): [HttpPost("send-email-confirmation")], [Idempotent], [AllowAnonymous] (:78-80); dispatches CreateSendCommand(request) (:89-91) and returns Accepted() on success, HandleFailure(result.Errors) otherwise (:93-95).
      • ConfirmEmailAsync (:114): [HttpPost("confirm-email")], [Idempotent], [AllowAnonymous] (:106-108); the link carries the address and token in the URI fragment, so the page reads them client-side and posts them here and neither reaches a server log or a Referer header (:98-101). It returns NoContent() on success (:122-124) and declares 400, 401 and 429 (:111-113).
    • Why it's built this way: unlike the credential-issuing endpoints in AuthControllerBase, neither action mints a token pair, so both opt in with [Idempotent] (ADR-017): a retried send or confirm replays the stored answer instead of re-running the handler. Both methods are virtual so an app can wrap them. Errors go through the shared HandleFailure, so a failed confirm is the same RFC 9457 shape as every other endpoint.
    • Where it's used: subclassed by ADC's EmailConfirmationController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/Controllers/EmailConfirmationController.cs:29). Both actions are listed by name in the framework's anonymous-endpoint architecture gate (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:42-43), so their [AllowAnonymous] is an approved exception. Framework coverage is EmailConfirmationControllerBaseTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/Auth/EmailConfirmationControllerBaseTests.cs).

    OAuthControllerBase

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Controllers · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/OAuthControllerBase.cs:56 · Level 6 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the base controller for external sign-in (Google, GitHub, Apple, and any configured generic OIDC provider). It runs the challenge/callback/complete/exchange dance so a browser or native head can log in through a provider and receive a local JWT pair without ever exposing tokens in a redirect URL, and it answers the home-realm discovery question "which organization provider owns this email domain".
    • Depends on: IAuthenticationService (ExternalLoginAsync), ICacheService (SetAsync, GetFromSharedStoreAsync, RemoveAsync), IConfiguration, an optional IDistributedLock (TryAcquireAsync), ExternalAuthExtensions (the scheme constant, OAuthControllerBase.cs:68), OidcProviderRegistry (Find, FindByEmail, resolved optionally from RequestServices), OidcDiscoveryResponse, WebApplicationBuilderExtensions (RateLimitPolicyAuthIp), NonIdempotentAttribute, AuthenticationResponse, OAuthCodeExchangeRequest, and Error; the Google, GitHub, and Apple OAuth packages and System.Security.Cryptography.
    • Concept introduced: the code-exchange OAuth completion pattern. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how credentials move through the system; the design's whole point is that the redirect after a successful provider login carries only a single-use opaque code, never the access/refresh tokens, so tokens never land in the address bar, browser history, the Referer header, or upstream access logs (OAuthControllerBase.cs:245-247). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]: the base is hoisted from the app hosts so every service reuses the identical flow, with the sealed subclass supplying only [Route("auth/oauth")] and versioning, and the burn check reads the shared cache store so the single-use guarantee holds across replicas. A subclass can go further and pass an IDistributedLock to the four-argument primary constructor (:56-60), which makes the read-then-burn one critical section across replicas (:304-323); AddCaching registers a Redis-backed lock when an IConnectionMultiplexer is present, and the three-argument constructor (:102) leaves the lock null, so single-use then holds per replica only. See ADR-036.
    • Concept introduced: generic OIDC providers and home-realm discovery. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]. Beyond the three named providers, any provider configured under OAuth:Oidc:<Name> (registered by ExternalAuthExtensions.AddExternalAuthProviders, :144-145) is reachable through one parameterized route. OidcLogin (:158, [HttpGet("{provider}")] and [AllowAnonymous] at :154-155) looks the name up ignoring case through OidcProviders?.Find(provider) and either challenges with the provider's registered name or answers 404 (:160-161). The literal google, github, and apple routes take precedence and those names are reserved, so an OIDC provider can never shadow them, and MAUI heads reach it through the same auth/oauth/{provider} URL the external auth broker already builds (:146-148). DiscoverOidcProvider (:179; [HttpGet("discover")], [AllowAnonymous], and [EnableRateLimiting(WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimitPolicyAuthIp)] at :174-176) maps the domain of an email to the provider whose Domains list claims it through FindByEmail (:181) and answers an OidcDiscoveryResponse(Name, DisplayName) or 404 (:182-184), so a sign-in page can offer one "Sign in with your organization" step instead of a button per identity provider. The answer reveals only which configured provider owns a domain, never whether an account exists, and it is throttled per client IP like the other anonymous auth endpoints (:164-171). The registry comes from OidcProviders (:188), an optional GetService lookup, because AddExternalAuthProviders registers it only when at least one OIDC provider is configured (:187); a host with none answers 404 on both actions.
    • Walkthrough
      • OAuthExchangeCodePrefix (OAuthControllerBase.cs:73) and a 2-minute OAuthExchangeCodeLifetime (:87) namespace and time-box the server-side token stash; the short TTL matches the single redirect-then-POST round trip. A second constant, ClientStateItemKey = "clientState" (:77), names a separate AuthenticationProperties.Items slot for the client's own opaque per-attempt value, deliberately not called "state" because that name belongs to the OAuth handler's own protocol value (:75-76). The redeem lock uses a 10-second lease and a 5-second wait (RedeemLockTimeToLive, RedeemLockWait, :92-93), matching the password-reset token service: the critical section is one cache read and one remove. UIBaseUrlConfigKey = "OAuth:UIBaseUrl" (:66) is public so the AppHost can set the same key through WithUiLinks as OAuth__UIBaseUrl (:62-65).
      • GoogleLogin (:117), GitHubLogin (:127), and AppleLogin (:140) each take an optional state query parameter alongside returnUrl and carry [AllowAnonymous] directly (:116, :126, :139); all three, like OidcLogin, call ChallengeProvider (:456), which stashes both returnUrl and the client's state under ClientStateItemKey in AuthenticationProperties.Items and sets RedirectUri = "/auth/oauth/complete" (:458-470). Apple needs no special action here: its callback arrives as a cross-site form POST (response_mode=form_post is forced by the name/email scopes) that the middleware handles at /auth/callback/apple like any other provider (:132-134).
      • CompleteAsync (:207) carries [AllowAnonymous] (:205). It reads the UI base URL through UIBaseUrlConfigKey (:209), and after the middleware handles the provider callback it reads the external cookie (:210), redirects to /login?error=oauth_failed when the ticket did not survive (:212-217), reads both the stashed returnUrl and clientState via ReadChallengeState (:222, :258-259), extracts provider claims (ExtractClaims, :225), calls ExternalLoginAsync to find or create the local user and mint tokens (:232-233), signs out the temporary external cookie (:243), then mints a 32-byte hex exchangeCode (:248), stashes the token pair in the cache under it (:249-250), and redirects with the code and, when the client sent one, the echoed state (:252, URL built by BuildSuccessRedirectUrl at :261-275).
      • ReadChallengeState (:258-259) is a safe-lookup helper (GetString is TryGetValue under the hood): the challenge normally stashes both returnUrl and clientState, but a ticket minted without them (custom challenge, provider round-trip edge) falls back to "/" and null instead of throwing on the Items indexer.
      • BuildSuccessRedirectUrl (:261-275) appends &state= (URL-escaped) only when clientState is non-empty (:268-270), for both the web redirect and the native AppendQuery branch (:272-274), so callers that never sent a state see no change to the redirect shape.
      • Name handling is defensive and never yields an empty name, because user invariants reject an empty first or last name and an empty value would fail the first external sign-up outright (:82-85). ExtractName (:362) uses GivenName/Surname only when both are non-blank (:367-370); otherwise it takes the full name from the GitHub display-name claim urn:github:name (GitHubDisplayNameClaimType, :80), because the GitHub handler maps ClaimTypes.Name to the login handle, and falls back to ClaimTypes.Name when that claim is blank (:372-378). It then splits through SplitFullName (:391), which breaks at the first space, trims, and returns the "User" / "User" placeholders (:84-85) for a blank or single-token name or an empty remainder (:393-406). A blank given or family name is replaced individually by its fallback (:381-382), so a provider that returns only a display name still yields a creatable local account. That fallback matters most for Apple, which returns name claims on the first authorization only.
      • Native heads (ADR-043): GetAllowedMobileReturnUrl (:431) returns the stashed returnUrl as the redirect target only when it is an absolute URI whose custom scheme is listed in OAuth:AllowedReturnUrlSchemes; http/https never match (:433-438), so the allowlist cannot become an open redirect, and a missing or empty section (or a test double returning null from GetSection) means "no allowlist", the exact pre-ADR-043 behavior (:440-444). Failures route to the same surface through RedirectError (:419-422), so a native window closes on an error instead of stranding on a web login page.
      • ExchangeAsync (:293): [HttpPost("exchange")] with [NonIdempotent(...)] and [AllowAnonymous] (:289-291); the UI swaps the code for the real AuthenticationResponse out-of-band. A blank code is answered as an invalid code (:297-300). With no lock it calls RedeemExchangeCodeAsync directly (:304-307); with an IDistributedLock it first takes lock:{cacheKey} through TryAcquireAsync (:312-314), answers an invalid code if the lock cannot be taken within the wait (:315-318), and redeems inside await using on the handle (:320-323). Two replicas that both read before either removes would otherwise both hand out the token pair (:309-311). RedeemExchangeCodeAsync (:326) does the read and the burn: the lookup goes through ICacheService.GetFromSharedStoreAsync (:332) rather than the ordinary read, because a code already burned on another replica must be a miss here, not a stale local copy that would mint a second token pair (:330-331). Because the response is a struct, a cache miss yields a default value rather than null, so the miss is detected via an empty AccessToken (:333-336). The code is then removed (:339), making it single-use so a leaked or replayed code cannot mint a second token pair. Every failure path returns the same opaque 400 "Invalid sign-in code" (InvalidCode, :344-350).
    • Why it's built this way: carrying tokens in a redirect is the classic OAuth token-leak vector; the single-use code plus a short-lived server-side stash closes it while keeping the client flow a plain redirect and one POST. Reading the stash from the shared store keeps "single-use" true when the API runs on more than one replica, where a per-node copy could otherwise outlive the burn. The [NonIdempotent] justification on ExchangeAsync (:290) records why this one endpoint must stay outside the replay contract: replaying the stored response would defeat the burn, letting a leaked code mint the same tokens again for the whole retention window. The lock is optional so a single-node host pays nothing, while a multi-replica host opts in by constructor argument; a caller that loses the lock race is answered as an invalid code, never as a second success (:309-311). The AppendQuery helper (:447) deliberately uses OriginalString rather than ToString(), because Uri normalization appends a trailing slash to authority-only URIs (e.g. myapp://oauth-complete) and native authenticator callback matching can be exact (:449-451). The client-supplied state is carried opaquely: the server never interprets or trusts it, only stores and echoes it back so the client can bind the completion to the flow it started (:465-467). Generic OIDC providers ride the same challenge and completion path rather than a parallel one, so every guarantee above applies to them unchanged.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the provider scheme registration, the OIDC provider registry, and the concrete ExternalLoginAsync implementation live outside this base (ExternalAuthExtensions, OidcProviderRegistry, and the app's IAuthenticationService); this file assumes they are wired. How GetFromSharedStoreAsync bypasses a local tier is the cache implementation's concern (ICacheService), not this file's. The complete and exchange actions are hidden from OpenAPI with [ApiExplorerSettings(IgnoreApi = true)] (:206, :292) because they are browser redirects, not a documented client contract; OidcLogin and DiscoverOidcProvider carry no such attribute and declare their responses (:156-157, :177-178). This base derives ControllerBase directly (:60), not ApiControllerBase.
    • Where it's used: subclassed by each app's sealed OAuth controller, today ADC's OAuthController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/Controllers/OAuthController.cs:21), which adds only the class-level routing and versioning attributes. ExchangeAsync is one of the endpoints the framework's anonymous-endpoint architecture gate lists by name (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:31), and the challenge, completion, OidcLogin, and DiscoverOidcProvider actions are listed there too (AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:57-64), so each [AllowAnonymous] is an approved exception rather than an oversight. The Aspire hosting side writes UIBaseUrlConfigKey through IdentityLinkExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aspire.Hosting/IdentityLinkExtensions.cs). Framework coverage is OAuthControllerBaseTests and OAuthControllerBaseOidcTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/Auth/), and ADC exercises the exchange end to end in OAuthExchangeTests (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Integration/MMCA.ADC.Identity.IntegrationTests/Auth/OAuthExchangeTests.cs).

      • MaxPageSize (:58-65) resolves IOptions<ApplicationSettings> per-request from HttpContext.RequestServices, falling back to 500, and clamps the result to the range 1 to EntityQueryPipeline.MaxUnboundedResultLimit (:63; the ceiling is 1000 at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Services/Query/EntityQueryPipeline.cs:23). EntityName (:91) is typeof(TEntity).Name, used in log messages and in the export refusal.

(:187), rather than mixing it into the body, [Rubric §9] again, and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] for the clamp.

      • GetAllForLookupAsync (:321, [HttpGet("lookup")] at :318): returns CollectionResult<BaseLookup<TIdentifierType>>, a lightweight id/label pair, with a [Required] nameProperty (:322) choosing the label. The same TryGetValue unwrap (:333) feeds the lookups into the CollectionResult items (:335-339).
      • GetByIdAsync (:362, [HttpGet("{id}")] at :357): includeFKs defaults to true for the single-entity case (:364), and on success it calls the inherited SetConcurrencyETag(result.Value) before returning (:383-384).
      • GetCursorPageAsync (:408) and GetChangesAsync (:461) are covered as their own concept below.
      • HandleFailure override (:485-499): logs the first error at Warning, guarded by Logger.IsEnabled (:488), before delegating to ApiControllerBase.HandleFailure, so the read path gets observability ([Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]) without changing the response mapping. The logged message goes through SingleLine (:495, defined at :505-506), which strips every carriage return and line feed so a logged message is always one line whatever the sink. Note it logs the first error while the base ranks the status by the most severe one: the log line is a breadcrumb, not the status decision.
      • Every read action that takes the option passes asTracking: false to the query service (for example :124), because a read endpoint never mutates what it loaded.
    • Concept introduced: one row-scoping hook for every read the controller serves. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether an authorization decision can be reproduced consistently across every path that returns the same rows; [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether that decision lives in one place. GetReadSpecificationAsync(cancellationToken) (:627-629) returns the Specification<TEntity, TIdentifierType> applied by all seven read actions: both GetAllAsync overloads, GetAllForLookupAsync, GetByIdAsync, ExportAsync, GetCursorPageAsync, and GetChangesAsync (each resolves it at :115, :170, :325, :369, :271, :422, and :469; the list is on the hook's doc at :592-594). Four properties are worth internalizing, all stated on the hook's own doc (:591-626).
      • It is asynchronous because row scoping usually is (:603-608). Scope is rarely a pure function of the current principal: it comes from a query handler, a claim lookup that hits a store, a tenancy read. A synchronous hook forced such a controller to override every read action by hand purely to get an await in before the query. An override with nothing to await returns ValueTask.FromResult(...) and allocates nothing.
      • It narrows, it never replaces (:611-615). The query service ANDs the specification with the caller's filters dictionary and fields projection, so a caller can only narrow what the specification already allows; a filter naming excluded rows yields an empty page rather than leaking them (:138-141).
      • A rejected row is a 404, not a 403 (:618-620, restated on GetByIdAsync at :351-356). The specification narrows the query, so the row is simply absent. Answering "forbidden" would confirm the id exists and turn a scoped read into an existence oracle a caller could walk.
      • The lookup endpoint carries the scope as a predicate (:311-317). GetAllForLookupAsync has no specification parameter, so the scope travels as specification?.Criteria (:329); a null specification passes a null predicate, the unscoped query this endpoint always issued. A dropdown that lists what the list endpoint hides would be an oracle of its own. GetExportSpecification() (:657) is the synchronous half: it returns null by default and is what GetReadSpecificationAsync returns by default (:629). A controller that can build its scope without awaiting overrides this one and gets all seven actions scoped; a controller that needs an await overrides the async hook instead, and then this one is no longer consulted (:639-643). For the JSON reads a null specification still means unscoped; for the export it means refused (next concept), so a row-scoped controller that overrides neither hook gets a 403 on /export rather than handing every caller the whole table (:646-649). See ADR-033 for the ownership model this hook reproduces in the query.
    • Concept introduced: a bulk read that fails closed when no scope was declared. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether the default on a sensitive path is the safe one. ExportAsync is the one read that can hand a caller a whole table in one request, so it does not treat a null specification as "unscoped": when the hook resolves to null and AllowUnscopedExport is false, it returns before any query runs (:274-275) with the Error.Forbidden built by UnscopedExportRefused (:664-669), which HandleFailure turns into a 403 Problem Details carrying the code ExportRowScopeRequiredErrorCode = "Export.RowScopeRequired" (:528; the 403 is declared on the action at :256). The error message names the three ways out: override GetReadSpecificationAsync, override GetExportSpecification, or opt in.
      • AllowUnscopedExport (protected virtual bool, default false, :549) is the deliberate opt-in. Its doc (:530-548) limits it to controllers whose rows every caller allowed to reach the endpoint may see (reference data, a catalog, an admin-only table already behind a role gate), and notes it is read per request, so it may depend on the principal: return null from the read hook for an administrator and a specification for everyone else, and opt in only for the administrator.
      • A non-null specification never consults the property (:545-546): a scoped export needs no opt-in. The effect is that a controller which forgot to scope its export serves no rows rather than every row (:232-239).
    • Concept introduced: opt-in keyset paging and a change feed. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] (ADR-144). Both actions carry [OptInAction(...)], so they exist only on a controller that declares the matching attribute: GetCursorPageAsync needs SupportsCursorPagingAttribute (:403-404) and GetChangesAsync needs SupportsChangeFeedAttribute (:456-457). Both clamp the page size to MaxPageSize (:419, :467), read the same row-scoping hook, and unwrap with TryGetValue into Ok or HandleFailure (:429-431, :474-476).
      • GET /cursor ([HttpGet("cursor")], :403) returns one seek page after an opaque cursor, ordered by sortColumn with Id as the tie-break, plus the next page's cursor (null on the last page). It validates the sort direction first (:415-417) and calls QueryService.GetPageByCursorAsync with a KeysetPageRequest (:424-427). Unlike the paged endpoint it has no total, no pagination header, no field projection, no includes, and no filter dictionary: the keyset read takes a specification only, and a malformed cursor or an unknown sort column is a 400 (:398-402).
      • GET /changes ([HttpGet("changes")], :456, default page size 100 at :464) returns one page of EntityChange<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> rows changed at or after since, ordered by (LastModifiedOn, Id), each an upsert carrying the DTO or a tombstone for a soft-deleted row (:435-438), through QueryService.GetChangesSinceAsync (:471-472). The bound is inclusive, so a client pages with the same since until the cursor is null, then keeps the largest changedOn as its next since, and applies the repeated boundary rows idempotently by id and row version; a row that left the read scope without being deleted yields no tombstone (:447-453).
    • Concept introduced: streaming a bulk extract from a paged read. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether a large response is bounded and whether memory grows with the result set; [Rubric §11, Security] covers who may pull a whole table in one request. ExportAsync answers the "export what you filtered" request without any new query path (ADR-078). The action itself is a thin adapter over EntityCsvExporter<TEntityDTO>, which owns the page loop, the column resolution, and the CSV format; this controller keeps only the HTTP concerns.
      • A dedicated route, not content negotiation ([HttpGet("export")], :253). The remarks name the two behaviors that make an Accept: text/csv formatter wrong here (:198-203): the public output-cache policy varies by query string but not by Accept, so a cached JSON body could be replayed to a CSV request, and AddAPI sets ReturnHttpNotAcceptable = false (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:49), so a negotiation miss falls back to JSON silently instead of returning 406. A distinct path has neither failure mode.
      • Field validation before a byte moves (:266-268): EntityCsvExporter<TEntityDTO>.ValidateFields rejects a fields= request naming a property the CSV cannot render, as an Error.InvalidEntityField failure, rather than quietly dropping the column.
      • Row scoping through the shared hook, fail-closed: the specification is resolved once, before the first page (:271), and refused when null without the opt-in (:274-275, previous concept), so the same closed-over instance filters every page the fetch delegate reads, and it is the same hook the list endpoints read, so an export cannot drift wider than the list it mirrors.
      • The page loop lives in the exporter: ExportAsync builds a fetch delegate that calls QueryService.GetAllAsync (:282-293) at pageSize = Math.Max(1, MaxPageSize) (:278) and hands it, beginResponse, and onFailureAfterStart to EntityCsvExporter<TEntityDTO>.WriteAsync (:280); the loop, its termination conditions, and the truncation bookkeeping are documented on that type.
      • Navigations for computed columns, never child columns: the export takes no includeChildren parameter, but the fetch delegate loads children when ExportIncludeChildren is overridden to true and foreign keys when either the request's includeFKs or ExportIncludeFKs is set (:283-284). Both are protected virtual bool defaulting to false (:557, :564), for a DTO that computes a scalar from a loaded navigation (a count of children, a parent's name); the collections themselves still earn no CSV column (:551-556, :222-225).
      • Headers first, then body (BeginExportResponse, :675): content type text/csv; charset=utf-8 (CsvContentType, :516, set at :679), a Content-Disposition attachment whose file name is {controller}-{yyyyMMdd'T'HHmmss'Z'}.csv built invariantly from an injected TimeProvider (:677, :680, BuildExportFileName at :691-694, prefix ExportFileNamePrefix at :576-589), and X-Export-Row-Limit (ExportRowLimitHeaderName, :522, appended at :681) so a client can tell "exactly at the limit" from "coincidentally that many rows".
      • Truncation rides in the body. Headers freeze the moment the first body byte flushes, so a truncated export ends with a # export truncated at N rows record (marker built by EntityCsvExporter<TEntityDTO>.TruncationMarker; the remarks at :213-219 name the same line) and a mid-stream query failure ends with an incomplete marker plus a Warning log (LogExportPageFailure, :702-714, wired as onFailureAfterStart at :298). A failure on the FIRST page, before anything was written, still returns Problem Details through HandleFailure (:302), which is exactly what "constructing the writer sends nothing" protects on the exporter side.
      • Column resolution is derived, not invented: EntityCsvExporter<TEntityDTO>.ResolveColumns takes the shaped keys of the first row, so the CSV columns for a given fields= request are the same camelCase JSON names the JSON endpoints emit; an empty result still gets a header row built from the DTO's own properties in declaration order. UnexportablePropertyNames on that type drops the properties that cannot render a faithful scalar cell, byte[]/ReadOnlyMemory<byte> concurrency tokens and every collection type except string, computed once per closed DTO type. Value objects and other class-typed properties are deliberately NOT dropped, because a record or value object has a meaningful invariant ToString. See EntityCsvExporter<TEntityDTO> for the full walkthrough.
    • Why it's built this way: the controller stays thin. All filtering/sorting/paging lives in IEntityQueryService<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>, and manual DTO mapping (ADR-001) keeps entities off the wire. The controller only translates HTTP concerns: query strings, headers, status codes. The ETag emission and its per-type reflection live on ApiControllerBase, so a conditional write answering from a non-entity controller emits the same header the by-id read does. The export reuses the paged read wholesale precisely so it cannot disagree with the grid it was launched from, and the row ceiling (DefaultMaxExportRows = 100_000, :513, matching ApplicationSettings.MaxExportRows's own default) is a number an operator can reason about rather than an unbounded connection hold. The fail-closed default puts the cost of a forgotten scope on the controller author (a 403 in their own tests) instead of on the data. The cursor and change-feed actions are opt-in so an existing controller's route surface does not grow until its author asks for it.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the export carries no authorization attributes of its own. It inherits whatever [Authorize] or [FeatureGate] the derived controller declares, so a controller that exposes paged anonymously exposes export anonymously once it scopes the rows or opts in; the symmetry is deliberate and documented (:206-210). The fail-closed rule applies to ExportAsync only: the JSON reads, including the cursor and change-feed actions, still run unscoped on a null specification. The export is also not output-cached.
    • Where it's used: the base for every read-only module controller, for example ADC's child-collection controllers SessionSpeakersController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Sessions/SessionSpeakersController.cs:61) and CategoryItemsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Categories/CategoryItemsController.cs:70). Extended by AggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest> for entities that also create and delete. The scoping hooks are widely overridden: the async GetReadSpecificationAsync by ADC's SpeakersController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Speakers/SpeakersController.cs:116), SessionsController (SessionsController.cs:80), RoomsController (RoomsController.cs:130) and their child controllers, and by Store's owner-scoped ShoppingCartsController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/ShoppingCartsController.cs:200); the synchronous GetExportSpecification by ADC's EventsController (EventsController.cs:73) and SessionQuestionAnswersController (SessionQuestionAnswersController.cs:111) and by Store's OrdersController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.API/Controllers/OrdersController.cs:241). AllowUnscopedExport is overridden two ways. Unconditional true on reference and catalog data: ADC's ConferenceCategoriesController (ConferenceCategoriesController.cs:44), QuestionsController (QuestionsController.cs:43) and CategoryItemsController (CategoryItemsController.cs:73), and Store's ProductsController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Catalog/MMCA.Store.Catalog.API/Controllers/ProductsController.cs:51), CategoriesController (CategoriesController.cs:48), InventoryItemsController (InventoryItemsController.cs:43) and CustomersController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.API/Controllers/CustomersController.cs:48), whose export sits behind CustomersManage and whose list endpoints are Admin-only rather than row-scoped (:90-104). Per principal, where the read hook returns null to a privileged caller: ADC's SpeakersController (SpeakersController.cs:126), SessionsController (SessionsController.cs:98), RoomsController (RoomsController.cs:148), EventsController (EventsController.cs:81), SessionQuestionAnswersController (SessionQuestionAnswersController.cs:123) and their siblings, and Store's OrdersController (OrdersController.cs:249) and ShoppingCartsController (ShoppingCartsController.cs:209). Framework coverage lives in EntityControllerBaseTests, EntityControllerBaseExportTests (opt-in doubles at EntityControllerBaseExportTests.cs:597 and :652), EntityControllerBaseETagTests, and EntityControllerBaseReadSpecificationTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/), the last of which drives both hooks through purpose-built doubles (EntityControllerBaseReadSpecificationTests.cs:358 and :377).

    AggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest>

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Controllers · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:29 · Level 8 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the read-plus-create-plus-delete tier of the controller hierarchy. It extends EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (the read endpoints) by adding a CreateAsync (POST) and a DeleteAsync (DELETE) for aggregate-root entities.
    • Depends on: EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (base), IAggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest> (implements), ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> (create and delete handlers), DeleteEntityCommand<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> (constraint), ICreateRequest (constraint), IdempotentAttribute; ASP.NET Core MVC and Asp.Versioning.
    • Concept introduced: idempotent creation guarded at the endpoint. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses safe mutation; CreateAsync carries [Idempotent] (AggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:76, beside [HttpPost] at :75), which wires IdempotencyFilter so a retried POST carrying the same Idempotency-Key replays the original 201 (flagged X-Idempotent-Replay: true, IdempotencyFilter.cs:41) instead of creating a duplicate aggregate, exactly what mobile and flaky-network clients need. A duplicate that arrives while the first request is still running and cannot take the lock within the 5-second LockWait (IdempotencyFilter.cs:105, awaited at IdempotencyFilter.cs:251) is answered with 409 Conflict rather than a replay (IdempotencyFilter.cs:305-310). Because the fitness rule reads attributes with inherit: true, every concrete controller that inherits this action satisfies its POST idempotency-intent obligation through this base (see NonIdempotentAttribute). [Rubric §1, SOLID]: the four constraints (AggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:42-45, notably TEntity : AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType>) enforce at compile time that only aggregate roots reach this create/delete surface.
    • Walkthrough
      • Primary constructor (AggregateRootEntityControllerBase.cs:29-40): four parameters, where queryService and logger are forwarded to the EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> base (:40), plus createHandler and deleteHandler. The logger is typed ILogger<EntityControllerBase<...>>, not of this class, because ILogger<T> is not covariant and the base ctor requires that exact type; the #pragma warning disable S6672 (:37-39) is a justified, narrowly-scoped suppression documenting exactly that ([Rubric §15, Best Practices]).
      • CreateHandler property (:50): protected, so a derived controller that overrides CreateAsync to build a more specific command can still reach the handler. deleteHandler stays a captured constructor parameter, used directly at :115, because nothing overrides delete today.
      • GetByIdRouteName (:57): a protected virtual string defaulting to $"Get{EntityName}ById", the route name CreateAsync links the new resource to. A derived controller that names its by-id route differently overrides it.
      • CreateAsync (:80-98): [HttpPost] plus [Idempotent] (:75-76), body bound [FromBody, Required] (:81); it dispatches the create command (:84) and unwraps the DTO with result.TryGetValue(out var created) (:86), returning HandleFailure on a miss (:86-89), so the success path reads a non-null created with no ! suppression. On success it resolves the Location itself, before returning (:93-95), and returns Created(location, created) (:97). The remarks (:67-74) give the reason: a CreatedAtRoute naming a route the derived controller does not declare throws only when the result executes, after the entity was saved, so the client would get a 500 for a create that succeeded. Url.Link(GetByIdRouteName, ...) supplies an absolute URL when the route resolves (:93-94); otherwise CollectionMemberPath (:126-131) appends the escaped id to the request's own path (PathBase + Path, trailing slash trimmed), a host-relative Location that RFC 9110 permits and where the inherited GET {id} answers. Each branch is parsed with its own UriKind, because RelativeOrAbsolute reads /x/1 as a file URI on Unix (:91-92).
      • DeleteAsync (:111-120): [HttpDelete("{id}")] (:106); builds a DeleteEntityCommand<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, dispatches it, and returns NoContent() on success. Delete here means soft-delete: the handler loads the aggregate and calls its Delete() method, so the domain, not the controller, decides whether the removal is allowed.
    • Why it's built this way: splitting the read-only base from the aggregate-root base means a child-collection controller (add/remove associations, not create whole aggregates) can extend the read base without inheriting create/delete it should not expose ([Rubric §1, SOLID], Interface Segregation), while the actual work stays in injected Application-layer handlers ([Rubric §3, Clean Architecture]) that the CQRS decorator pipeline already wraps with validation, transactions, and cache invalidation (ADR-014). Update is deliberately NOT here: it needs a fifth type parameter, so it lives on CrudEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest, TUpdateRequest> instead of changing this type's generic arity.
    • Where it's used: concrete aggregate controllers in the modules extend this, for example ADC's EventsController (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/Events/EventsController.cs:58) and SessionsController (SessionsController.cs:60), and Store's CustomersController (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.API/Controllers/CustomersController.cs:43); child-only controllers deliberately extend the read-only base instead. Framework coverage lives in AggregateRootEntityControllerBaseTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/AggregateRootEntityControllerBaseTests.cs).

    CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.FeatureManagement · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/FeatureManagement/CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor.cs:68 · Level 8 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the ITargetingContextAccessor that supplies the audience (a user id plus that user's groups, including a tenant:<tenantId> group when the request resolved a tenant) which the feature-management Targeting filter evaluates, read from the current HTTP request.
    • Depends on: Microsoft.FeatureManagement.FeatureFilters.ITargetingContextAccessor and TargetingContext, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.IHttpContextAccessor, System.Security.Claims, ClaimsPrincipalExtensions for the user-id read, and ITenantContext resolved from the request's own services (CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor.cs:1-6). Registered by AddAPI; a sibling of DisabledFeatureHandler in the same folder.
    • Concept introduced: a percentage rollout that is sticky per user rather than random per request. A Percentage feature filter with no targeting rolls a die on every evaluation, so the same user sees the feature on one request and off the next: unusable for a UI. The Targeting filter fixes that by hashing the audience's user id, which makes the answer deterministic for a given user across requests and across instances, and this accessor is what supplies that id (:11-16). [Rubric §29, Resilience, Reliability & Business Continuity] assesses whether a cross-cutting toggle is applied uniformly; [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §17, DevOps] both bear on the rollout being an operational lever rather than a deploy. See ADR-031. Two source decisions are worth carrying. First, the user id is the standard sub claim TokenService emits, read through ClaimsPrincipalExtensions so the ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier form the bearer handler maps it to resolves identically, the same read CurrentUserService and IdempotencyFilter perform (:18-22); the principal's name is the fallback for a token carrying neither. Second, the accessor is a singleton (that is the lifetime WithTargeting gives it), so it cannot take the scoped ICurrentUserService; it reads IHttpContextAccessor instead and re-derives the roles itself, which the doc calls out explicitly (:25-26).
    • Concept introduced: tenant as a targeting group. [Rubric §29, Resilience, Reliability & Business Continuity] and [Rubric §17, DevOps]: a flag can be turned on for one tenant without a per-tenant configuration store. When the request's ITenantContext has resolved a tenant (ADR-073), the groups also carry tenant:<tenantId>, so an audience group such as tenant:acme turns a flag on for every request of that tenant (:29-34). The prefix is the public constant TenantGroupPrefix = "tenant:" (:75), and the public TenantGroup(string tenantId) (:83) builds the name exactly as the accessor emits it (rejecting a null or blank id at :85, concatenating at :86), so configuration tooling and tests cannot spell the group differently. ITenantContext is scoped, so ResolveTenantGroups (:128) reads it from HttpContext.RequestServices rather than taking it as a dependency of this singleton, and a host that never registered it, or a request that resolved no tenant, contributes no group (:126-127, :130-131). The group only matters to an audience that names it, so a host that targets nothing by tenant sees no change (:33-34).
    • Walkthrough: GetContextAsync() (:95) reads the current HttpContext (:97), its principal (:98), and the tenant groups (:99) up front. An unauthenticated or absent principal yields a context with UserId = null and only the tenant groups (:101-108, Groups = tenantGroups at :106), so a targeted feature is off for anonymous callers unless the audience opts everyone in or names their tenant (:37-39); the method never returns null, because a feature filter must not be able to fail a request (:90-92). For an authenticated caller it collects the role claims, accepting each claim type the JWT middleware may produce: the standard ClaimTypes.Role URI when inbound claim mapping is on, or the raw role / roles claim when it is off (:110-114), and appends the tenant groups (:116). Finally it builds the TargetingContext with user.FindUserIdValue() ?? user.Identity.Name (:121) and those groups (:122).
    • Why it's built this way: accepting three role claim types is not defensive padding, it is the concrete consequence of ASP.NET Core's inbound claim mapping being configurable; matching only ClaimTypes.Role would silently drop every group when a host turns mapping off, and a group-targeted rollout would then behave as an ungrouped one. Folding the tenant into the existing Groups list, rather than adding a custom filter, keeps the stock Targeting filter and its configuration shape unchanged. The class doc carries a worked FeatureManagement configuration example (:41-65) showing a rollout that always includes one role (Reviewers) and every request of tenant acme, includes 25 percent of everyone else, and pins two named users, which is the fastest way to see what the context is actually feeding.
    • Where it's used: registered inside AddAPI as services.AddFeatureManagement().WithTargeting<CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:108-109), immediately after AddHttpContextAccessor() (:90, which is TryAdd-based and therefore safe to call here as well as elsewhere, the reasoning recorded at :84-89). From there it is consumed only by the Targeting feature filter, whose verdicts reach the HTTP edge through [FeatureGate] and DisabledFeatureHandler, and the CQRS layer through FeatureGateCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>. Framework coverage is CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessorTests and, for the tenant group end to end, TenantTargetedFeatureFlagTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/FeatureManagement/).

    CrudEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest, TUpdateRequest>

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Controllers · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/CrudEntityControllerBase.cs:55 · Level 8 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the top rung of the generic controller chain. It adds the one endpoint AggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest> leaves out, a conditional PUT /{id}, completing read, create, update, and delete with no per-entity action bodies at all.
    • Depends on: AggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest> (base), ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> with UpdateEntityCommand<TEntity, TUpdateRequest, TIdentifierType>, SupportsIfMatchAttribute, IdempotentAttribute, AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> and ICreateRequest (constraints, CrudEntityControllerBase.cs:70-73); ASP.NET Core MVC and Asp.Versioning.
    • Concept introduced: adding an endpoint without changing a shipped generic arity. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether a capability can be added without disturbing what already works, and [Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain] covers what a version bump costs a consumer. The update endpoint needs a fifth type, the update request. Adding that parameter to the shipped four-parameter base would change that type's arity, and every controller in every consuming app would stop compiling on the next version bump (CrudEntityControllerBase.cs:23-30). So this base is purely additive: a controller offering only create and delete keeps inheriting the four-parameter base; one that also offers update inherits this and gains the action. Note also what did not change: IAggregateRootEntityControllerBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest> gained no UpdateAsync member, for the same reason.
