The grouped shape is chosen to match what ASP.NET Core's own model-state validation emits (comment, ValidationExceptionHandler.cs:46-47), so a client form component can render field errors with one code path regardless of whether the failure came from model binding or from a validator running in the CQRS validating decorator.
    • Walkthrough: TryHandleAsync (ValidationExceptionHandler.cs:23) type-tests and passes on non-validation exceptions (:28-29), logs at LogWarning (:31, not LogError: an invalid payload is a client mistake, not a system fault), sets 400 (:33), builds the problem document titled "Validation Exception" (:34-44), then groups validationException.Errors by PropertyName into a Dictionary<string, string[]> (:48-53) and adds it under the "errors" extension key (:54) before writing (:56).
    • Why it's built this way: the grouping consolidates several failures for one field into one array, which is exactly the ModelStateDictionary serialization front ends already understand. Note the key is the raw PropertyName from FluentValidation, not a camelCased alias, and that Extensions.Add (:54) would throw on a duplicate key, which cannot happen here because the document was just constructed.

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Middleware · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:245 · Level 0 · class (internal sealed, attribute)

    • What it is: a marker attribute for the one action a view-as token may call with a non-safe HTTP method: ending the view. It has no members; its presence in the routed endpoint's metadata is the whole signal.
    • Depends on: System.Attribute only. It is declared with [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method, Inherited = true)] (ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:244) in the same file as its only reader, ViewAsGuardMiddleware.
    • Concept: endpoint metadata as an allow-list. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether a read-only support session (ADR-137) can reach a write: the guard refuses every non-safe method under a view-as token, and this attribute is the single exemption, read from the endpoint rather than matched by path, so the exemption follows the action wherever a host routes its auth controller (doc comment, ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:238-243).
    • Walkthrough: the declaration is one line, internal sealed class ViewAsEndEndpointAttribute : Attribute; (ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:245). The guard's IsEndViewAsEndpoint (:109-111) treats a request as the end-view-as call only when the method is POST and context.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<ViewAsEndEndpointAttribute>() is not null.

    DbUpdateExceptionHandler

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Middleware · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:18 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the IExceptionHandler that turns an EF Core DbUpdateException into an HTTP 409 Conflict RFC 9457 response with a deliberately generic body, while the full exception is logged server-side.
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.IExceptionHandler, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.IProblemDetailsService, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbUpdateException, and the internal ConcurrencyConflictMetrics counter (using MMCA.Common.API.Concurrency; at DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:6). Siblings in the same chain: OperationCanceledExceptionHandler, DomainExceptionHandler, ValidationExceptionHandler, and the catch-all GlobalExceptionHandler.
    • Concept introduced: the IExceptionHandler chain. ASP.NET Core resolves registered IExceptionHandler implementations in registration order and calls TryHandleAsync on each: returning true claims the exception and stops the chain, returning false passes it on. The framework registers the chain in AddCommonExceptionHandlers() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:157-168) as OperationCanceled (:159), then Domain (:160), then DbUpdate (:161), then Validation (:162), then Global (:163), and that same method calls AddProblemDetails with a customization that stamps a requestId extension from HttpContext.TraceIdentifier onto every problem document (DependencyInjection.cs:159-161). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether errors have one uniform, standards-based shape: every handler here writes RFC 9457 application/problem+json through the same IProblemDetailsService, so controllers never need a try/catch. [Rubric §11, Security] applies to this handler specifically, see below.
    • Walkthrough: TryHandleAsync (DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:24):
      • Type-tests with is not DbUpdateException dbUpdateException and returns false (DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:29-30) so the rest of the chain still gets its turn.
      • Logs the exception at LogError (:32).
      • When the exception is the DbUpdateConcurrencyException subtype, calls ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.RecordConflict(concurrencyException) (:36-39), which adds one to the persistence.concurrency.conflict counter tagged by entity type (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Concurrency/ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:37-47). The comment at DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:34-35 states why only that subtype is counted: a unique-key or foreign-key failure has its own remedy, and folding it in would hide the contention signal.
      • Sets StatusCodes.Status409Conflict (:41) for every DbUpdateException, concurrency or not.
      • Builds the client-facing detail as the fixed string "A data conflict occurred. Please retry or contact support." (:45), with the comment stating why (:43-44): leaking the EF message would expose table, column and constraint names. The full exception is already in the log.
      • Assembles a ProblemDetailsContext titled "Database Update Exception" (:47-57) and returns await problemDetailsService.TryWriteAsync(context) (:59), so the response body is whatever the configured ProblemDetailsService writes.
    • Why it's built this way: 409 is the honest status for a write rejected by a constraint or a concurrency token, and the split between a rich server-side log and a generic client body is the standard information-disclosure posture.
    • Where it's used: registered third in AddCommonExceptionHandlers() (DependencyInjection.cs:164), ahead of GlobalExceptionHandler. Note that a DbUpdateConcurrencyException on an action carrying SupportsIfMatchAttribute never reaches this handler: that filter converts it to 412, records the same conflict metric itself, and sets ExceptionHandled = true (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Concurrency/SupportsIfMatchAttribute.cs:181-188). A given exception reaches exactly one of the two, so each conflict is counted once (ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:14-17).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: no alert ships on the conflict counter (ConcurrencyConflictMetrics.cs:20-21); a sustained rate on one entity type is read as a design question about contended rows, not an incident. The class doc comment (DbUpdateExceptionHandler.cs:10-15) matches the code: a fixed generic detail, no constraint name leaked.

    DomainExceptionHandler

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Middleware · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/DomainExceptionHandler.cs:16 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the handler that translates a DomainException into a 400 Bad Request problem document whose detail is the domain message itself.
    • Depends on: DomainException (MMCA.Common.Shared.Exceptions, imported at DomainExceptionHandler.cs:5), IProblemDetailsService, ILogger<DomainExceptionHandler>; chain concept at DbUpdateExceptionHandler.
    • Concept: [Rubric §4, DDD] assesses whether the domain's vocabulary survives the trip to the edge, and [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] whether the status code tells the truth about who is at fault. A domain exception is a broken business rule, not a system fault, so two things differ from the other handlers: it logs at LogWarning (DomainExceptionHandler.cs:30) rather than LogError, and it is the one handler that puts the raw exception message into the client-facing Detail (:41). That is safe precisely because a DomainException message is authored by the domain layer for humans, unlike an EF or infrastructure message.
    • Walkthrough: TryHandleAsync (DomainExceptionHandler.cs:22) type-tests and returns false otherwise (:27-28), logs the warning (:30), sets StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest (:32), and writes a problem document titled "Domain Exception" with the domain message as its detail (:33-45).
    • Why it's built this way: it sits second in the chain (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:163), ahead of the infrastructure handlers, so a business-rule violation never gets mislabeled as a database conflict or an internal error. Remember that the framework's primary path for business failures is the Result pattern; this handler covers the code that still throws.
    • Where it's used: AddCommonExceptionHandlers() (DependencyInjection.cs:163).

    GlobalExceptionHandler

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Middleware · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/GlobalExceptionHandler.cs:30 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the last handler in the IExceptionHandler chain. It claims anything the specific handlers declined and answers HTTP 500 as RFC 9457 problem details, with two exception types mapped on the way: a CrossTenantWriteException is answered 400 instead, and a BadHttpRequestException is answered with the status it carries (413 or 400 typically).
    • Depends on: IProblemDetailsService and ILogger<GlobalExceptionHandler> (primary-constructor injected, GlobalExceptionHandler.cs:30-33), plus CrossTenantWriteException from MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Persistence.Interceptors (imported at :5). Chain concept introduced at DbUpdateExceptionHandler.
    • Concept: [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether error handling is factored out of business code, and [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] whether failures are always recorded. This handler is the guarantee for both: no exception can escape the pipeline as a raw stack trace or an unlogged 500, because it never returns false on a type test. [Rubric §11, Security] covers the second half: the cross-tenant detail is deliberately free of everything the exception carries, because echoing a tenant id back tells an unauthorized caller which tenant owns the row it just tried to write (GlobalExceptionHandler.cs:38-43). The bad-request path applies the same restraint: its detail is a fixed sentence, never the exception message (:93-95).
    • Walkthrough: TryHandleAsync (GlobalExceptionHandler.cs:49) has three paths.
      • CrossTenantWriteTitle (:36) and CrossTenantWriteDetail (:44-46) are internal const strings, so the tests assert against the same literals the handler writes.
      • The tenant-boundary path (:54-72): a CrossTenantWriteException is logged at LogWarning (:58), because the request was refused exactly as designed and a tenant-scoped API answering 400 to an untenanted write is routine rather than a server fault (:56-57). It sets Status400BadRequest (:60) and returns TryWriteAsync with the two constants (:61-71).
      • The bad-request path (:74-98): a BadHttpRequestException (Kestrel or model binding rejected a malformed or oversize request) is a caller fault, so it is logged at LogWarning with its status code (:80) and answered with the status the exception already carries, passed through unchanged (:82). The title is "Payload Too Large" when that status is Status413PayloadTooLarge and "Bad Request" otherwise (:90-92), and the detail follows the same split (:93-95).
      • The catch-all path (:100-113): logs "Unhandled exception occurred" with the exception at LogError (:100), sets StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError (:102), and returns the result of problemDetailsService.TryWriteAsync(...) (:103-113) with the generic title "Internal Server Error" and a "please try again" detail (:110-111). The exception object is attached to the ProblemDetailsContext (:106) so a configured customization can enrich the document (in development, for example) without this class deciding what to expose.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc explains why the cross-tenant mapping lives here rather than in a handler of its own (GlobalExceptionHandler.cs:13-19): CrossTenantWriteException derives from InvalidOperationException, so nothing ahead of this handler claims it, while every other save-time invariant failure of that family still ends at the 500. The BadHttpRequestException mapping is documented beside it (:20-26): the exception already knows which client status applies, so the handler passes it through rather than collapsing an oversize body into a 500. Returning TryWriteAsync's own boolean rather than a hard-coded true keeps the handler honest: if no problem-details writer can serve the request, the framework is told the exception was not fully handled instead of silently swallowing it. Registration order is the only thing that makes it the fallback, so it is registered last (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/DependencyInjection.cs:166); its own doc says so (DependencyInjection.cs:153-154).
    • Where it's used: AddCommonExceptionHandlers() (DependencyInjection.cs:166); every host that calls it inherits the same 500 contract, the same tenant-boundary 400 and the same bad-request pass-through.

    CorrelationIdMiddleware

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Middleware · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs:20 · Level 9 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: convention-based middleware that establishes one correlation ID per request, publishes it on the scoped ICorrelationContext, and echoes it back to the caller in the X-Correlation-ID response header.
    • Depends on: ICorrelationContext (injected per invoke, so it is resolved from the request scope) and System.Diagnostics.Activity (CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs:1-3).
    • Concept: distributed trace correlation is introduced at ICorrelationContext; this is the type that populates it. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether one logical operation can be reconstructed across log entries and services: with this middleware second in the pipeline, every later log line, outbox row and downstream call can carry the same ID.
    • Walkthrough
      • HeaderName = "X-Correlation-ID" (CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs:23) is a public const, so clients, tests and downstream code all name the header from one place.
      • MaxLength = 64 (:26) is an internal const: the width of the persisted correlation columns (its doc comment at :25).
      • InvokeAsync(HttpContext, ICorrelationContext) (:35): the second parameter is per-invoke injected, which is how convention-based middleware consumes a scoped service from a singleton middleware instance. Both arguments are null-guarded (:37-38).
      • The resolution waterfall (:40-43): an inbound X-Correlation-ID header wins when it is not null, empty or whitespace (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace) and survives Sanitize (:41); otherwise Activity.Current?.TraceId (the W3C trace ID that OpenTelemetry propagates, :42), else ASP.NET's HttpContext.TraceIdentifier (:43). The chain is null-coalescing, so a header that Sanitize rejects falls through to the generated ID exactly as a blank one does. A usable caller-supplied ID is therefore honored, and the ID always exists.
      • Sanitize (:61-65) cuts a caller value longer than MaxLength to its first 64 characters with a range slice (:63), then keeps it only when every character is printable ASCII, >= ' ' and <= '~' (:64); any other character yields null.
      • correlationContext.SetCorrelationId(correlationId) (:45) publishes it, then context.Response.OnStarting(...) (:46-50) registers a callback that writes the response header. Writing it in OnStarting rather than after next(...) completes is the only safe way: once the response has begun, header writes throw.
      • return next(context) (:52) continues the pipeline. InvokeAsync is a plain Task-returning method, not async (:35): it has no work after the call, so it hands back the downstream task directly instead of allocating a state machine.
    • Why it's built this way: accepting the client's ID makes cross-system correlation possible when the caller already has a trace, and falling back to Activity.Current means the correlation ID and the OpenTelemetry trace ID are the same value in a normally instrumented host. Truncating at the boundary rather than at the database means the id echoed in the response header is exactly the one stored (class comment, :13-15), and treating a blank header as absent keeps an empty value from displacing the trace-ID fallback. Replacing a non-ASCII or control-character value with the generated ID is a defense for the echo itself: Kestrel refuses to write such a value into a response header, which would fail the request after its handler had already run (class comment, :15-17).
    • Where it's used: it is the second step of the default pipeline, right after the exception handler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:38-40, following ExceptionHandler at :34-36), so everything downstream (including the exception handlers above) logs under a known ID. The step is named MiddlewarePipelineStepNames.CorrelationId (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineStepNames.cs:20), which is the handle a host uses to insert its own middleware around it. The CQRS logging decorators read the same context.

    ErrorHttpMapping

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Middleware · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ErrorHttpMapping.cs:14 · Level 3 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the single table that maps domain ErrorType values to HTTP status codes, the ranking rule that picks one status for a whole failure, and the builder for the errors extension array that problem documents carry.

[Rubric §27, i18n] applies through the localizer parameter.
