    AppAssociationEndpointExtensions

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Startup.Endpoints · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/AppAssociationEndpointExtensions.cs:15 · Level 1 · class (static, extension block)

    • What it is: a mapping helper that serves the two well-known app-association documents from an AppAssociationOptions: Android Digital Asset Links at /.well-known/assetlinks.json and the Apple App Site Association at /.well-known/apple-app-site-association.
    • Depends on: AppAssociationOptions (Level 0) for every value; ASP.NET IEndpointRouteBuilder and Results.Json.
    • Concept (anonymous, machine-verified association documents). Both endpoints are anonymous by design because the OS and Apple's CDN fetch them without credentials, which the doc comment states (AppAssociationEndpointExtensions.cs:12-13). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: the exact JSON shape is a contract a third party parses, so the code builds it structurally out of dictionaries rather than formatting strings by hand.
    • Walkthrough
      • Two path constants: AssetLinksPath (AppAssociationEndpointExtensions.cs:18) and AppleAppSiteAssociationPath (:24). The comment on the Apple constant (:20-23) records that the path deliberately has no file extension because Apple requires that exact path, while the content type must still be JSON.
      • MapAppAssociationEndpoints(AppAssociationOptions options) (:35) null-guards the options (:37), builds both documents once at map time because they are static for the process lifetime (:39-40), then maps two GETs that each return Results.Json(...), are .AllowAnonymous() and are .ExcludeFromDescription() so they never leak into the OpenAPI document (:42-48).
      • BuildAssetLinks (:54) emits the delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls relation with the Android package name and the fingerprint list (:56-65).
      • BuildAppleAppSiteAssociation (:68) emits the applinks details block, projecting each configured URL pattern into a { "/": pattern } component (:78-80), plus the webcredentials apps list naming the same app id (:84-87).
    • Why it's built this way: building the payload once at map time avoids a per-request allocation for a document that never changes [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability], and holding the RFC 8615 well-known paths as public constants keeps them from drifting between hosts or between the endpoint and any gateway forwarding rule.
    • Where it's used: the ADC Blazor web host maps them once at startup (MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:144), which is the host that ships a companion MAUI Hybrid app. Both documents' exact shapes are asserted by AppAssociationEndpointTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Startup/AppAssociationEndpointTests.cs).

    JwksEndpointExtensions

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Startup.Endpoints · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/JwksEndpointExtensions.cs:15 · Level 1 · class (static, extension block)

    • What it is: maps /.well-known/jwks.json, serializing the active JsonWebKeySet of the Identity service so other services can validate its RS256 tokens.
    • Depends on: IJwksProvider, resolved from DI per request, whose implementation is RsaJwksProvider; plus Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens.JsonWebKeySet and System.Text.Json.
    • Concept (the public-key distribution endpoint of cross-service auth). [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]: with RS256 only the Identity service holds the private key, and every other service fetches the public keys from here, so no shared secret ever crosses a service boundary (ADR-004). The endpoint is .AllowAnonymous() (JwksEndpointExtensions.cs:39) because clients fetch it before they have a token, which is what JWKS means (RFC 7517; the doc comment says so at :27-28).
    • Walkthrough: the DefaultJwksPath constant (JwksEndpointExtensions.cs:20) pins the RFC 8615 path. MapJwksEndpoint() (:31) maps a single GET whose handler takes HttpContext and IJwksProvider as parameters (:33), calls GetJsonWebKeySet() (:35), serializes with JsonSerializer (:36), sets application/json; charset=utf-8 explicitly (:37), and writes the body (:38). The whole endpoint is under ten lines because the key material and its rotation live behind the provider.
    • Why it's built this way: non-Identity hosts still map it (the JwksEndpoint step is unconditional in the default pipeline, MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:143-150); their provider returns an empty key set rather than erroring, so the wiring is uniform across every host and a single gateway forwarder rule for /.well-known/* covers JWKS discovery for the whole platform. That same prefix is one of the paths the global rate limiter bypasses (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:79).
    • Where it's used: applied as the JwksEndpoint step of the default pipeline seeded by MiddlewarePipelineBuilder (MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:150), so every host that adopts the shared pipeline serves it; the path it owns is the jwks_uri value that OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions advertises, which is in turn what AddForwardedJwtBearer (on WebApplicationBuilderExtensions) reaches through OIDC discovery. Its behavior is covered by JwksEndpointTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Startup/JwksEndpointTests.cs).

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Uploads · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Uploads/FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:24 · Level 2 · record (sealed, positional)

    • What it is: the result of ReadCsvAsync: the raw upload beside the parsed table, so one read serves both the edge's own validation and dry run and a command that stores or re-parses the file (doc comment FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:18-23).
    • Depends on: UploadedFileContent (Level 0) for File, and CsvTable for Table.

    • Walkthrough: two positional components (:24). File is the raw upload, bytes unchanged (:22); Table is the parsed table (:23).

    • Where it's used: built only by ReadCsvCoreAsync on success (FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:128).     IFeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/FeatureFlags/IFeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:14 · Level 2 · interface

    • What it is: the cached whole-table snapshot of the stored feature-flag overrides that every flag evaluation reads, plus the invalidation every write performs (ADR-031; doc comment IFeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:5-8).
    • Depends on: FeatureFlagOverrideResponse, the element type it returns.
    • Concept (one snapshot, not a lookup per flag). A flag check sits on the request path, so loading every override in one query on a slow interval, and again right after an edit, keeps that check a cache read; the remarks borrow the reasoning of the permission-grant cache (IFeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:9-13). [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether hot-path reads avoid a database round trip; [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] applies to the staleness bound that FeatureFlagOverrideSettings.OverrideCacheSeconds states.
    • Walkthrough
      • GetAsync (IFeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:19) returns the active overrides, from the cache when it holds them.
      • InvalidateAsync (:24) drops the cached snapshot so the next read reloads it from the store.
    • Why it's built this way: separating the cached read from the store (IFeatureFlagOverrideStore) keeps the evaluator off the database. The shipped implementation, the internal FeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot, holds the whole table as one entry in the host's ICacheService under a key that carries the host's application name and the data source name, and invalidates by prefix, so on a host with the two-level cache a write on one replica retires the snapshot on every replica (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:11-37). It is a singleton that opens its own DI scope per load because the store is scoped (:35-36, :104).
    • Where it's used: registered as a singleton by AddReloadableFeatureFlags (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.FeatureFlags.cs:74); read by StoredOverrideFeatureDefinitionProvider (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/StoredOverrideFeatureDefinitionProvider.cs:33) and invalidated by the shipped IFeatureFlagAdministrationService after each write (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:33). Fallback behavior is covered by StoredOverrideFallbackTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/FeatureFlags/StoredOverrideFallbackTests.cs).

    OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Startup.Endpoints · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Endpoints/OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions.cs:22 · Level 2 · class (static, extension block)

    • What it is: maps a minimal OpenID Connect discovery document at /.well-known/openid-configuration. It returns just enough for token validation (the issuer and jwks_uri fields, plus three supported-value arrays), so a downstream service that points its JWT authority here can discover the signing keys automatically. When no issuer is configured it returns 404.
    • Depends on: JwksEndpointExtensions.DefaultJwksPath to compose the jwks_uri (OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions.cs:72); IConfiguration for Jwt:Issuer; System.Text.Json.
    • Concept (OIDC discovery as the bootstrap for JWKS-based validation). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] and [Rubric §11, Security]: AddForwardedJwtBearer sets an Authority, and the JWT bearer middleware fetches {authority}/.well-known/openid-configuration to learn the issuer and the JWKS URL. This endpoint answers that fetch, which is the other half of ADR-004 alongside JwksEndpointExtensions.
    • Walkthrough
      • DefaultOidcDiscoveryPath constant (OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions.cs:27).
      • Three static arrays (token, public, RS256, :32-34) and an OidcJsonOptions with PropertyNamingPolicy = null (:43-46). Disabling the naming policy is load-bearing: the field names are already OIDC snake_case per RFC 8414, and camelCasing jwks_uri to jwksUri would leave OpenIdConnectConfigurationRetriever unable to recognise the document (:36-42). The fields sit under a scoped #pragma warning disable IDE0052 (:31, restored :47) because the analyzer does not look into C# extension blocks for field usage, and the comment records that (:29-30).
      • MapOidcDiscoveryEndpoint() (:58) maps a GET that is .AllowAnonymous() (:86) and reads Jwt:Issuer (:62); a blank issuer returns Results.NotFound() (:63-66), safe because no downstream points its authority at a non-Identity host. Otherwise it derives jwks_uri from the configured issuer rather than the inbound request (:76) and returns the issuer, that URI, and the three supported-value arrays (:78-85).
    • Why it's built this way: the comment at :68-75 documents the subtle reason jwks_uri is built from the configured issuer and not from the request. Aspire/DCP fronts the Identity service on per-launchSettings ports and rewrites Host via X-Forwarded-Host to canonical ports that internal callers cannot always reach, so reusing the issuer keeps issuer and jwks_uri origin-aligned (a common OIDC client requirement) and routes both through the same gateway that fronts /Auth, which means one forwarder rule for /.well-known/* covers everything.
    • Where it's used: applied unconditionally as the OidcDiscoveryEndpoint step of the default pipeline (MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:152-154); consumed by the bearer middleware that AddForwardedJwtBearer configures on WebApplicationBuilderExtensions, which deliberately leaves ValidIssuer unset so the issuer comes from this document (WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:90-103). Covered by OidcDiscoveryEndpointTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Startup/OidcDiscoveryEndpointTests.cs).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the pre-forwarded scheme and host captured into HttpContext.Items by the PreForwardedCapture step exist for exactly this endpoint's benefit (WebApplicationExtensions.cs:18-35), but the current handler composes jwks_uri from the configured issuer only, so those items are not read on this path today.

    IFeatureFlagAdministrationService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/FeatureFlags/IFeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:17 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the administration surface of the reloadable feature flags (ADR-031): list the flags this service declares, and set or clear their stored overrides. Registered by AddReloadableFeatureFlags and served by FeatureFlagsControllerBase (doc comment IFeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:6-10).
    • Depends on: Result; FeatureFlagStatusResponse and SetFeatureFlagOverrideRequest.
    • Concept (only a declared flag can be overridden). The declared set is what FeatureFlagRegistry.Describe reports over the assemblies the host passed to AddReloadableFeatureFlags, so an override cannot be written for a name no code reads: a typo is refused with FeatureFlag.Undeclared rather than stored and left silently inert (IFeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:11-16). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: failures come back as Result values naming the cause, not as exceptions. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: an operator changes a flag at runtime through one audited surface.
    • Walkthrough
      • ListAsync (IFeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:22) lists every declared flag with its configured value, its override and its effective value, ordered by name.
      • SetOverrideAsync(name, request) (:28) stores the override of one declared flag and invalidates the cached snapshot, returning the flag's state afterwards or a failure (an undeclared name, an invalid override).
      • ClearOverrideAsync(name) (:38) clears the override and invalidates the snapshot; it fails only for an undeclared name.
    • Why it's built this way: the declared-name check, the store write and the invalidation live in one service so a controller cannot skip a step. The shipped internal FeatureFlagAdministrationService also records that the invalidation never fails a committed write: a cache fault after the row is saved is logged and the call still succeeds, and the entry lifetime bounds how long the old snapshot can be served (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:9-24).
    • Where it's used: registered scoped by AddReloadableFeatureFlags (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.FeatureFlags.cs:75); injected into FeatureFlagsControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/FeatureFlagsControllerBase.cs:38), which the ADC Conference and Engagement AdminFeatureFlagsController subclasses receive (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/FeatureFlags/AdminFeatureFlagsController.cs:23, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/Controllers/AdminFeatureFlagsController.cs:23). Covered by FeatureFlagsControllerBaseTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/Administration/FeatureFlagsControllerBaseTests.cs).

    • What it is: the persistence of stored feature-flag overrides (ADR-031). The shipped implementation is the EF store AddReloadableFeatureFlags registers over the owning service's own database (doc comment IFeatureFlagOverrideStore.cs:6-9).
    • Depends on: Result; FeatureFlagOverrideResponse and SetFeatureFlagOverrideRequest.

The store does not check that a name is a declared flag, and its writes do not invalidate the cached snapshot: the administration service does both, around each call (IFeatureFlagOverrideStore.cs:10-14). [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]: each rule has exactly one owner, so the store stays a plain persistence boundary.

      • GetAllAsync (IFeatureFlagOverrideStore.cs:20) reads every active override, ordered by flag name; cleared ones are not included.

    • Why it's built this way: the overrides live in the owning service's own database (database per service), selected by FeatureFlagOverrideSettings.DataSourceName; keeping the interface in Application lets a host substitute a store without touching the evaluator or the snapshot.
    • Where it's used: registered scoped as the internal EFFeatureFlagOverrideStore by AddReloadableFeatureFlags (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.FeatureFlags.cs:73; implementation at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/FeatureFlags/EFFeatureFlagOverrideStore.cs:33); read by the snapshot in a fresh scope per load (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot.cs:104) and written by the shipped administration service (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:32). See IFeatureFlagOverrideSnapshot and IFeatureFlagAdministrationService.

    FormFileUploadExtensions

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Uploads · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Uploads/FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:31 · Level 4 · class (static, extension block)

    • What it is: bounded upload reads for a controller action that takes an IFormFile: the size check, the single exact read and the refusal error in one call, instead of a hand-written check plus a MemoryStream copy per action (doc comment FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:26-30).
    • Depends on: UploadedFileContent and CsvUpload (the two result shapes); Result and Error; CsvReader for the CSV parse; ASP.NET Core IFormFile.
    • Concept introduced (bound the file, not only the request). [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assess whether untrusted input is bounded before it costs memory. An action's [RequestSizeLimit] bounds the request body; this bounds the file itself, and a declared length over the limit is refused before any byte is read (remarks at FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:45-48). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: every refused file returns the caller's own Error unchanged, so each action keeps its documented error code.
    • Walkthrough
      • One extension(IFormFile? file) block (FormFileUploadExtensions.cs:33), so the methods also accept a missing file.
      • ReadBoundedAsync(maxBytes, invalidUpload) (:49) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for maxBytes below 1 or above Array.MaxLength and ArgumentNullException for a null error (:51-53), then delegates to ReadBoundedCoreAsync.
      • ReadCsvAsync(maxBytes, invalidUpload) (:72) applies the same argument guards (:74-76) and delegates to ReadCsvCoreAsync.
      • ReadBoundedCoreAsync (:82) refuses a null, empty or oversize file with invalidUpload (:88-89), checks cancellation, allocates one byte[] of the declared length (:93) and fills it with ReadExactlyAsync (:99). A stream shorter than its declared length raises EndOfStreamException, which is answered with the same invalidUpload (:101-104). Success carries the declared file name and content type (:107).
      • ReadCsvCoreAsync (:110) reuses the bounded read, passing its errors through (:117-118), then parses the buffer through a read-only MemoryStream with CsvReader.ReadTableAsync (:121-125). A parse failure returns the reader's own errors unchanged (MalformedCode with the line in Target, or EmptyCode, per the doc comment :65-69); success returns a CsvUpload (:127-129).
    • Why it's built this way: the public methods validate their arguments synchronously and hand off to private async cores, so a programming error throws at the call rather than inside a faulted task. One buffer of the declared length, read exactly once, is the cheapest correct read; a truncated stream is treated like any other bad upload rather than surfacing as an exception. Every await uses ConfigureAwait(false) (:99, :116, :124), as packaged non-UI code requires.
    • Where it's used: ADC actions call it directly: ReadBoundedAsync for session assets and user photos (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/SessionAssets/SessionAssetsController.cs:197, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/Controllers/UsersController.cs:171) and ReadCsvAsync for the ticket roster import (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.API/Controllers/TicketRosterImportController.cs:77). Covered by FormFileUploadExtensionsTests and FormFileCsvUploadTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Uploads/). A body over the endpoint limit never reaches it: OversizeFormResourceFilter answers 413 first.

    MiddlewarePipelineBuilder

    MMCA.Common.API · MMCA.Common.API.Startup.Pipeline · MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:15 · Level 10 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the mutable, ordered list of MiddlewarePipelineStep values behind UseCommonMiddlewarePipeline. CreateDefault() seeds the framework's eighteen-step edge pipeline; a host may then insert, replace, or remove steps by name; and Build() re-checks four load-bearing adjacencies before anything is applied.
    • Depends on: MiddlewarePipelineStep and MiddlewarePipelineStepNames; CorrelationIdMiddleware, TenantResolutionMiddleware and SoftDeletedUserMiddleware (the three custom middlewares it wires); WebApplicationBuilderExtensions for the two CORS policy names; JwksEndpointExtensions and OidcDiscoveryEndpointExtensions for the two always-mapped well-known endpoints; WebApplicationExtensions for UseCommonRequestLocalization and the two pre-forwarded HttpContext.Items keys; CommonForwardedHeaders for the shared forwarded-headers options; ASP.NET forwarded-headers primitives.
    • Concept introduced (a customization point that validates itself, not a free-for-all). The tension a shared pipeline has to resolve: one fixed order is safe but blocks any host with a legitimate extra step, while an open Action<WebApplication> hook gives the order back to every host and re-opens exactly the bugs the shared pipeline closed. The resolution here is a scoped escape hatch with startup-enforced invariants: the host may edit the list, but four adjacencies are re-asserted afterwards and a violation throws while the host is starting, naming the invariant it broke and printing the current order. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether a change can be made locally without breaking distant behavior; encoding the rationale as an executable check rather than a comment is what makes that true here. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] also applies: the failure modes these invariants prevent (an unreachable jwks_uri, a tenant that never resolves, a per-user rate cap that never engages) all look like configuration bugs at runtime, so converting them into a startup exception with a named cause is a large operability win. See ADR-079.
    • Walkthrough
      • One field, _steps (MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:17), and a private constructor (:19), so the only way in is CreateDefault(). StepNames (:24) projects the current names in application order, which is what the fitness function asserts on and what error messages print.
      • CreateDefault() (:31-150) seeds the eighteen steps. Reading it top to bottom is the fastest way to learn the edge: exception handler (:34-36), correlation id (:38-40), request localization (:42-47, with the ADR-027 note that this runs early so edge error localization uses the caller's culture), the pre-forwarded scheme and host capture (:49-61, which stores both values in HttpContext.Items before the forwarded-headers rewrite; nothing in the framework reads those two Items today, since the OIDC discovery endpoint derives jwks_uri from Jwt:Issuer), forwarded headers via CommonForwardedHeaders.Create() clearing KnownProxies/KnownIPNetworks for cloud reverse proxies (:63-68; UI hosts take the same options through UseCommonUiForwardedHeaders), an HTTPS redirect wrapped in UseWhen that skips negotiated-h2c requests via IsCleartextHttp2 (:70-86) so gRPC-over-cleartext calls are not 307-redirected, response compression (:88-90), routing (:92-94), CORS choosing the development or production policy by environment (:96-100), authentication (:102-104), tenant resolution (:106-112), the rate limiter (:114-120), the soft-deleted-user filter (:122-124), authorization (:126-128), output cache (:130-132), the always-mapped JWKS (:134-141) and OIDC discovery (:143-145) endpoints, and finally MapControllers() (:147-149). Each Configure delegate is static, so no closure is allocated per step.
      • IsCleartextHttp2(HttpContext) (:349-355, public static) is the HTTPS-redirect exemption predicate, defined at the bottom of the class and pulled out to its own method under SEC-Common-44: it null-checks the context (:351) and returns true only when !Request.IsHttps and HttpProtocol.IsHttp2(Request.Protocol) (:353-354), i.e. the connection negotiated HTTP/2 without TLS. It replaced a Content-Type: application/grpc string check, which any caller could forge in a header; the negotiated protocol is settled by Kestrel at connection setup and cannot be faked by a request header. The method is public specifically so a host that rebuilds the HttpsRedirection step reuses the same predicate instead of reintroducing the forgeable check.
      • Four mutators, all returning this for chaining and all validating first: InsertBefore (:160), InsertAfter (:177), Replace (:197) and Remove (:218). Replace keeps the replaced step's position and permits a different name, but rejects a name another step already carries (:202-208).
      • Build() (:251) runs the four checks and returns a defensive copy (:273). Two adjacency checks: PreForwardedCapture immediately before ForwardedHeaders (:253-256) and Authentication immediately before TenantResolution (:258-261). Two precedence checks: Authentication before RateLimiting (:263-266, ADR-019) and ForwardedHeaders before HttpsRedirection (:268-271). Every check carries its rationale string, which is what the exception message prints.
      • The private helpers hold the guard semantics. RequireIndexOf (:279) rejects a blank name and, for an unknown one, throws listing every known step (:290-293), which turns a typo into a self-answering error. RequireUniqueName (:298) enforces name uniqueness across the list. RequireImmediatelyBefore (:308) and RequirePrecedes (:323) share one subtle rule: an invariant binds only when both of its steps are still present (:314, :329), so a host that removes a whole capability (both members of a pair) stays legal, while a host that removes only one half is not constrained by a rule that no longer has anything to say.
    • Why it's built this way: the "both present or the rule is silent" clause is the design decision worth internalizing. Without it, Remove(MiddlewarePipelineStepNames.TenantResolution) on a single-tenant host would fail the authentication adjacency check for no reason, and the escape hatch would be unusable. With it, the invariants constrain reordering rather than composition, which is what they were written to protect. Constructing the defaults as data rather than as calls also means the whole order can be asserted with no WebApplication built at all, which is what puts the fitness function in the fast unit tier. The IsCleartextHttp2 extraction is the same "encode the invariant, don't comment it" instinct the class applies to step ordering: SEC-Common-44 turned a header the caller controls into a protocol fact Kestrel controls, closing a path where a forged Content-Type could have served plaintext gRPC traffic that should have been redirected.
    • Where it's used: only through WebApplicationExtensions.ApplyPipeline (WebApplicationExtensions.cs:140-151), which both UseCommonMiddlewarePipeline overloads route through, so the zero-argument path is exactly the validated default pipeline. MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:31) subclasses into each app's architecture tier (ADC, Store, Helpdesk, and Common's own testing tier) and freezes the eighteen-name order; MiddlewarePipelineBuilderTests covers the mutators and the invariants directly.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the builder validates order, not semantics. A Replace that keeps a step's name but swaps in an unrelated middleware passes every check, because nothing inspects the Configure delegate.

    JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Http · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Http/JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler.cs:17 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: an HTTP DelegatingHandler that copies the inbound Authorization header from the current HttpContext onto every outgoing request of the client it is attached to, so a service-to-service HTTP call travels on the caller's own bearer token.
    • Depends on: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.IHttpContextAccessor (constructor-injected, JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler.cs:17), System.Net.Http.Headers.AuthenticationHeaderValue. Its gRPC twin is JwtForwardingClientInterceptor, which the doc comment names explicitly (:12).
    • Concept introduced (token propagation at the transport boundary). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether authorization survives a hop: the downstream service authorizes the user, not the calling service, which means the caller's JWT has to arrive with the request. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] is the other half: because the forwarding lives in a message handler, application code that calls a typed client is identical whether the module is in-process or extracted, and no handler has to know a token exists. [Rubric §29, Resilience, Reliability & Business Continuity]: this is the classic chain-of-responsibility shape of HttpClient, one concern per handler.
    • Walkthrough
      • SendAsync (:22) guards the request (:24), then returns straight to base.SendAsync in two cases. First, when request.Headers.Authorization is already set (:27-30), because a previous handler or the caller stated its own credentials and must win. Second, when there is no inbound header to copy (:32-36): httpContextAccessor.HttpContext?.Request?.Headers.Authorization.ToString() is null-conditional the whole way, so a background processor or an outbox dispatch with no ambient request simply passes through untouched.
      • When there is a value, it normalizes the scheme (:40-43): an inbound "Bearer <token>" has the prefix sliced off case-insensitively, and anything else is treated as the parameter itself. The result is assigned as a structured AuthenticationHeaderValue(BearerScheme, token) (:45) rather than as a raw string, so the outgoing header is always well-formed Bearer <token> with the constant scheme from :19.
    • Why it's built this way: the no-op-without-HttpContext behavior (:13-14) is what makes the handler safe to attach unconditionally: background work uses its own credentials and is not accidentally given the last request's token. Slicing and re-forming the scheme instead of copying the string verbatim means a malformed or scheme-less inbound value still leaves the client with a valid header.
    • Where it's used: wired by the framework's typed-service-client helper, AddTypedServiceClient<TInterface, TImplementation> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:155), which calls AddHttpContextAccessor() and TryAddTransient<JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler>() (:147-148) and then chains .AddHttpMessageHandler<JwtForwardingDelegatingHandler>() onto the typed HttpClient (:151-153) alongside Aspire service discovery and the standard resilience handler (:156).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: no shipped app calls AddTypedServiceClient today. The helper's own doc scopes it to HTTP contracts that do not warrant a gRPC binding (webhook receivers, public REST endpoints, third-party wrappers) and points at MMCA.Common.Grpc.AddTypedGrpcClient as the preferred service-to-service path (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:142-145), which is the path the cross-service calls in ADC and Store actually take. This handler is therefore live framework code on a currently unused registration path.

    ICorrelationContext

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/ICorrelationContext.cs:8 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the Application-layer abstraction for "the correlation ID of the work currently in flight": one reader and one writer, resolved per scope.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party, BCL string only. Implemented by CorrelationContext in Infrastructure.
    • Concept introduced (request correlation as an injected ambient value). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether one logical request can be reassembled from disjoint logs; a correlation ID is the value that makes that possible. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] is the reason this interface exists at all: handlers, decorators and interceptors need the ID, but they must not reach for HttpContext, so the contract sits in Application and the holder sits in Infrastructure, keeping the dependency arrow pointing inward. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: nothing in the business path sets or threads the ID, it is populated once at the edge and read wherever it is needed.
    • Walkthrough: two members. string CorrelationId { get; } (ICorrelationContext.cs:11) is read-only to consumers. void SetCorrelationId(string correlationId) (ICorrelationContext.cs:15) is the single write path, on the same interface, so the edge component that populates the value can do it through the DI-resolved instance without a second, internal interface. The doc comment (ICorrelationContext.cs:3-6) states the intended lifecycle: set by middleware from the X-Correlation-ID header or generated, then carried through the handler pipeline in structured-logging scopes.
    • Why it's built this way: a two-member interface is small enough that a test or a background host can supply its own holder, and putting the setter here (rather than on the concrete class) keeps middleware depending on the abstraction. ITenantContext is deliberately modelled on it, and says so: one scoped instance per request, populated once at the edge (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/ITenantContext.cs:11).
    • Where it's used: registered as TryAddScoped<ICorrelationContext, CorrelationContext>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:342). Populated by CorrelationIdMiddleware, which takes it as a method-injected parameter of InvokeAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/CorrelationIdMiddleware.cs:35). Consumed by LoggingCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/LoggingCommandDecorator.cs:20) and LoggingQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult> (.../LoggingQueryDecorator.cs:16), which wrap the ID into their log scope for the duration of the pipeline.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: not every component can use it. The audit-trail interceptor is a singleton and records the ambient Activity trace id instead of this scoped value, and says so in its own comment (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/AuditTrail/AuditTrailEntry.cs:94).

    OutboundAddressPolicy

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Http · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Http/OutboundAddressPolicy.cs:11 · Level 0 · class (public, static)

    • What it is: the address and target rules an outbound call to an operator-supplied URL is held to, so a stored target cannot reach the host's own network (OutboundAddressPolicy.cs:5-9). Two public predicates: IsPublicAddress and IsAcceptableTargetUri.
    • Depends on: BCL only (System.Net.IPAddress, System.Net.Sockets.AddressFamily, System.Uri).
    • Concept introduced (server-side request forgery defense). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether the system refuses attacker-steerable requests to internal resources. SSRF is the attack where a server is talked into calling a URL the attacker chose (a webhook target, say) that resolves into the private network, loopback, or the cloud host's metadata endpoint. This class is the single rule set for that check, applied twice by its callers: once to the URI as written and once to every address the name resolves to at connect time, which is what defeats DNS rebinding.
    • Walkthrough
      • DeniedIPv4 (:18-32) is a deny-list of (network, prefix) pairs: 0/8, 10/8, 100.64/10, 127/8, 169.254/16, 172.16/12, 192.0.0.0/24, 192.168/16, 198.18/15, 224/4, 240/4, plus the single address 168.63.129.16/32 (:31), the cloud platform's host endpoint that is reachable from every VM although it is public space (:13-17).
      • IPv6 is an allow-list instead: only global unicast 2000::/3 (GlobalUnicastIPv6, :40-41), because several formats outside it embed an IPv4 address the stack may still dial (IPv4-compatible ::/96, both NAT64 prefixes) and a range added later is refused without anyone listing it (:34-39). Inside it, DeniedGlobalIPv6 (:48-54) still refuses Teredo 2001::/32, 6to4 2002::/16 and the documentation prefixes 2001:db8::/32 and 3fff::/20.
      • IsPublicAddress (:68) unwraps an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address to its IPv4 form first (:72-75), checks IPv4 against the deny-list (:77-80), returns false for any family that is neither IPv4 nor IPv6 (:82-85), and for IPv6 requires "inside 2000::/3 and in none of the denied ranges" (:87-89).
      • IsAcceptableTargetUri(target, allowInsecure) (:100) always requires the callable shape: absolute, https or http, no user info, a non-empty host (HasCallableShape, :114-118). Unless allowInsecure (Development only, per the parameter doc), it also requires https, a host that is not localhost or *.localhost (IsLocalHostName, :123-125), and, for an IP-literal host only, a public address (IsPublicIfLiteral, :128-130); a host name passes here because its addresses are checked when it is resolved (:127).
      • IsInRange (:135-151) compares the whole prefix bytes with SequenceEqual, then masks the remaining bits of the next byte (:149).
    • Why it's built this way: one public static class means the validation-time and connect-time checks cannot drift apart. ADR-142 covers the outbound-webhook design this serves.
    • Where it's used: DnsWebhookTargetValidator applies IsAcceptableTargetUri and then requires every resolved address to pass IsPublicAddress (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Webhooks/DnsWebhookTargetValidator.cs:31, :52). HttpWebhookSender re-checks the URI before sending (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Webhooks/HttpWebhookSender.cs:46), and WebhookConnectCallback refuses a non-public address at connect time (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Webhooks/WebhookConnectCallback.cs:48).

    RemainingWindowFixedWindowRateLimiter

    Linked source (compiled into MMCA.Common.API, Aspire, UI.Web and Gateway) · MMCA.Common.RateLimiting · MMCA.Common/Source/Build/RateLimiting/RemainingWindowFixedWindowRateLimiter.cs:31 · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

    • What it is: the in-memory fixed-window limiter with an honest Retry-After hint. The framework's FixedWindowRateLimiter stamps every rejection with the whole window length, so a 429 always said Retry-After: 60 however much of the minute was left; this wraps it, tracks when the current window opened, and rewrites the hint to the time remaining (RemainingWindowFixedWindowRateLimiter.cs:5-12).
    • Depends on: System.Threading.RateLimiting (ReplenishingRateLimiter base, an inner FixedWindowRateLimiter), TimeProvider. Nested RejectedLease. Its distributed counterpart is RedisFixedWindowRateLimiter, whose figure this one now matches (:10-11).
    • Concept introduced (decorating a BCL limiter to correct its metadata). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether responses tell clients the truth they need to behave well: a Retry-After that overstates the wait makes well-behaved clients back off longer than necessary. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns]: a decorator over FixedWindowRateLimiter that forwards every permit decision unchanged and rewrites only the rejection metadata.
    • Walkthrough
      • The constructor (:45) copies the options into a new inner FixedWindowRateLimiter with AutoReplenishment = false forced (:49-56), because the owning partitioned limiter drives replenishment. It sets ReplenishmentPeriod to the window (:57), takes TimeProvider.System when none is injected (:58), and stamps the window start (:59).
      • IsAutoReplenishing is false (:63); IdleDuration and GetStatistics forward to the inner limiter (:69, :72).
      • TryReplenish (:75) resets its own window start when at least one period has elapsed (:77-80), then delegates (:82). The remarks explain why this agrees with the inner limiter's own window to within one timer tick (:23-28).
      • TimeUntilNextWindow (:87-91) is period minus elapsed, clamped at zero.
      • AttemptAcquireCore and AcquireAsyncCore (:94, :98) both pass the inner lease through WithRemainingRetryAfter (:121): an acquired lease, or a rejection with no RetryAfter hint (a request larger than the whole allowance, :119-120), is returned untouched (:123-126); any other rejection is disposed and replaced by a RejectedLease carrying TimeUntilNextWindow() (:128-129).
      • Dispose(bool) and DisposeAsyncCore dispose the inner limiter before the base (:102-117).
    • Why it's built this way: one source file is linked as an internal type into each package that runs an in-memory fixed window, keeping the Gateway package free of any MMCA reference; it cannot sit in MMCA.Common.Shared because System.Threading.RateLimiting ships in the ASP.NET Core shared framework, which Shared (also loaded by Blazor WebAssembly) does not reference (:13-22). ADR-088 covers the gateway edge limiter it serves.
    • Where it's used: every in-memory fixed-window partition: RateLimitPartitions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/RateLimiting/RateLimitPartitions.cs:48), AddCommonRateLimiting in WebApplicationBuilderExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:312), the gateway edge limiter (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aspire/Gateway/GatewayRateLimitingExtensions.cs:329), the gateway route policies (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Gateway/RateLimiting/GatewayRoutePolicyExtensions.cs:145) and the Blazor host's edge limiter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hardening/UiRateLimitingExtensions.cs:167).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the class doc cites a Store local test run ("X-18", :9) as the trigger; that run is not in source.

    IBaseDTO<TIdentifierType>

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.DTOs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/DTOs/IBaseDTO.cs:9 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: a one-property marker interface. Every DTO that carries an entity identifier exposes TIdentifierType Id { get; init; } (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/DTOs/IBaseDTO.cs:13).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party, and nothing external beyond the generic constraint. It lives in MMCA.Common.Shared, the bottom layer, so a Blazor WebAssembly client and an EF-backed service can both reference it.
    • Concept introduced (the DTO and the marker/role interface). [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses DTOs decoupled from domain entities and stable wire contracts: a DTO (Data Transfer Object) is the shape that crosses the wire, deliberately separate from the domain entity. IBaseDTO lets generic machinery treat any DTO uniformly through its Id, which is what makes a single generic read service, a single generic controller base, and a single generic UI service possible instead of one hand-written trio per entity. This is also [Rubric §1, SOLID]: a textbook Interface Segregation interface, with one member (the only thing a generic consumer needs), so clients never depend on more than they use.
    • Walkthrough: generic over TIdentifierType with a where TIdentifierType : notnull constraint (IBaseDTO.cs:10); the single Id is get; init; (IBaseDTO.cs:13), settable at construction and immutable after. The init-not-set choice recurs across these contracts (see the primer on immutability with required/init). The doc comment (IBaseDTO.cs:3-6) names the two consumers it exists for: the generic query service and the controller bases.
    • Why it's built this way: making the identifier type a generic parameter, rather than hard-coding int, lets a DTO match its entity's strongly-typed id alias (see identifier aliases), so a Guid-keyed aggregate and an int-keyed one share the same generic pipeline; the notnull constraint forbids Id being a nullable type, which keeps the generic code free of null checks on the one value it always needs.
    • Where it's used: it is the constraint on every generic read/write pipeline in the framework, each declaring the same where TEntityDTO : IBaseDTO<TIdentifierType> line: IEntityQueryService<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Mapping/IEntityQueryService.cs:21), IEntityDTOMapper<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Mapping/IEntityDTOMapper.cs:16), the generic create handler CreateEntityHandlerBase<TCreateRequest, TEntity, TIdentifierType, TEntityDTO> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Crud/CreateEntityHandlerBase.cs:50), the controller hierarchy (EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/EntityControllerBase.cs:41), and the UI's EntityServiceBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Api/EntityServiceBase.cs:39). Implemented directly by BaseLookup<TIdentifierType> and by every module DTO in ADC, Store, and Helpdesk (for example MMCA.Helpdesk/Source/Modules/Tickets/MMCA.Helpdesk.Tickets.Shared/Tickets/TicketDTO.cs:10).

    IConcurrencyAware

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.DTOs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/DTOs/IConcurrencyAware.cs:15 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the contract for read DTOs that expose the current optimistic-concurrency token (byte[] RowVersion). The API renders that token as the response ETag, and the client echoes it back in the If-Match header of its next write.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. It is the wire-side half of a pair whose persistence-side half is IWriteRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType>.SetOriginalRowVersion; the header encoding of the same bytes is ConcurrencyETag, which names this interface as the byte-array side of the translation (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Http/ConcurrencyETag.cs:7).
    • Concept introduced (optimistic concurrency, header-only). [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses deliberate persistence: transactions, migrations, soft-delete, audit, and concurrency control. The token is a version stamp that changes on every save of a row: on SQL Server it is a server-generated rowversion, and on PostgreSQL and SQLite it is stamped on every save instead (IConcurrencyAware.cs:17). A read DTO carries the current RowVersion so the client can state a precondition on the next write, and the persistence layer can then refuse a conflicting concurrent edit instead of silently overwriting it. The doc comment (IConcurrencyAware.cs:3-7) spells out the full round trip: DTO to ETag to If-Match to SetOriginalRowVersion. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] applies too, because the precondition is expressed in HTTP's own vocabulary rather than in a body field.
    • Walkthrough: one property, byte[] RowVersion { get; init; } (IConcurrencyAware.cs:19), and it is not nullable. The remark (IConcurrencyAware.cs:9-13) is the reason: the token is the If-Match header's whole content, so it is never optional. A DTO read from a persisted aggregate always has one (AuditableBaseEntity.RowVersion is non-null), and a write that states no precondition is refused with 428 Precondition Required rather than falling back to last-write-wins. The same remark states the other half of the current design: update requests carry no token, because the precondition travels in the header alone. Note the [SuppressMessage("Performance", "CA1819")] on IConcurrencyAware.cs:18: exposing a byte[] property normally trips the "properties should not return arrays" analyzer rule, but it is required to round-trip the EF token, and the suppression is justified inline ([Rubric §15, Best Practices]: suppressions are tracked and explained, not blanket-disabled).
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-035 puts the precondition on the resource read rather than on each request model, so a module adds conditional writes by making its read DTO concurrency-aware plus tagging the action, and no request record has to loosen its immutability to receive a token. Keeping the contract in Shared means the same interface is visible to the Blazor client that must echo the tag and to the Infrastructure repository that consumes the bytes.
    • Where it's used: implemented by the read DTOs across the apps: ADC's SessionDTO (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Shared/Sessions/SessionDTO.cs:15) and LivePollDTO (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/LivePolls/LivePollDTO.cs:8), Store's OrderDTO (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.Shared/Orders/OrderDTO.cs:9) and InventoryItemDTO (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.Shared/Inventory/InventoryItemDTO.cs:9), and Helpdesk's TicketDTO (MMCA.Helpdesk/Source/Modules/Tickets/MMCA.Helpdesk.Tickets.Shared/Tickets/TicketDTO.cs:10). On the server, ApiControllerBase.SetConcurrencyETag writes the ETag response header (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/ApiControllerBase.cs:125-134), called from EntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (EntityControllerBase.cs:383) and CrudEntityControllerBase<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType, TCreateRequest, TUpdateRequest> (CrudEntityControllerBase.cs:113). It does not test for this interface: it reads a public byte[] RowVersion property off the row's runtime shape (or the rowVersion entry of a field-projected dictionary row), cached per type (ApiControllerBase.cs:26-30, :112-116), so a shaped response keeps its tag. On the client, EntityServiceBase<TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType>.ConcurrencyTagOf pattern-matches the same interface to build the outgoing If-Match value, treating an empty array as no token (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Api/EntityServiceBase.cs:193-197).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the "update requests carry no token" half is a convention this interface cannot enforce by itself; it is pinned by the shipped fitness rule UpdateRequests_ShouldNotImplement_IConcurrencyAware (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Domain/ConcurrencyConventionTestsBase.cs:14), which each consumer app subclasses.

    ServiceHostAuthentication

    MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/ServiceHostAuthentication.cs:6 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: the two-value switch that tells the composed service host how it validates bearer tokens: ForwardedJwtBearer = 0 (ServiceHostAuthentication.cs:12) for every service that receives tokens, and TokenIssuer = 1 (ServiceHostAuthentication.cs:18) for the one Identity service that mints them.
    • Depends on: nothing; it is read by ServiceHostBuilderExtensions and carried on MmcaServiceHostOptions.
    • Concept (issuer versus relying party). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses authentication and token handling. A service that only consumes tokens validates them against the issuer's published signing keys (JWKS discovery against Authentication:JwtBearer:Authority, ServiceHostAuthentication.cs:8-11), while the issuer validates in process with its own Jwt settings and reads no authority at all (:14-17). The dual-fetch model itself is taught in the primer under ADR-004; this enum only picks which half a host runs.
    • Walkthrough: the zero value is the forwarded mode, so a default-constructed options object is a relying party, and MmcaServiceHostOptions.Authentication defaults to it explicitly (MmcaServiceHostOptions.cs:52). AddMmcaServiceHost branches on it: TokenIssuer calls AddCommonAuthentication, anything else calls AddForwardedJwtBearer with the authority from GetRequiredJwtAuthority() and an audience from JwtAudience.RequireConfigured (ServiceHostBuilderExtensions.cs:132-143).
    • Why it's built this way: a selector, rather than a callback, keeps the fail-closed audience check inside the package for every relying-party host, and it gives the architecture rule a literal to look for. ArchitectureRules.ForwardedJwtBearerAudienceIsFailClosed exempts a host file only when it names ServiceHostAuthentication.TokenIssuer (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Api/ArchitectureRules.ForwardedJwt.cs:10, :41), surfaced through ForwardedJwtAudienceTestsBase.
    • Where it's used: ADC's Identity service is the one host that selects TokenIssuer (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Service/Program.cs:117); ADC's Conference, Engagement and Notification services keep the default.

Note the consequence for required: an expression-tree MemberInit constructs the record without the compiler's required-member check, which is legal because required is a compile-time contract, not a runtime one.     • Walkthrough: the constructor is internal (MmcaServiceHost.cs:13), so only ServiceHostBuilderExtensions can create one. ModuleHost (:23) is public: the same module host the ConfigurePipeline callback received (bound settings, the module loader, the discovery step). BootstrapLoggerFactory (:29) is internal: the factory the module loader's logger came from, kept alive for the life of the host and disposed on ApplicationStopped.

    MmcaServiceHostOptions

    MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/MmcaServiceHostOptions.cs:16 · Level 4 · sealed class

    • What it is: the values and callbacks that differ between service hosts. Its defaults are the REST plus gRPC service profile: an Http2-only cleartext endpoint, forwarded JWT validation, no Redis-backed output cache (MmcaServiceHostOptions.cs:11-15).
    • Depends on: ServiceHostAuthentication, MmcaApplicationPipelineBuilder, ModuleHostContext; externals HttpProtocols, OutputCacheOptions, WebApplicationBuilder, IServiceCollection, Assembly.
    • Concept (options object plus ordered callbacks). [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses deliberate pattern use: this is a Template Method expressed as data. The package owns the fixed registration order, and each Action property is a hook invoked at one named point in it, so a host supplies only what differs. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] applies too: every extracted service starts the same way, which is what lets a module move out of the monolith without a hand-written startup (ADR-059).
    • Walkthrough: three required members. LogFilePath (:22) is the rolling Serilog file, skipped in Production; ModuleAssemblies (:28) lists only the host's own module assemblies so peer modules are never loaded; ConfigurePipeline (:35) is the application-pipeline body (ADR-014), typically pipeline.Register(moduleHost.RegisterModules) plus gRPC clients and AddBrokerMessaging. Defaulted values: Protocols is HttpProtocols.Http2 (:42; Http1AndHttp2 for the ADR-012 mixed profile), RedeclareCleartextEndpoint is true (:49; false for a host that declares endpoints under Kestrel:Endpoints), Authentication is ForwardedJwtBearer (:52), UseRedisOutputCaching is false (:55). The optional callbacks, by the point they run: ConfigureConfigurationSources first of all, before any configuration is read (:66); AfterServiceDefaults right after AddServiceDefaults(), the place for vendor exporters and the shared DataProtection key ring (:72); ConfigureOutputCache after the always-present no-cache base policy (:60); ConfigureServices after AddAPI (:78); RegisterBrokerTransports immediately before the pipeline, because AddBrokerMessaging picks its transport while it registers (:84).
    • Why it's built this way: vendor calls (Key Vault, the Azure Monitor exporter, a cloud broker transport) arrive only as callbacks, so the package stays cloud-neutral (ADR-134); the options type is sealed with init-only members, so a host cannot change it after the call.
    • Where it's used: passed as new() { ... } to AddMmcaServiceHost by each ADC service host (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service/Program.cs:58, MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Notification.Service/Program.cs:58, MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Service/Program.cs:79).

    ServiceHostBuilderExtensions

    MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/ServiceHostBuilderExtensions.cs:30 · Level 5 · static class

    • What it is: the composed service-host registration, one extension(WebApplicationBuilder) method, AddMmcaServiceHost(MmcaServiceHostOptions) (ServiceHostBuilderExtensions.cs:65), that holds the start-up list every extracted service host would otherwise repeat, in the one order that is correct for all of them (:20-25).
    • Depends on: MmcaServiceHostOptions, ServiceHostAuthentication, ServiceHostOpenApi, MmcaServiceHost, ModuleHostExtensions, ModuleLoader, SerilogHostExtensions, JwtAudience, JwtAuthorityExtensions, MiniProfilerExtensions; it spans the API, Aspire, Grpc and Infrastructure packages (:6-16).
    • Concept: C# extension(T) blocks are taught in the primer. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses composition at the edge: this is the composition root for a service host, and the only place that knows the order. The CA1708 suppression (:26-29) is justified inline as an extension(T) false positive [Rubric §15, Best Practices].
    • Walkthrough: guards first: null builder or options, and an empty ModuleAssemblies throws ArgumentException (:67-74). Then, in order: ConfigureConfigurationSources (:79) so a vault value is seen by every eager bind below; Kestrel endpoints with the health-probe listener (:81); AddCommonSerilog then AddServiceDefaults() then AfterServiceDefaults (:84-86); AddRedisCaching, the Redis output cache when asked for, and the hybrid cache when Redis is configured (:91-97); a bootstrap logger factory and AddModuleHost (:101-104); infrastructure health checks with requireDatabase: true (:106); CORS, API versioning and rate limiting (:108-110); the output cache with a no-cache base policy then the host's policies (:112-116); response compression (:118); the OpenAPI 3.1 pin as named options on the "v1" document, then AddCommonOpenApi() (:127-130), so a bare AddOpenApi() made before or after still emits 3.1 on both framework lines (ADR-141); token validation by Authentication (:132-143); exception handlers, AddInfrastructure, AddAPI (:145-147); AddMiniProfilerIfEnabled (:151); ConfigureServices (:153); RegisterBrokerTransports (:156); AddMmcaApplicationPipeline with the host's ConfigurePipeline as its body (:158); AddApplicationProfiling only when ApplicationSettings:UseMiniProfiler is true, after the pipeline because TryDecorate wraps only what is registered (:162-165); AddGrpcServiceDefaults (:167); and last the per-module health checks, which can only see modules discovery found (:170). It returns a new MmcaServiceHost (:172).
    • Why it's built this way: the doc comment (:49-59) records two contracts. The host keeps its own builder.Services.AddOpenApi() line, because XML-comment summaries attach only at a call site compiled in the host project (enforced at startup by ServiceHostOpenApi). And after the call the application pipeline is sealed, so anything registered afterwards (gRPC endpoint services, a service-token client, MCP) must not register command or query handlers. Composition order and module contract: ADR-059.
    • Where it's used: every ADC service host (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:82, MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Service/Program.cs:79, and the Engagement and Notification hosts at Program.cs:58); its layer placement is pinned by Common's LayerDependencyTests and CloudVendorIsolationTests.

    MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/ServiceHostProfiling.cs:11 · Level 11 · static class (internal)

Placing it right after tenant resolution means HttpContext.User is populated when the profiler answers its own result routes, and the controllers, the CQRS pipeline and EF Core all run inside the profiled request (:16-22).

Who may read the results is decided by MiniProfilerOptions.ResultsAuthorize, which AddMiniProfilerIfEnabled limits to Development (:20-21) [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability].

    MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common.ServiceHost · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/ServiceHostApplicationExtensions.cs:19 · Level 12 · static class

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagLifetime.cs:9 · Level 0 · enum

Permanent is "a capability a host chooses to run with or without (push notifications, a data-subject export endpoint)" and must NOT carry a removal date (FeatureFlagLifetime.cs:11-15); Temporary "exists only until a migration, rollout or experiment finishes", must carry a removal date, and the build fails once that date has passed (:17-21). The enforcement itself lives on FeatureFlagAttribute and the governance architecture rule that reads it.
    • Walkthrough: two members, Permanent (FeatureFlagLifetime.cs:15) and Temporary (:21), each documented inline with the consequence it carries.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-031 is the feature-flag management scheme this lifetime enforces.
    • Where it's used: the Lifetime argument every [FeatureFlag] attribute application supplies, across MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Shared/EngagementFeatures.cs, MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Shared/ConferenceFeatures.cs, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Notifications/NotificationFeatures.cs, and MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Privacy/PrivacyFeatures.cs; read back by FeatureFlagRegistry.Describe into each FeatureFlagDescriptor.Lifetime, surfaced to operators as FeatureFlagStatusResponse.Lifetime, and checked by the governance architecture rule that fails a Temporary flag past its RemoveBy date (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Governance/ArchitectureRules.FeatureFlags.cs:70). That rule compares the lifetime by its name string (ArchitectureRules.FeatureFlags.cs:13-14), not through this enum, because the architecture-testing package takes no framework reference (:7-9).

    FeatureFlagOverrideMode

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideMode.cs:10 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: what a stored, operator-set override does to a declared flag: Off, On, Percentage, or Targeting (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagOverrideMode.cs:10-29).
    • Depends on: System.Text.Json.Serialization.JsonStringEnumConverter<T> (BCL), applied at :9.
    • Concept: the runtime half of ADR-031. Where FeatureFlagLifetime describes a flag's declared life cycle, this enum describes what an operator has set it to without a new revision. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a wire contract can evolve without breaking clients: the type doc says it is "Serialized by name, so a client reads a newer mode as an unknown string rather than a bare number" (:6-7), and the explicit numeric values (= 0 to = 3) pin the stored column against a reorder.
    • Walkthrough: Off = 0 is the kill switch (:13); On = 1 is on for everyone (:16); Percentage = 2 is on for a stable percentage of users through the targeting filter's default rollout, "so one user keeps the same answer from request to request" (:18-22); Targeting = 3 is on for named users and groups plus an optional percentage of everyone else, and groups are how a tenant-wide override is expressed (:24-28).
    • Why it's built this way: each mode maps one-to-one onto a Microsoft.FeatureManagement definition in FeatureFlagDefinitions.ToDefinition (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagDefinitions.cs:33-46): On becomes an always-on filter, Percentage and Targeting become a targeting filter, Off becomes a definition with no filter, and an unknown mode also evaluates to off (:44-45), which fails closed.
    • Where it's used: carried by SetFeatureFlagOverrideRequest.Mode, FeatureFlagOverrideResponse.Mode, and stored on FeatureFlagOverride.Mode, which also decides which modes carry a percentage or an audience; the admin page MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/FeatureFlagAdmin.razor.cs offers the four modes to the operator.

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagValueKind.cs:10 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: the coarse state a flag definition puts a flag in, as the administration surface reports it: Off, On, or Conditional (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagValueKind.cs:5-20).
    • Depends on: JsonStringEnumConverter<T> (BCL), applied at :9; serialized by name like FeatureFlagOverrideMode.

    • Walkthrough: Off = 0 covers "everyone, including a flag the configuration never mentions" (:12-13); On = 1 is on for everyone (:15-16); Conditional = 2 is "decided per evaluation by one or more feature filters" (:18-19).
    • Why it's built this way: FeatureFlagDefinitions.Describe is the one place that collapses a definition into this enum (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagDefinitions.cs:51-75): a missing or disabled definition is Off (:53-56), a definition with no named filter is Off (:63-66), a definition whose filters are all always-on (or any always-on under RequirementType.Any) is On (:68-72), and anything else is Conditional with its filter names (:74).
    • Where it's used: the Configured and Effective fields of FeatureFlagStatusResponse, filled by FeatureFlagAdministrationService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAdministrationService.cs:125-130), and rendered by FeatureFlagAdmin.razor.cs.

    SupportedCultures

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Globalization · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Globalization/SupportedCultures.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: the framework-wide allowlist of supported UI cultures (ADR-027). A static class holding the default culture, the full supported set, the Development-only pseudo-localization locale, a closest-match resolver, and two membership tests.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Uses only BCL types (IReadOnlyList<string>, StringComparison).
    • Concept introduced (internationalization allowlist as one source of truth). [Rubric §27, i18n] assesses whether locale support is centralized, discoverable, and drift-resistant rather than scattered string checks. Every consumer that decides "is this a language we support" reads this one list: the host request-localization setup, the culture switcher, the MAUI head's culture resolution, and the domain guard on a user's preferred culture. Adding a locale means adding a .<culture>.resx sibling set plus one entry here, with no other infrastructure change (SupportedCultures.cs:3-8).
    • Walkthrough
      • Default = "en-US" (SupportedCultures.cs:12) is the fallback used when no cookie, profile, or Accept-Language preference resolves.
      • All (SupportedCultures.cs:18) is the supported set, default first, and today it is exactly [Default, "es"]: English and Spanish. Both the request-localization options and the culture switcher iterate it.
      • PseudoLocale = "qps-Ploc" (SupportedCultures.cs:28) is the Windows-standard pseudo-localization locale, deliberately not part of All so the translation-completeness fitness gate does not demand a .qps-Ploc.resx sibling (:21-23). It is wired into request localization, the culture-switch endpoint, and the culture switcher in Development only, where it runtime-transforms every resolved resource string (accents, padding, bracket sentinel) to surface hard-coded strings, truncation, and string concatenation without translating anything (:23-26).
      • IsSupported(string?) (SupportedCultures.cs:35-37) returns true for a non-empty culture matched case-insensitively against All; IsPseudoLocale(string?) (SupportedCultures.cs:76-77) tests case-insensitively against PseudoLocale. Both take a nullable string so callers can pass an unvalidated cookie, query value, or profile field straight in.
      • ResolveClosest(string?) (SupportedCultures.cs:51) is the fallback ladder: blank returns Default (:53-56), an exact case-insensitive All match wins (:58-62), otherwise the language subtag is matched, so "es-MX" resolves to "es" (:64-66), and anything left over falls to Default (:68). The subtag split is done by the private LanguageOf (:83-87), which returns the input unchanged when there is no -, avoiding an allocation for an already-neutral culture. Because PseudoLocale is not in All, this method can never return it (stated at :42).
    • Why it's built this way: a single const plus IReadOnlyList allowlist keeps the localization middleware, the switcher UI, the fitness gate, and the domain guard from drifting apart; separating PseudoLocale from All lets a diagnostic locale ship in Development without polluting the production culture set or the resx-completeness gate. ResolveClosest exists because web heads get language-level fallback for free from request localization's Accept-Language matching, while a head with no request pipeline (the MAUI Blazor Hybrid, which resolves against the device locale) has to do it itself, and the doc comment (SupportedCultures.cs:43-48) says explicitly that the point is to keep the two paths from diverging.
    • Where it's used: WebApplicationExtensions.UseCommonRequestLocalization builds the supported list from All (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationExtensions.cs:76), appends PseudoLocale only in Development (:80), and sets Default as the default culture (:85); the culture-switch endpoint validates the incoming value with IsSupported or, when pseudo is allowed, IsPseudoLocale (:107). MmcaCultureBootstrap falls back to Default when the stored culture is not supported (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Culture/MmcaCultureBootstrap.cs:30), and PseudoStringLocalizer activates only under IsPseudoLocale (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Globalization/PseudoStringLocalizer.cs:17). The MAUI head is the ResolveClosest caller: MauiCultureStore resolves the device culture when nothing is stored (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Globalization/MauiCultureStore.cs:41-43), and MauiCultureApplier refuses an unsupported culture outright (.../MauiCultureApplier.cs:32). The domain guard is CommonInvariants.EnsurePreferredCultureIsValid, which allows null or an IsSupported culture (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Invariants/CommonInvariants.cs:144).

    FeatureFlagAttribute

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAttribute.cs:32 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the attribute a *Features constant class applies to each flag field, carrying a FeatureFlagLifetime, an optional RemoveBy date, and an optional Owner (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagAttribute.cs:32-67).

RemoveBy is a string? rather than a DateOnly? because "an attribute argument must be a compile-time constant" (FeatureFlagAttribute.cs:44), so TryParseRemoveBy (:60-66) is what turns the constant string back into a real date for the check, parsed strictly against RemoveByFormat = "yyyy-MM-dd" (:35,63). TryParseRemoveBy is the one static method: a thin wrapper over DateOnly.TryParseExact with DateTimeStyles.None (:60-66), so a malformed date fails to parse rather than being silently coerced.

The governance architecture rules FeatureFlagsDeclareLifetime and TemporaryFeatureFlagsAreNotPastRemoveBy (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Governance/ArchitectureRules.FeatureFlags.cs:28,70) do not reference this type: they match it by its full name string (:10) and read its properties reflectively (:95-98), keeping their own copy of RemoveByFormat (:12).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: because the governance rule duplicates the format and lifetime names as strings (ArchitectureRules.FeatureFlags.cs:12-14), a rename here is not a compile error there.

Percentage is 0 to 100, required for Percentage mode, the share of everyone outside the named audience for Targeting, and ignored otherwise (:11-15).     FeatureFlagRegistry

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagRegistry.cs:35 · Level 2 · class (static)

    • What it is: the reflection scanner that turns a set of *Features constant classes into a flat, ordered list of FeatureFlagDescriptor rows, given the assemblies to scan (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagRegistry.cs:35-124).
    • Depends on: FeatureFlagDescriptor, FeatureFlagAttribute; System.Reflection (BCL).
    • Concept introduced (the flag inventory built entirely by convention). [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance & Documentation] assesses whether the set of flags in play is discoverable rather than tribal knowledge. A *Features class is recognized purely by shape: IsFeatureClass requires a static, abstract, sealed type (the C# pattern for a static class) whose name ends in FeatureClassSuffix = "Features" (:38,77,81-82); FlagFields then takes only its public const string fields (:91,95-97). No registration call, no central list to keep in sync: adding a flag is adding a const string field to the module's *Features class.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Describe(IEnumerable<Assembly>) (:46) scans every loadable type across the given assemblies, filters to feature classes, flattens to their flag fields, maps each to a descriptor, and orders the result by FlagName with StringComparer.Ordinal (:50-55) so the inventory is deterministic regardless of assembly load order.
      • Describe(Assembly) (:64) is the single-assembly overload, delegating to the collection one (:68).
      • LoadableTypes (:112) guards Assembly.GetTypes() against ReflectionTypeLoadException, falling back to the subset of types that did load via ex.Types.OfType<Type>() (:118-121), so one broken type in an assembly does not blank out every flag in it.
      • The private Describe(FieldInfo) (:100) reads the optional FeatureFlagAttribute with inherit: false (:102) and the field's raw constant value via GetRawConstantValue(), defaulting to an empty string (:106).
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-031 is the convention this registry executes; scanning by name suffix rather than a marker interface keeps a *Features class a plain constant holder with no base type or registration boilerplate.
    • Where it's used: FeatureFlagCatalog calls Describe lazily over every assembly the host passed to AddReloadableFeatureFlags (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagCatalog.cs:11-22), which is what limits stored overrides to declared flags; MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared.Tests/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagRegistryTests.cs exercises Describe, IsFeatureClass, and FlagFields directly.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the governance architecture rule does not call this registry. It re-implements the same shape test and field filter over the Shared layer of the architecture map (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Governance/ArchitectureRules.FeatureFlags.cs:87-93) with its own FeatureClassSuffix constant (:11), because that package takes no framework reference (:7-9); the two copies must be kept in step by hand. FeatureClassSuffix is a public constant ("Features"), but nothing enforces that every constant class ending in that suffix is meant to hold flags: a coincidentally named class would be scanned as one.

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.FeatureFlags · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/FeatureFlags/FeatureFlagStatusResponse.cs:15 · Level 2 · record (sealed)
